title: Dynamic Influence-Weighted Distillation for Single-IMU Activity Recognition
summary: Inertial sensors at multiple body locations can improve activity recognition, but requiring every sensor at inference increases the deployment burden. We study whether four synchronized IMUs available during training can improve a student that uses only the right-arm IMU during fitting and inference. A frozen four-IMU teacher provides logit and feature targets. Fixed-weight knowledge distillation applies each target with the same strength to every fitting sample, although the student may not benefit equally from them. We introduce dynamic influence weighting (DIW), which tests a one-step candidate update on separate fold-internal training participants. DIW then assigns separate sample-wise gates to the logit and feature losses. On WEAR, we evaluate 19 labels and 68,298 complete windows from 22 participants using subject-disjoint five-fold cross-validation. Pooled out-of-fold macro-F1 is 0.561820 for Supervised and 0.571623 for Fixed-weight KD. DIW reaches 0.638451, gains of 7.66 and 6.68 percentage points, respectively. It exceeds Supervised for 18 of 19 labels and 21 of 22 held-out participants. All three routes retain the same 80,915-parameter right-arm student at inference. Under this protocol, DIW converts training-only multi-position information into a stronger single-IMU model without changing deployed sensing or the student forward graph.

AI.tldr: Dynamic Influence Weighting (DIW) improves single-IMU activity recognition by intelligently weighting knowledge distillation from a multi-sensor teacher during training, boosting performance without changing deployed hardware.
AI.motivation: While using multiple inertial sensors (IMUs) on different body parts improves activity recognition, requiring all sensors during deployment increases burden. The paper explores whether training with four synchronized IMUs can improve a student model that only uses a single right-arm IMU during both training and inference.
AI.method: A frozen four-IMU teacher provides logit and feature targets to a right-arm student. Instead of fixed-weight knowledge distillation, they introduce Dynamic Influence Weighting (DIW), which tests candidate updates on separate fold-internal training participants and assigns sample-wise gates to logit and feature losses based on their expected benefit to the student.
AI.result: DIW achieves pooled out-of-fold macro-F1 of 0.638451, representing gains of 7.66 percentage points over supervised learning (0.561820) and 6.68 percentage points over fixed-weight knowledge distillation (0.571623). It outperforms supervised learning for 18 of 19 activity labels and 21 of 22 held-out participants.
AI.conclusion: DIW successfully converts training-only multi-position sensor information into a stronger single-IMU model without changing deployed sensing hardware or the student model architecture, providing an effective way to leverage richer training data while maintaining simple deployment requirements.

title: BVR Sim: An Open and High-Throughput Environment for Heterogeneous Air-Combat Reinforcement Learning
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Code and reproducibility artifacts available at the project repository
summary: Beyond-visual-range (BVR) air combat is a challenging reinforcement-learning domain characterized by partial observability, long-horizon decision making, energy management, and limited weapons. We present BVR Sim, an open-source Gymnasium-style environment designed for heterogeneous air-combat reinforcement learning. BVR Sim supports multiple JSBSim aircraft models, including the F-15, F-16, F/A-18, and F-22, with configurable weapons, sensors, controllers, and opponents. A unified tactical action interface specifies desired heading, altitude, speed, and weapon release above aircraft-specific inner-loop controllers, enabling policies to operate across heterogeneous platforms. The environment provides interchangeable Python and accelerated C++ backends, entity-oriented observations, compositional rewards, scripted opponents, replay and visualization, and adapters for multi-agent learning frameworks. At a 0.4-s decision interval, the C++ backend achieves 104 simulated seconds per wall-clock second in 1-vs-1 and remains practical through 10-vs-10 scenarios. A policy trained only on the F-16 transfers without retraining to four unseen aircraft, reaching a 45.5% mean win rate with aircraft-specific controller adaptation. MAPPO and HAPPO experiments further verify end-to-end compatibility with standard multi-agent reinforcement-learning pipelines.

AI.tldr: BVR Sim is an open-source Gymnasium-style environment for heterogeneous air-combat RL that supports multiple aircraft models, provides interchangeable Python/C++ backends, and enables policy transfer across different platforms without retraining.
AI.motivation: Beyond-visual-range air combat is challenging for reinforcement learning due to partial observability, long-horizon decision making, energy management, and limited weapons. Current environments lack support for heterogeneous aircraft platforms and the ability to train policies that can transfer across different aircraft types.
AI.method: Developed BVR Sim, an open-source environment with: 1) Multiple JSBSim aircraft models (F-15, F-16, F/A-18, F-22), 2) Unified tactical action interface that works across platforms, 3) Interchangeable Python and accelerated C++ backends, 4) Entity-oriented observations and compositional rewards, 5) Support for scripted opponents and multi-agent frameworks, 6) Aircraft-specific inner-loop controllers with policy-level abstraction.
AI.result: 1) Achieves 104 simulated seconds per wall-clock second at 0.4-s decision interval in 1-vs-1 scenarios, remaining practical through 10-vs-10 scenarios. 2) Policy trained only on F-16 transfers without retraining to four unseen aircraft, achieving 45.5% mean win rate with only controller adaptation. 3) Verified compatibility with standard multi-agent RL pipelines (MAPPO and HAPPO).
AI.conclusion: BVR Sim provides a flexible, high-performance environment for heterogeneous air-combat RL that enables policy transfer across different aircraft platforms, significantly reducing training requirements and supporting both single-agent and multi-agent learning scenarios.

title: GreenLeaf Law Embed Tiny: A Compact Embedding Model for Legal Domain Retrieval
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, IEEE dual-column format. Submitted to arXiv for preprint distribution
summary: We present GreenLeaf Law Embed Tiny, a 0.6B parameter embedding model for legal domain retrieval. GreenLeaf-Tiny achieves 75.11% on the Massive Legal Embedding Benchmark (MLEB) and 64.38% on MTEB(Law, v1),demonstrating competitive performance among models under 1B parameters. Our approach combines a two-stage training pipeline that first distills knowledge from a larger teacher model into a compact student architecture, then applies domain-specific fine-tuning with hard negative mining; a carefully curated dataset of 3.4 million query-passage pairs, including 150,000 human-curated samples across diverse legal jurisdictions; and an efficient inference architecture supporting multiple quantization levels (BF16, INT8, binary) enabling deployment in resource-constrained environments. We provide detailed analysis of our training methodology, architectural choices, and comprehensive evaluation across legal retrieval tasks. Our results demonstrate that domain-specific training with high-quality data can improve performance for specialized domain applications

AI.tldr: GreenLeaf Law Embed Tiny is a 0.6B parameter embedding model for legal domain retrieval that achieves competitive performance through knowledge distillation, domain-specific fine-tuning, and efficient quantization for resource-constrained deployment.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to create a compact yet effective embedding model specifically for legal domain retrieval that can operate efficiently in resource-constrained environments while maintaining competitive performance compared to larger models.
AI.method: The method uses a two-stage training pipeline: 1) knowledge distillation from a larger teacher model into a compact student architecture, 2) domain-specific fine-tuning with hard negative mining. This is combined with a curated dataset of 3.4M query-passage pairs (including 150K human-curated samples) and an efficient inference architecture supporting multiple quantization levels (BF16, INT8, binary).
AI.result: The model achieves 75.11% on Massive Legal Embedding Benchmark (MLEB) and 64.38% on MTEB(Law, v1), demonstrating competitive performance among models under 1B parameters. The efficient architecture enables deployment in resource-constrained environments.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that domain-specific training with high-quality data can significantly improve performance for specialized domain applications, and demonstrates that compact models can achieve competitive legal retrieval performance when properly trained with domain-specific knowledge and efficient architectures.

title: Trust-Aware Sequential Decision Making and Rollout Planning for Resilient Multi-Robot Systems
summary: Sequential decision-making in multi-robot systems typically assumes that planning information is reliable and that agents execute the actions anticipated by the planner. Compromised agents can violate both assumptions, creating a mismatch between the planning model and physical execution. We study this problem in online multi-robot routing under localization spoofing. We introduce a distance-constrained spoofing model for monitor-aware adversaries, together with a tiered bipartite matching strategy that maximizes assignment influence while limiting spoofing magnitude. To mitigate such attacks, we develop a trust-aware monitor that combines probabilistic localization trust, calibrated using real GPS spoofing data, with behavioral evidence from task execution to classify agents and remove detected adversaries from subsequent planning. We further show that undetected adversaries can cause rollout to lose its expected cost-improvement behavior by violating planner-execution consistency. Trust-aware removal restores this consistency after detection, enabling stable routing and recovery of rollout's empirical advantage over the base policy. Experiments using real GPS spoofing datasets and San Francisco taxicab demand demonstrate effective detection and resilient routing across varying spoofing capabilities, adversarial fleet sizes, adaptive attacks, monitoring configurations, and rollout horizons.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses security vulnerabilities in multi-robot routing systems against localization spoofing attacks, developing detection methods and resilient planning strategies to maintain system performance under adversarial conditions.
AI.motivation: Sequential decision-making in multi-robot systems assumes reliable planning information and proper agent execution, but compromised agents can violate both assumptions through localization spoofing attacks, creating dangerous mismatches between planning models and physical reality.
AI.method: 1. Introduces a distance-constrained spoofing model for monitor-aware adversaries with tiered bipartite matching strategy. 2. Develops a trust-aware monitor combining probabilistic localization trust (calibrated with real GPS data) and behavioral evidence. 3. Implements trust-aware removal to restore planner-execution consistency after detection.
AI.result: The approach effectively detects adversaries and enables resilient routing across varying spoofing capabilities, adversarial fleet sizes, adaptive attacks, monitoring configurations, and rollout horizons, restoring rollout's empirical advantage over base policies.
AI.conclusion: Trust-aware monitoring and adversary removal can effectively mitigate localization spoofing attacks in multi-robot routing systems, maintaining planning consistency and recovering performance advantages of rollout methods even under sophisticated adversarial conditions.

title: Multi-Modal Anomaly Detection: A Survey
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Big Data
summary: Multi-Modal Anomaly Detection (MMAD) detects rare abnormal events from heterogeneous data sources and is increasingly used in safety- and reliability-critical applications such as industrial inspection and cybersecurity. Yet the literature is fragmented across domains and modality combinations, and existing surveys usually group methods by architecture rather than by how abnormality is defined and separated in multi-modal settings. We survey MMAD from an assumption-driven perspective. We formalize the problem, identify five intrinsic characteristics underlying its core challenges, and organize prior work into two complementary paradigms. The first, normality-assumption methods, models regularity via representation learning, cross-modal alignment, and knowledge enhancement. The second, anomaly-assumption methods, sharpens decision boundaries through coarse-grained, structural, and semantic anomaly injection. We also investigate how foundation models are reshaping MMAD through scalable pretraining, flexible cross-modal transfer, and emerging reasoning capabilities. Finally, we compile representative benchmarks and evaluation protocols across domains and highlight open problems and future directions for robust, adaptive, and interpretable MMAD systems.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey of Multi-Modal Anomaly Detection (MMAD) that organizes methods by assumptions about abnormality rather than architecture, covering normality-based and anomaly-based paradigms, foundation models, benchmarks, and future directions.
AI.motivation: The literature on Multi-Modal Anomaly Detection is fragmented across domains and modality combinations, with existing surveys focusing on architectural groupings rather than fundamental assumptions about how abnormality is defined and detected in multi-modal settings.
AI.method: The paper takes an assumption-driven perspective, formalizing the MMAD problem, identifying five intrinsic characteristics of its core challenges, and organizing prior work into two complementary paradigms: normality-assumption methods (modeling regularity) and anomaly-assumption methods (sharpening decision boundaries through anomaly injection).
AI.result: The survey provides a systematic taxonomy of MMAD methods, analyzes how foundation models are reshaping the field through scalable pretraining and cross-modal transfer, compiles representative benchmarks and evaluation protocols across domains, and highlights key research challenges.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a unified framework for understanding MMAD from an assumption-driven perspective, identifies current research gaps, and points toward future directions for developing more robust, adaptive, and interpretable MMAD systems.

title: HypoForge: A Self-Improving Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Hypothesis Generation and Testing via Scientific Skill Learning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled AI scientist systems to automate scientific discovery, yet existing approaches most rely on static prompting or fixed workflows and fail to accumulate experience for continual improvement. We propose HypoForge, an experience-guided multi-agent framework that learns reusable scientific skills for automated hypothesis generation and hypothesis testing. HypoForge is built on the observation that these two stages involve different supervision signals. For hypothesis generation, where explicit feedback is unavailable, HypoForge adopts an adversarial generator--discriminator mechanism to improve reasoning through comparative critique. For hypothesis testing, where empirical feedback is available, HypoForge learns testing skills from execution outcomes and ground-truth results. By matching skill learning strategies with stage-specific supervision, HypoForge enables continual improvement without fine-tuning foundation models. Experiments on hypothesis generation and testing benchmarks show that HypoForge consistently outperforms existing AI scientist frameworks and skill-level variants. Further analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed stage-specific skill learning paradigms.

AI.tldr: HypoForge: An experience-guided multi-agent framework that learns reusable scientific skills for automated hypothesis generation and testing, using stage-specific learning strategies without fine-tuning foundation models.
AI.motivation: Existing AI scientist systems relying on static prompting or fixed workflows fail to accumulate experience for continual improvement. Current approaches don't adapt learning strategies to the different supervision signals available in hypothesis generation vs. hypothesis testing stages.
AI.method: HypoForge uses an experience-guided multi-agent framework with stage-specific skill learning: (1) For hypothesis generation (no explicit feedback), employs adversarial generator-discriminator mechanism with comparative critique; (2) For hypothesis testing (empirical feedback available), learns testing skills from execution outcomes and ground-truth results.
AI.result: Experiments on hypothesis generation and testing benchmarks show HypoForge consistently outperforms existing AI scientist frameworks and skill-level variants. Further analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed stage-specific skill learning paradigms.
AI.conclusion: HypoForge enables continual improvement of scientific discovery by matching skill learning strategies to stage-specific supervision signals, without requiring fine-tuning of foundation models, representing an advancement in AI scientist systems.

title: ExFold: Unified Expert Folding for Training-Free MoE Prefill-Decode Acceleration
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale capacity for strong quality while keeping per-token compute bounded through sparse expert activation. Yet low-latency MoE serving is increasingly challenging, because it spans two inference phases with fundamentally different bottlenecks: prefill is dominated by token-wise expert computation, whereas decode is constrained by memory traffic from the batch-wise activated expert set. However, existing training-free acceleration methods optimize only a single resource proxy, either the experts each token executes or the experts a batch activates, and either discard the excluded experts' contribution or leave it only implicitly approximated. In this paper, we propose ExFold, a unified training-free expert-folding framework for jointly accelerating MoE prefill and decode. ExFold casts both prefill and decode as one budgeted output-approximation problem: execute only a phase-specific constrained expert set while projecting the contribution of budget-excluded experts onto retained experts using calibrated scalar projectors. Motivated by the observation that many expert outputs are directionally aligned but differ in magnitude, ExFold calibrates a pairwise scalar-projector matrix on unlabeled data and uses it at inference time to fold excluded expert contributions into retained experts. Under this view, prefill acceleration becomes token-level Top-K folding, and decode acceleration becomes batch-level expert-pool folding. The two phases differ only in how retained experts are selected, while excluded contributions are recovered by one shared folding mechanism. We implement ExFold as a plug-and-play plugin in vLLM, with a lightweight expert-folding CUDA kernel, delivering up to 1.41x TTFT and 2.45x TPOT speedups while retaining about 99% of the original average quality.

AI.tldr: ExFold is a training-free framework that accelerates both prefill and decode phases of MoE inference by approximating excluded expert contributions through calibrated scalar projection onto retained experts.
AI.motivation: Current MoE serving faces latency challenges due to different bottlenecks in prefill (token-wise expert computation) and decode (memory traffic from batch-wise expert activation). Existing methods only optimize one resource proxy and either discard excluded expert contributions or approximate them implicitly.
AI.method: ExFold frames both prefill and decode as a budgeted output-approximation problem, using calibrated scalar projectors to fold excluded expert contributions into retained experts. It calibrates pairwise scalar-projector matrices on unlabeled data and applies them at inference. Prefill uses token-level Top-K folding while decode uses batch-level expert-pool folding.
AI.result: Implemented as a plug-and-play plugin in vLLM with lightweight CUDA kernels, ExFold achieves up to 1.41x TTFT and 2.45x TPOT speedups while maintaining about 99% of original quality.
AI.conclusion: ExFold provides a unified training-free framework that jointly accelerates both prefill and decode phases of MoE inference through expert folding, effectively addressing their different bottlenecks while preserving model quality.

title: AI Agentic Selective Laser Sintering Process Optimization
summary: Agentic systems enable the intelligent automation of complex workflows, specific to additive manufacturing this is applicable for complex tasks such as process parameter optimization for mechanical properties. This work investigates the AI enabled agentic process optimization within Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) to iteratively improve the tensile and flexural properties of 3 different materials on the Inova Mk1. These materials include PA12 GF, PA11 Onyx, and PA12 Blend (volume mixture of 25% PA12 GF and 75% PA12 White) and with using knowledge from previous builds and minimal guidance from the user, the agentic system was able to optimize process parameters over a small number of iterations to achieve comparable TDS specified mechanical properties. This work showcases the ability for an agentic system to continually learn from updated data, enabling the intelligent automation of complex tasks such as process parameter optimization for selective laser sintering.

AI.tldr: AI agentic system optimizes SLS process parameters through iterative learning to achieve target mechanical properties for multiple PA materials with minimal human guidance.
AI.motivation: Intelligent automation of complex additive manufacturing workflows, specifically for process parameter optimization in Selective Laser Sintering to achieve desired mechanical properties with minimal user intervention.
AI.method: AI-enabled agentic system that iteratively improves tensile and flexural properties by learning from previous builds and using minimal user guidance to optimize process parameters for three PA materials (PA12 GF, PA11 Onyx, PA12 Blend) on Inova Mk1 system.
AI.result: Agentic system successfully optimized process parameters over few iterations to achieve mechanical properties comparable to TDS specifications, demonstrating continual learning from updated data.
AI.conclusion: Agentic systems can effectively automate complex SLS process optimization through iterative learning, enabling intelligent parameter optimization with minimal human guidance for improved mechanical properties.

title: VLM-based automatic multi-granularity graph representation of building layouts for design informatics
summary: Architectural floorplan images encode rich relational knowledge among functional spaces, which underpins design retrieval, knowledge-based reasoning, and BIM enrichment through the building lifecycle. However, it remains challenging to automatically construct task-adaptive graph representations for public buildings. To address this gap, we first define a multi-granularity Level-of-Graphs (LoGs) for public building layouts. Methodologically, we present a Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based automatic LoG construction through node identification, edge inference, text parsing, and graph coarsening. VLM-generated representations are systematically evaluated and tested in real-world tasks, using 147 academic library floorplans worldwide as a case study. Experiments showed VLM-generated graphs were broadly consistent with human-labeled graphs (matched node ratio >= 92%; 509.3 s per floor plan for three-LoG graph generation). Meso-grained graphs yield the best node-level zone prediction (Macro F1 = 0.647, at 65% of fine-grained complexity), while coarse-grained graphs are most effective for graph-level layout quality evaluation (Spearman's \r{ho} = 0.610, at 16% of fine-grained complexity). By enabling scalable, annotation-free extraction of structured layout information from floorplan images, this study advances design informatics by converting plan images into knowledge representations, thereby enhancing the utilization of design information across the building life cycle.

AI.tldr: A method for automatically constructing multi-granularity graph representations of architectural floorplans using Vision-Language Models, enabling annotation-free extraction of structured layout knowledge for building informatics applications.
AI.motivation: Floorplan images contain rich relational knowledge about functional spaces that's valuable for design retrieval, knowledge-based reasoning, and BIM enrichment, but automatic construction of task-adaptive graph representations for public buildings remains challenging.
AI.method: Proposes a multi-granularity Level-of-Graphs (LoGs) framework with Vision-Language Model-based automatic construction through node identification, edge inference, text parsing, and graph coarsening, tested on 147 academic library floorplans.
AI.result: VLM-generated graphs were highly consistent with human-labeled graphs (≥92% node match, 509.3s per floorplan for three-LoG generation). Meso-grained graphs worked best for node-level zone prediction (Macro F1=0.647 at 65% complexity), while coarse-grained graphs were most effective for graph-level layout quality evaluation (Spearman's ρ=0.610 at 16% complexity).
AI.conclusion: The approach enables scalable, annotation-free extraction of structured layout information from floorplan images, advancing design informatics by converting plan images into knowledge representations that enhance utilization of design information across the building lifecycle.

title: When Does Frequency Decomposition Benefit Physics-Informed Neural Networks? A Preliminary Ablation Study
summary: Partial differential equations (PDEs) often have high-frequency and multi-scale features that neural networks struggle to approximate. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) build the governing equations directly into training, but suffer from spectral bias: they learn low-frequency components faster than high-frequency ones. Techniques such as Fourier feature embeddings and sinusoidal activations address this, but most studies assume they help across the board without checking which spectral regimes actually benefit. We introduce a dual-branch, spectrally-gated architecture (DBSG-PINN) that splits low- and high-frequency components into separate subnetworks joined by an adaptive gate, and use it to run a partially controlled ablation of frequency decomposition and spectral routing. We test this on five one-dimensional benchmark PDEs, ranging from smooth, single-scale problems to oscillatory, multi-scale ones. Frequency decomposition helps most on the spectrally complex benchmarks, cutting relative $L_2$ error by up to $59.2\%$ on a multimodal wave problem, but gives little benefit on smoother PDEs. On one benchmark (1D Wave), it performs substantially worse than a simpler fixed-combination variant. The gate's benefit scales with how spectrally rich the target solution is: the full model's advantage over the ablations is largest on multi-scale benchmarks and smallest (or negative) on single-scale ones, consistent with the gate exploiting frequency structure rather than acting as noise,though we do not directly visualize or quantify its spatial activations in this study. All results come from a single training seed across five 1D benchmarks, so we present this as an exploratory study meant to raise questions rather than answer them, and outline the additional seeds and benchmarks needed to test whether the pattern holds.

AI.tldr: DBSG-PINN architecture splits low/high-frequency components with adaptive gate, showing frequency decomposition helps most on spectrally complex PDEs but offers little benefit on smoother problems.
AI.motivation: PINNs suffer from spectral bias, learning low-frequency components faster than high-frequency ones. While techniques like Fourier feature embeddings address this, it's unclear which spectral regimes actually benefit from such approaches.
AI.method: Introduced dual-branch, spectrally-gated architecture (DBSG-PINN) that splits low- and high-frequency components into separate subnetworks with adaptive gate. Used it for controlled ablation study of frequency decomposition and spectral routing on five 1D benchmark PDEs.
AI.result: Frequency decomposition helps most on spectrally complex benchmarks (up to 59.2% error reduction on multimodal wave problem), but gives little benefit on smoother PDEs. On 1D Wave benchmark, it performed worse than simpler fixed-combination variant. Gate's benefit scales with spectral richness of target solution.
AI.conclusion: This is an exploratory study showing DBSG-PINN's effectiveness depends on problem complexity, with frequency decomposition most beneficial for multi-scale PDEs. Results based on single training seed highlight need for more comprehensive evaluation to establish pattern robustness.

title: Praxist: From Experimental Artifacts to Solution Lineages
summary: Autonomous R\&D agents now write, run, and improve executable artifacts under automated evaluation---but largely as laboratory instruments: shown on curated benchmarks, with gains that are hard to trace to a cause and costs well above what sustained engineering practice absorbs. The limitation is structural. Most systems treat each attempt as nearly self-contained, so logs, memories, and search trees record what happened without establishing which design element produced an improvement, whether its evidence survived validation, or how it recombines with others. Long campaigns therefore keep re-learning the same lessons. We introduce Praxist, a lineage-centered generational system that converts reproducible artifacts and evaluator outcomes into a typed evidence graph of findings, lane-structured frontiers, and agendas. Separating local artifact construction from cohort-level evidence synthesis lets later attempts inherit validated mechanisms, unresolved claims, and useful constraints, and leaves results attached to an inspectable lineage. On the standardized 75-task MLE-bench suite, the finalized official-grader results give Praxist 60 medals (80.0\%), 49 of them gold, against 55 medals (73.3\%) and 34 gold for a Claude Code baseline on Claude Opus 4.8---at a recorded model spend of US\$3,054 versus US\$38,370, roughly a twelfth of the cost. Four case studies---quantitative trading, LiDAR-inertial-visual SLAM, tokamak magnetic control, and rocket landing---carry the same process into open-ended engineering problems, improving on each task-native baseline in headline accuracy, survival, or resource cost, with the discovery path on record. Stronger artifacts at an order of magnitude less spend, each backed by an auditable lineage, are, to our knowledge, first brought together here: the operating profile production research requires, not the one a benchmark demonstration establishes.

AI.tldr: Praxist is a lineage-centered generational system for autonomous R&D agents that separates artifact construction from evidence synthesis, enabling validated mechanisms to be inherited across attempts, leading to stronger results at 1/12th the cost.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous R&D systems treat each attempt as nearly self-contained, causing them to repeatedly re-learn the same lessons without tracking which design elements produced improvements, whether evidence survived validation, or how elements recombine. This makes gains hard to trace and costs too high for sustained engineering practice.
AI.method: Praxist converts reproducible artifacts and evaluator outcomes into a typed evidence graph with findings, lane-structured frontiers, and agendas. It separates local artifact construction from cohort-level evidence synthesis, allowing later attempts to inherit validated mechanisms, unresolved claims, and useful constraints with inspectable lineage.
AI.result: On the 75-task MLE-bench suite: Praxist achieved 60 medals (80.0%) with 49 gold vs. Claude Code baseline's 55 medals (73.3%) with 34 gold. Praxist cost only $3,054 vs. baseline's $38,370 (roughly 1/12th). Four case studies (quantitative trading, LiDAR-inertial-visual SLAM, tokamak magnetic control, rocket landing) improved on native baselines in accuracy, survival, or resource cost with discovery paths recorded.
AI.conclusion: Praxist demonstrates that lineage-centered generational systems can produce stronger artifacts at an order of magnitude less cost, each backed by an auditable lineage - providing the operating profile that production research requires rather than just benchmark demonstration capabilities.

title: SIMGUIDE: Procedurally Grounded Multi-Context Representations for Personalized Agent Planning
summary: Personalized AI agents overwhelmingly treat users as single entities: a flat profile concatenated into a prompt. This fails when the same person holds different priorities across life contexts -- and fails catastrophically when those priorities conflict. The core problem is not that agents lack information about users; it is that the format of user representations determines whether an agent can act on that information at all. We introduce SIMGUIDE, a method that structures user context into typed, domain-specific blocks called Sims and grounds each constraint with procedural examples drawn from past decisions. To evaluate this, we construct SIMBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 47 preference-conditioned planning tasks where the correct plan depends on which user context is active -- a property no existing benchmark tests. Declarative Sim constraints alone do not outperform retrieval-based personalization (RAG). Procedurally grounded Sims outperform RAG on GPT-4o (+7.9 Preference Adherence points, $p = 0.013$), and this advantage replicates on 100 $τ$-bench tasks across both GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet~4.5 ($p \leq 0.023$). At the parametric level, the same principle holds: training distribution dominates whether parametric adaptation succeeds at all. Task-matched LoRA fine-tuning improves generation quality by 12.8 ROUGE-L points over the unadapted base model, and routing adapters by Sim type rather than user identity adds a further 7.3 points, robust to 28% routing error. Representation format -- not representation content -- is the first-order design variable.

AI.tldr: SIMGUIDE is a method that structures user context into typed, domain-specific blocks called Sims with procedural examples, improving AI agent personalization by enabling context-aware planning when users have conflicting priorities across different life contexts.
AI.motivation: Current personalized AI agents fail when users have different priorities across life contexts because they treat users as single, flat entities. The core problem is not lack of user information, but that the format of user representations prevents agents from acting appropriately on contextual information.
AI.method: SIMGUIDE structures user context into typed, domain-specific blocks called Sims and grounds each constraint with procedural examples drawn from past decisions. The approach is evaluated using SIMBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 47 preference-conditioned planning tasks where correct plans depend on active user context.
AI.result: Procedurally grounded Sims outperform retrieval-based personalization (RAG) on GPT-4o (+7.9 Preference Adherence points, p=0.013), with advantages replicating on 100 τ-bench tasks across GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (p≤0.023). Task-matched LoRA fine-tuning improves generation quality by 12.8 ROUGE-L points, and routing adapters by Sim type adds further 7.3 points, robust to 28% routing error.
AI.conclusion: Representation format — not representation content — is the first-order design variable for personalized AI agents. Structuring user context into typed, domain-specific blocks with procedural grounding enables agents to handle conflicting priorities across different life contexts.

title: FAMPWQ: Fisher Information-based Adaptive Mixed Precision Weight Quantization for Effective LLM Inference
summary: Recent years have witnessed remarkable achievements of Large Language Models (LLMs) in multiple domains, while the excessive resource requirements of LLMs hinder the deployment on resource-constrained devices. Although model quantization stands out as an effective approach, conventional quantization approaches typically incur severe performance degradation due to uniform bit-width or simple heuristic sensitivity evaluation. In this paper, we propose a novel Fisher information-based Adaptive Mixed Precision Weight Quantization approach, i.e., FAMPWQ, which performs layer-adaptive weight quantization for effective LLM inference on commodity GPUs. First, we propose a system model with a novel Fisher information metric to measure the layer-wise sensitivity to quantization. Second, we propose a reinforcement learning-based bit-width allocator in FAMPWQ, which generates an adaptive bit-width allocation strategy based on the Fisher information sensitivity metric. Extensive experiments on 7 models and 5 benchmarks demonstrate that FAMPWQ significantly outperforms 7 baseline approaches in terms of PPL (up to 3.39 smaller), accuracy (up to 6.87% higher), and LLM-as-a-judge comparison (up to 76% win rate).

AI.tldr: FAMPWQ is a novel Fisher information-based adaptive mixed precision weight quantization method for LLMs that uses reinforcement learning to allocate optimal bit-widths per layer based on Fisher sensitivity, achieving significant improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs require excessive resources that hinder deployment on resource-constrained devices. While model quantization is effective, conventional approaches suffer from severe performance degradation due to uniform bit-width allocation or simplistic sensitivity evaluation methods.
AI.method: 1) Proposes a system model with a novel Fisher information metric to measure layer-wise sensitivity to quantization. 2) Develops a reinforcement learning-based bit-width allocator that generates adaptive bit-width allocation strategies based on the Fisher sensitivity metric.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 7 models and 5 benchmarks show FAMPWQ significantly outperforms 7 baseline approaches: achieves up to 3.39x smaller perplexity (PPL), up to 6.87% higher accuracy, and up to 76% win rate in LLM-as-a-judge comparisons.
AI.conclusion: FAMPWQ provides an effective adaptive mixed precision quantization approach for LLM inference on commodity GPUs, overcoming limitations of conventional quantization methods through Fisher information-based sensitivity analysis and reinforcement learning optimization.

title: Poisoning Agentic Alpha: Adversarial Vulnerabilities Across Roles and Architectures in Multi-Agent Trading Systems
summary:
LLM-based multi-agent trading systems, in which specialized agents collaborate through structured communication to produce trading decisions, are moving rapidly from research prototypes to live deployments that control real assets. The same inter-agent communication that makes them effective also exposes them: a corrupted signal can propagate to the final decision and translate into realized financial loss. Unlike prior attacks that presume privileged access to system internals, we restrict the adversary to what is practically reachable---the source data and prompts agents consume---yielding a low-barrier, and thus democratized threat model instantiated as role-specific adversaries.
  We present the first systematic empirical study in the financial domain to characterize how an adversarial signal enters a multi-agent trading system and how far it survives toward the decision. Along the role axis, we decompose a widely-used trading pipeline into four functional roles---Analyst, Researcher, Trader, and Risk Manager---and pair each with an attack matched to its interface. Along the structural axis, we evaluate four communication topologies under data- and agent-level attacks, using the Adversarial Signal Preservation Score (APS) as a post-hoc lens on why some designs are more robust than others. We conduct experiments across five assets, two backbones, and two target directions. A central finding is that no architecture is inherently robust. These findings provide insights for the future design of safer and more robust agentic trading systems.

AI.tldr: First systematic study of adversarial attacks on LLM-based multi-agent trading systems using role-specific attacks through accessible interfaces (data/prompts) rather than privileged access.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent trading systems are moving from research to real deployments controlling real assets. While inter-agent communication makes them effective, it also exposes them to attacks where corrupted signals can propagate to final decisions and cause financial losses. Unlike prior attacks requiring privileged access to system internals, the authors focus on practically reachable attack surfaces: source data and prompts agents consume.
AI.method: 1. Decompose trading pipeline into four functional roles (Analyst, Researcher, Trader, Risk Manager) and pair each with role-specific attacks matched to their interfaces. 2. Evaluate four communication topologies under data- and agent-level attacks. 3. Use Adversarial Signal Preservation Score (APS) as post-hoc analysis tool to understand why some designs are more robust. 4. Conduct experiments across five assets, two LLM backbones, and two target directions.
AI.result: Central finding: no architecture is inherently robust against adversarial signals. The study provides empirical characterization of how adversarial signals enter multi-agent trading systems and how far they survive toward final decisions. APS analysis reveals why some system designs are more robust than others.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide insights for designing safer and more robust agentic trading systems, highlighting that current architectures have vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit through practical, low-barrier attack vectors focused on data and prompts.

title: Reliable LLM-Powered Decision Engines for Large-Scale Supply Chain Operations: Architecture, Safety, and Performance Guarantees
summary: Current large-scale supply chains are highly uncertain, dynamic, and disruption prone that are challenging to serve up timely and resilient decisions through traditional rule-based and optimization-only systems. The increasing supply of heterogeneous data sources, such as transactional demand signals and unstructured disruption report, presents a chance of intelligent systems, which could reason, adapt and optimize at the same time. A hybrid architecture that combines large language models (LLMs) with mathematical optimization, probabilistic forecasting, and safety-constrained decision filtering is proposed in this paper as a performance of a Decision Engine, which is called LLM-Powered Decision Engine (LLM-DE). In comparison to purely data-driven or heuristic solutions, LLM-DE integrates semantic reasoning with LLM with a set of performance and safety guarantees that allow safe decision-making in large-scale supply chain processes. The suggested framework enables the end-to-end decision making such as demand forecasting, inventory optimization, and transportation routing and disruption mitigation. The findings affirm that language-based reasoning combined with optimization and formal constraints can be used to come up with not only smarter but also safer and more scalable supply chain decisions. This research provides a new architecture, a complete pipeline of algorithm, and a formulation based on mathematical constructs of the operational decision systems incorporating LLM. The proposed model offers a pragmatic and theoretical basis of the next-generation intelligent supply chain infrastructures that can be implemented to work dependably in the face of uncertainty and massive complexity.

AI.tldr: LLM-Powered Decision Engine (LLM-DE) combines large language models with mathematical optimization and safety constraints for intelligent, safe supply chain decision-making under uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Current large-scale supply chains face challenges with uncertainty, dynamics, and disruptions that traditional rule-based and optimization-only systems struggle to handle. The availability of heterogeneous data sources presents an opportunity for intelligent systems that can reason, adapt, and optimize simultaneously.
AI.method: Proposes a hybrid architecture combining large language models (LLMs) with mathematical optimization, probabilistic forecasting, and safety-constrained decision filtering. LLM-DE integrates semantic reasoning from LLMs with performance and safety guarantees, enabling end-to-end decision making for demand forecasting, inventory optimization, transportation routing, and disruption mitigation.
AI.result: The findings demonstrate that language-based reasoning combined with optimization and formal constraints enables smarter, safer, and more scalable supply chain decisions compared to purely data-driven or heuristic solutions.
AI.conclusion: The research provides both a new architecture and a complete algorithmic pipeline that offers pragmatic and theoretical foundations for next-generation intelligent supply chain infrastructures capable of reliable operation under uncertainty and massive complexity.

title: MacroAgent: Regularity-Aware Macro Legalization with LLM-Agent-Designed Contour Algorithms
summary: Macros constitute a large part of the core area in modern very large-scale integration (VLSI) designs. Moreover, macro positions have a significant impact on the final quality of result (QoR), and macro legalization is typically the final step in determining the macro positions. However, existing approaches related to macro legalization either lack robustness or incur substantial computational costs or neglect the regularity between macros. To address these limitations, we introduce MacroAgent. The novel framework is a four-stage approach: clustering, contour generation, template matching, and inter-cluster refinement. We propose leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to discover multiple, effective heuristic regularity-aware contour algorithms. This framework successfully generates robust and effective algorithmic solutions for macro legalization. Compared with state-of-the-art macro legalization works, experimental results on TILOS and Chipyard benchmarks demonstrate a 2 to 8 fold improvement in layout regularity, a 3% to 5% reduction in routed wirelength with comparable congestion after global routing, and significantly better robustness with an acceptable runtime. Furthermore, end-to-end evaluation through Cadence Innovus place-and-route confirms that the regularity improvements translate into tangible PPA gains, including 2.9% lower routed wirelength and 68.3% TNS improvement over the DREAMPlace macro legalization baseline; it also achieves 1.8% lower routed wirelength when integrated into the Innovus macro placement flow.

AI.tldr: MacroAgent is a novel four-stage framework for macro legalization in VLSI designs that uses LLMs to discover effective regularity-aware contour algorithms, significantly improving layout regularity and routing quality.
AI.motivation: Existing macro legalization approaches have three main limitations: lack of robustness, high computational costs, and neglect of regularity between macros. Since macro positions significantly impact final quality of results in modern VLSI designs and macro legalization is typically the final step in determining macro positions, there is a need for a better solution.
AI.method: A four-stage framework: 1) clustering, 2) contour generation, 3) template matching, and 4) inter-cluster refinement. The key innovation is leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to discover multiple effective heuristic regularity-aware contour algorithms.
AI.result: Experimental results show 2-8× improvement in layout regularity, 3-5% reduction in routed wirelength with comparable congestion, significantly better robustness with acceptable runtime. End-to-end evaluation demonstrates 2.9% lower routed wirelength and 68.3% TNS improvement over DREAMPlace baseline, and 1.8% lower routed wirelength when integrated into Innovus macro placement flow.
AI.conclusion: MacroAgent successfully addresses the limitations of existing macro legalization approaches by providing a robust, computationally efficient framework that considers macro regularity, resulting in tangible PPA (Power, Performance, Area) gains for VLSI designs.

title: Federation Is Nearly Free, Reasoning Is Not: Tradeoffs for AI Co-Scientists in Protein Characterization Workflows
comment: 24 Pages, 4 main figures, 5 main tables, 2 supplementary figures
summary: Natural language driven autonomous co-scientist workflows involve a fundamental trade-off between flexibility and reasoning at the expense of determinism, reproducibility, and observability. Such agents increasingly must communicate across institutional boundaries, where federation topology can shape latency and cost. We systematically evaluated these tradeoffs using a controlled ablation on a production agentic platform for science. We use a verifiable task: given a protein sequence, we ask an agent to confidently characterize its function by routing across common tools. We compare federation topology, classic RL vs LLM-driven harnesses, language model, and prompt expertise. We also stratify results by protein novelty. We find that the choice of LLM dominated prediction quality far more than topology or prompting (Opus ~92%-94% vs o4-mini ~40%-50%). The PPO policy was nearly as accurate as the best LLM (88%) at zero token cost, fastest latency, and perfect consistency, but yields no reasoning trace. Expert prompted LLMs reached the highest accuracy but were high-cost and less consistent; prompt dependence was largest when the task was hardest. Federation imposed a negligible penalty on performance. These results offer actionable guidance for deploying agents for scientific workflows: for routine, verifiable tasks, a cheap deterministic policy delivers near-frontier accuracy with complete reproducibility, while flexible LLM reasoning is best reserved for open-ended discovery.

AI.tldr: LLM-driven autonomous co-scientist workflows trade flexibility for determinism; evaluation shows LLM choice dominates quality, PPO policies offer near-top accuracy with perfect reproducibility, and federation has minimal impact on performance.
AI.motivation: There's a fundamental trade-off in natural language driven autonomous co-scientist workflows between flexibility/reasoning and determinism/reproducibility/observability. As these agents increasingly communicate across institutional boundaries, federation topology affects latency and cost, requiring systematic evaluation of these tradeoffs.
AI.method: Used a controlled ablation study on a production agentic platform for science with a verifiable task: given a protein sequence, the agent must characterize its function by routing across common tools. Evaluated federation topology, classic RL vs LLM-driven harnesses, language model selection, and prompt expertise. Stratified results by protein novelty.
AI.result: LLM choice dominated prediction quality (Opus ~92-94% vs o4-mini ~40-50%). PPO policy achieved nearly top accuracy (88%) with zero token cost, fastest latency, and perfect consistency but lacks reasoning trace. Expert-prompted LLMs reached highest accuracy but were high-cost and less consistent; prompt dependence was largest on hardest tasks. Federation imposed negligible performance penalty.
AI.conclusion: For routine, verifiable scientific tasks, cheap deterministic policies deliver near-frontier accuracy with complete reproducibility, while flexible LLM reasoning is best reserved for open-ended discovery. Provides actionable guidance for deploying agents in scientific workflows.

title: AI-Powered Mental Health Chatbots in Africa: A Systematic Review and Culturally Adaptive Framework
summary: Mental health challenges in Africa remain under-addressed due to inadequate infrastructure, stigma, and a chronic shortage of professionals. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots are emerging globally as low-cost, accessible tools that can offer psychological support. This paper presents a systematic review of 52 empirical studies published between 2017 and 2025, critically analysing their cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural relevance to African contexts. The findings demonstrate the potential of AI chatbots to improve accessibility, reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, and expand psychosocial support, yet reveal limited African-specific adaptation. Most systems remain rooted in Western models and English-language designs, leaving critical gaps in local relevance, inclusivity, and sustainability. Based on the findings, the authors develop a Culturally Adaptive Digital Mental Health (CADMH) framework that integrates African cultural values, multilingual design, mobile-first optimisation, and ethical safeguards. The study highlights opportunities and barriers for integrating AI chatbots into African healthcare, offering guidance for research, practice, and policy.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 52 studies shows AI chatbots have potential for mental health support in Africa but lack cultural adaptation, leading to a proposed framework for culturally adaptive digital mental health.
AI.motivation: Mental health challenges in Africa are under-addressed due to inadequate infrastructure, stigma, and shortage of professionals. AI chatbots offer potential as low-cost, accessible tools for psychological support, but their adaptation to African contexts needs evaluation.
AI.method: Systematic review of 52 empirical studies published between 2017-2025, critically analyzing their cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural relevance to African contexts.
AI.result: AI chatbots show potential to improve accessibility, reduce anxiety/depression symptoms, and expand psychosocial support in Africa. However, most systems lack African-specific adaptation, remaining rooted in Western models and English-language designs, creating gaps in local relevance, inclusivity, and sustainability.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose a Culturally Adaptive Digital Mental Health (CADMH) framework integrating African cultural values, multilingual design, mobile-first optimization, and ethical safeguards. The study highlights both opportunities and barriers for AI chatbot integration in African healthcare, offering guidance for research, practice, and policy.

title: CAT-GS: Balanced Multimodal Learning via Calibrated Gating and Fusion Surgery
comment: This article is accepted with minor revision in Neurocomputing Journal
summary: End-to-end training of multimodal neural networks often exhibits unstable neural dynamics characterized by three coupled failure modes that degrade learning: (i) modality imbalance, where one branch dominates gradient-based optimization; (ii) unstable gating, where noisy confidence cues induce erratic modality selection; and (iii) fusion interference, where modality-specific gradients conflict at the shared fusion layer. We propose CAT-GS (Calibrated, Adaptive, Thresholded Gating with Fusion Surgery), a neural dynamics-based optimization controller for intelligent computing applications. CAT-GS operates during backpropagation without modifying model architectures, fusion modules, or task losses. Through calibration of teacher-derived reliability via temperature scaling and EMA smoothing, CAT-GS stabilizes neural dynamics using a margin-thresholded policy to switch between warm-up dropout, weak-modality prioritization, and weak-biased blending, stabilizes gradient magnitudes under aggressive gating via capped gradient-budget renormalization, and applies fusion-only PCGrad to reduce destructive cross-modal interference at the primary shared bottleneck. We evaluate CAT-GS on audio--visual multimodal pattern recognition benchmarks (CREMA-D, AV-MNIST, and VGGSound), a tri-modal setting (UR-FUNNY), controlled synthetic data (CG-MNIST), and additional cross-domain benchmarks (AVE and CMU-MOSI). CAT-GS improves or matches fused multimodal accuracy against strong imbalance-aware baselines (including OGM-GE, G$^2$D, and UMT) across settings, and yields smoother gating behavior with fewer conflicting fusion gradients.

AI.tldr: CAT-GS is a neural dynamics-based optimization controller that stabilizes end-to-end multimodal training by addressing three failure modes: modality imbalance, unstable gating, and fusion interference, without modifying model architectures.
AI.motivation: End-to-end training of multimodal neural networks suffers from three coupled failure modes: (1) modality imbalance where one branch dominates optimization, (2) unstable gating due to noisy confidence cues causing erratic modality selection, and (3) fusion interference where modality-specific gradients conflict at shared fusion layers, all degrading learning performance.
AI.method: CAT-GS operates during backpropagation without architectural changes, using teacher-derived reliability calibration via temperature scaling and EMA smoothing, margin-thresholded policies for modality switching (warm-up dropout, weak-modality prioritization, weak-biased blending), capped gradient-budget renormalization for aggressive gating stability, and fusion-only PCGrad to reduce cross-modal interference at shared bottlenecks.
AI.result: CAT-GS improves or matches fused multimodal accuracy against strong imbalance-aware baselines (OGM-GE, G$^2$D, UMT) across multiple benchmarks including CREMA-D, AV-MNIST, VGGSound, UR-FUNNY, CG-MNIST, AVE, and CMU-MOSI, with smoother gating behavior and fewer conflicting fusion gradients.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CAT-GS framework effectively stabilizes multimodal neural dynamics by addressing coupled failure modes through calibration, adaptive policies, and gradient management, offering a flexible optimization controller that works across various multimodal settings without requiring architectural modifications.

title: Beyond Scaling: Self-Evolving LLM Agents for Hardware Kernel Optimization via an Experience-Driven Workflow and Experience Graph Memory
summary: Hardware kernel optimization requires repeated compilation, correctness testing, profiling, and revision. LLM agents can automate parts of this process, and stronger foundation models, longer context windows, and longer execution horizons have improved optimization within individual tasks. These advances alone do not enable an agent to learn from completed optimization runs. Existing kernel-optimization agents seldom preserve a decision, its observed execution feedback, and the later decisions that use that evidence. Retaining every prior trajectory is also impractical because an expanding history competes with the current task for context. We present KOPE, an experience-driven framework for hardware kernel optimization. KOPE records optimization trajectories with correctness and performance feedback in Experience Graph Memory, then uses Active Context Management and Injection to retrieve relevant experience under a fixed token budget. The graph retains decision order, observed outcomes, and alternative branches, allowing evidence collected on the target hardware to inform later optimization steps and tasks. Under the same GLM-5.2 setting, the geometric mean of KOPE's per-operator speedups is $1.54\times$ that of CANNBot, the strongest competing baseline. In a complete 53-operator ablation, Active Context Management and Injection raises pass rate from 60.0\% to 84.6\%, increases the evaluator-reported positive-field geometric mean from 0.0382 to 0.0661, and reduces optimization token consumption from 15.9B to 1.113B tokens relative to passive agent-led context construction. Enabling Experience Graph Memory raises full-suite pass rate from 55.2\% to 84.6\% and yields a $1.43\times$ geometric-mean speedup on valid timing comparisons. These results support continual optimization through external experience while the foundation model remains fixed.

AI.tldr: KOPE is an experience-driven framework for hardware kernel optimization that uses Experience Graph Memory to store and retrieve optimization trajectories, enabling agents to learn from past runs while managing context efficiently.
AI.motivation: Existing kernel-optimization agents fail to learn from completed optimization runs as they don't preserve decision history with execution feedback, and storing all prior trajectories is impractical due to context window limitations.
AI.method: KOPE records optimization trajectories with correctness/performance feedback in Experience Graph Memory, then uses Active Context Management and Injection to retrieve relevant experience under fixed token budgets. The graph preserves decision order, outcomes, and alternative branches.
AI.result: KOPE achieves 1.54× geometric mean speedup over strongest baseline (CANNBot). In 53-operator ablation, Active Context Management raises pass rate from 60.0% to 84.6%, improves positive-field geometric mean from 0.0382 to 0.0661, and reduces token consumption from 15.9B to 1.113B tokens.
AI.conclusion: KOPE enables continual optimization through external experience management while foundation models remain fixed, demonstrating significant improvements in optimization efficiency, success rates, and performance over existing approaches.

title: Measurement-Budget Allocation in Quantum Learning with Finite-Shot Generalization Guarantees
summary: On near-term quantum hardware, estimating a Born probability requires repeated circuit executions. A quantum learning experiment with a fixed measurement budget $B$ must therefore decide how many distinct training states $n$ to use and how many shots $S$ to allocate to each state. We study this tradeoff for binary quantum classifiers with fixed or independently selected measurement operators $M$, where the ideal score is $\Tr(Mρ)$. We prove a distribution-free generalization bound that separates the finite-sample and finite-shot contributions. The sample term scales as $\sqrt{d/n}$, while the shot term scales as $\sqrt{(\log n)/S}$; under the constraint $B=nS$, these two terms move in opposite directions. Minimising a conservative closed-form surrogate of the bound gives the allocation rule $\nstar = 2\sqrt{2dB/\log(2B/δ)}$ and $\Sstar = B/\nstar$. This surrogate has the same asymptotic scaling as the exact minimizer and yields a worst-case rate of $B^{-1/4}$. The guarantee is intentionally conservative, since it applies to the full class of binary quantum measurements. We complement the theory with PennyLane simulations using 2-qubit and 4-qubit variational quantum circuits on nine synthetic binary classification benchmarks. In all tested configurations, the one-sided empirical generalization gap remains below the theoretical bound. The result provides a conservative statistical guideline for allocating measurement budgets in finite-shot evaluation and pre-experimental planning for near-term quantum learning systems, complementing hardware-level scheduling and circuit-design considerations. Extending the guarantee to fully adaptive shot-noisy training remains an open problem.

AI.tldr: Study of optimal allocation between number of distinct quantum training states and measurement shots under fixed budget for binary quantum classifiers, providing theoretical bounds and practical guidelines.
AI.motivation: Near-term quantum hardware requires repeated circuit executions to estimate Born probabilities, creating a tradeoff between number of distinct training states and shots allocated per state under fixed measurement budget in quantum learning experiments.
AI.method: Proved distribution-free generalization bound separating finite-sample and finite-shot contributions, derived optimal allocation rule minimizing conservative surrogate bound, and validated with PennyLane simulations using 2-qubit and 4-qubit variational quantum circuits on nine synthetic binary classification benchmarks.
AI.result: Theoretical bound yields allocation rule n* ≈ 2√(2dB/log(2B/δ)) and S* = B/n* with worst-case rate B^{-1/4}. Empirical generalization gap remains below theoretical bound in all tested configurations, providing conservative statistical guidelines for measurement budget allocation.
AI.conclusion: The work provides conservative statistical guidelines for allocating measurement budgets in finite-shot evaluation for near-term quantum learning systems, complementing hardware-level scheduling and circuit-design considerations, though extending to fully adaptive shot-noisy training remains an open problem.

title: Demystifying Reinforcement Learning Post-Training of Language Models
comment: Link to website: https://minjang10.github.io/demystifying-rl-finetuning-web Link to code: https://github.com/sankarh-1/demystifying-rl-finetuning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has emerged as a powerful framework for enhancing the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), enabling impressive reasoning, math, and coding capabilities. Yet for many researchers and practitioners, the principles behind classical RL remain a "black box". In this work, we deconstruct the RL post-training algorithm, investigating each step to clarify what is actually happening beneath the surface. By isolating the mechanics of RL with Verifiable Rewards in a controlled and simplified environment, we examine how RL outcomes are shaped by the base model's prior distribution, the granularity of the reward signal, the diversity of the prompt distribution, and model scale. We use the entropy of the policy's output distribution as a lens to compare the distributions learned through pretraining, SFT, and RL post-training, revealing how each stage shapes model certainty. Our investigation sheds light on how these choices interact to affect post-training success. For example, we show that the effect of so-called 'spurious rewards' depends on the prompt distribution used for post-training. We also provide insight into why the success of RL post-training depends on whether the base model already places sufficient probability mass on the desired behavior, linking it to the classical concept of exploration in RL. Ultimately, we provide this primer as a resource to those in the NLP community wishing to incorporate RL as a tool in their toolbox.

AI.tldr: This paper demystifies RL post-training for LLMs by systematically examining its mechanics, showing how factors like prior distribution, reward granularity, and prompt diversity shape outcomes, and explaining RL success requires base models already have sufficient probability on desired behaviors.
AI.motivation: RL post-training has become powerful for enhancing LLM capabilities, but remains a "black box" for many researchers and practitioners. The authors aim to deconstruct and clarify the actual mechanics of RL post-training.
AI.method: Isolate mechanics of RL with Verifiable Rewards in controlled environments, examining how RL outcomes are shaped by: base model's prior distribution, reward signal granularity, prompt distribution diversity, and model scale. Use policy output distribution entropy to compare pretraining, SFT, and RL post-training.
AI.result: Reveals how choices interact to affect post-training success. Shows that 'spurious rewards' effect depends on prompt distribution. Explains RL success depends on whether base model already places sufficient probability mass on desired behavior, linking to classical RL exploration concepts.
AI.conclusion: Provides a primer as a resource for the NLP community to better understand and incorporate RL as a practical tool, demystifying the black box of RL post-training through systematic analysis of its underlying mechanics.

title: Candidate supply and answer selection shape the value of LLM judging in multi-agent systems
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) sometimes already have the potential to answer correctly, but still report a wrong answer. Explaining this outcome is difficult because generation, communication and final answer-selection rules usually change simultaneously. We conceptualize multi-agent reasoning as an evolutionary pipeline of candidate generation, peer communication and terminal selection, wherein consensus without quality control can exhibit patterns of memetic drift. We study two questions: (1) when an LLM judge provides effective selection pressure by supplying a signal of answer correctness for candidates generated in a multi-agent system, and (2) when using that signal improves the reported answer. To map judge reliability, we analysed 15,336 questions from MMLU-Pro, GPQA, MedXpertQA and MuSR, with Humanity's Last Exam analysed separately. To test these rules, we replayed 81,390 fixed candidate pools drawn from 16,278 questions across five benchmarks. We report three findings. (1) A correct answer is often already present among the generated candidates, but the system can still converge on and report a wrong answer. (2) Judge reliability is not a fixed trait of the model, but varies with the task, the generator and how rare the correct answer is. (3) Combining answer frequency with the judge's evaluation changed only the final answer-selection rule and raised accuracy from 63.82% to 70.82-70.95%, primarily by rescuing correct answers that were outnumbered by popular errors. In the systems studied here, the value of generating more candidates depends on whether those extra samples make correct answers present, frequent or recognisable. By isolating generation, recognition and selection, these findings establish a diagnostic basis for designing multi-agent architectures that protect generated correct answers from being lost.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM systems often generate correct answers but still select wrong ones due to poor consensus mechanisms. Adding judge-based selection pressure significantly improves accuracy by rescuing correct answers from being outvoted by popular errors.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems frequently have correct answers in their candidate pools but still report wrong answers due to complex interactions between generation, communication, and selection rules. Understanding when and how to apply effective selection pressure is crucial for improving system accuracy.
AI.method: Conceptualized multi-agent reasoning as an evolutionary pipeline with candidate generation, peer communication, and terminal selection. Analyzed judge reliability across 15,336 questions from multiple benchmarks. Tested selection rules by replaying 81,390 fixed candidate pools across 16,278 questions using five benchmarks. Combined answer frequency with judge evaluation to create improved selection rules.
AI.result: 1) Correct answers are often present in candidate pools but systems still converge on wrong answers. 2) Judge reliability varies with task, generator, and answer rarity. 3) Combining frequency with judge evaluation improved accuracy from 63.82% to 70.82-70.95%, primarily by rescuing correct answers that were outnumbered by popular errors.
AI.conclusion: The value of generating more candidates depends on whether extra samples make correct answers present, frequent, or recognizable. By isolating generation, recognition, and selection, the study provides diagnostic tools for designing multi-agent architectures that protect generated correct answers from being lost through improved selection mechanisms.

title: Natural Language Input, Semantic Track Representation, and LLM Inference: Making the Maritime Information Exchange Model Tractable
summary: We describe a practical architecture for making the Maritime Information Exchange Model (MIEM) and the broader Rich Semantic Track model tractable using current large language model (LLM) technology. The barrier to adoption of semantic track models in defense and law enforcement has been the requirement that operators learn formal ontology languages and manually encode observations as typed logical assertions. We propose eliminating this barrier entirely: operators contribute observations in natural language; an LLM translates these into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs), which are named case frames that capture n-ary relations in a single compact structure; a knowledge graph accumulates the SARs; and a second LLM pass performs inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking over the graph. We work through two detailed examples (a 9/11-era pre-attack indicator scenario and a maritime cargo inspection scenario) showing the full pipeline from natural language input to SAR representation to inference output. We argue that this architecture makes the Track Model and MIEM immediately deployable with current technology, establishes prior art against proprietary enclosure of the approach, and grounds the method in a theoretical framework connecting semantic track representations to neural manifold geometry.

AI.tldr: A practical LLM-based architecture that enables natural language input for maritime semantic track models, eliminating the need for operators to learn formal ontologies while maintaining semantic reasoning capabilities.
AI.motivation: The adoption of semantic track models (like MIEM) in defense/law enforcement has been hindered by requiring operators to learn formal ontology languages and manually encode observations as typed logical assertions. This creates a significant barrier to practical implementation.
AI.method: A two-stage LLM architecture: 1) Operators input observations in natural language, which an LLM translates into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs) - compact structures capturing n-ary relations as named case frames. 2) These SARs populate a knowledge graph, then a second LLM performs inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking over the graph.
AI.result: Demonstrated through two detailed scenarios: a 9/11-era pre-attack indicator scenario and a maritime cargo inspection scenario. The full pipeline from natural language input to SAR representation to inference output is shown to be functional with current technology.
AI.conclusion: This architecture makes semantic track models like MIEM immediately deployable with current LLM technology, establishes prior art against proprietary enclosure, and grounds the method in a theoretical framework connecting semantic track representations to neural manifold geometry.

title: AFDBench: A Reasoning-First AI Scientist for NationalWeather Service Forecast Discussions
summary: Large language models (LLMs) hallucinate numerical values when generating high-stakes meteorological text, posing risks for weather communication. We present AFDBench, an AI meteorologist that generates professional Area Forecast Discussions (AFDs) by reasoning through structured AI weather forecast data from Google's WeatherNext 2. We introduce AFDBench, the first benchmark for evaluating generative meteorological reasoning, comprising 7,732 expert written discussions from 13 National Weather Service (NWS) offices paired with real AI weather forecast inputs, and three complementary metrics: Met-Align (numerical accuracy), Style-Align (professional dialect adherence), and Input-Grounding (fidelity to source weather data). Zero-shot evaluations reveal that open-source LLMs achieve low Style-Align (~0.33) and moderate Input-Grounding (~0.88), failing to write in the professional NWS register or faithfully use their input data. We apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with domain-specific rewards targeting temperature accuracy, synoptic correctness, and format compliance. On 1,033 held-out samples from two unseen NWS offices, GRPO nearly doubles Style-Align from 0.318 to 0.619 and improves Input-Grounding from 0.881 to 0.940, demonstrating that reinforcement learning teaches a 7B-parameter model to write like a professional meteorologist and faithfully interpret AI weather data.

AI.tldr: AFDBench is a new benchmark and AI system that uses reinforcement learning to train LLMs to generate professional meteorological Area Forecast Discussions by improving numerical accuracy, style adherence, and data grounding.
AI.motivation: LLMs hallucinate numerical values when generating meteorological text, posing serious risks for weather communication, especially in high-stakes scenarios. Current models fail to write in professional National Weather Service style and don't faithfully use weather forecast data.
AI.method: Created AFDBench benchmark with 7,732 expert-written discussions from 13 NWS offices paired with AI weather forecast data. Uses three metrics: Met-Align (numerical accuracy), Style-Align (professional dialect adherence), and Input-Grounding (fidelity to source data). Applied Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with domain-specific rewards targeting temperature accuracy, synoptic correctness, and format compliance.
AI.result: On 1,033 held-out samples from two unseen NWS offices, GRPO nearly doubled Style-Align from 0.318 to 0.619 and improved Input-Grounding from 0.881 to 0.940. Open-source LLMs initially showed low Style-Align (~0.33) and moderate Input-Grounding (~0.88).
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning with domain-specific rewards can successfully teach a 7B-parameter model to write like a professional meteorologist and faithfully interpret AI weather data, significantly improving both style adherence and data fidelity in meteorological text generation.

title: ProgRouter: Online Progress-Guided Orchestration for Multi-Agent LLM Workflows under Quality-Cost Tradeoffs
comment: Accepted in Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026. Index Terms: Collaborative agentic workflows, LLM agent orchestration, Quality-cost trade-off, Task progress prediction, Online decision-making
summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflows have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving complex, open-ended tasks through collaborative reasoning among specialized LLM agents, but they incur substantial operating costs due to repeated LLM invocations and long-horizon context accumulation. Existing cascade routing methods make one-shot, query-level decisions and cannot adapt to the dynamic, state-dependent nature of multi-step workflows, in which the right LLM at each step depends on evolving task progress, remaining task difficulty, and cost-efficiency requirements. We present ProgRouter, an online progress-guided routing framework that adaptively selects LLM agents across workflow steps to preserve task-solving quality while adhering to time and cost budgets. ProgRouter introduces a multi-view task progress scorer that combines coarse workflow outcome regimes with fine-grained signals on subtask completion, progress trends, and workflow state quality. Then, a dual-path task progress predictor and an adaptive meta-gating mechanism estimate the progress gain for each candidate routed LLM.
