ProgRouter makes online step-wise routing decisions that balance progress gain, task time budgets, and long-term operating cost efficiency. Experiments on HumanEval Plus, MBPP, MATH-500, and ASQA, spanning agentic code generation, mathematical reasoning, and retrieval-augmented long-form question answering, demonstrate that ProgRouter reduces the operating cost relative to key baselines while maintaining strong task-solving performance.

AI.tldr: ProgRouter is an online progress-guided routing framework that dynamically selects LLM agents in multi-step workflows to reduce operating costs while maintaining task-solving quality, outperforming existing cascade routing methods.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM workflows for complex tasks incur high operating costs due to repeated LLM calls and context accumulation. Existing cascade routing methods make one-shot decisions and cannot adapt to the dynamic, state-dependent nature of multi-step workflows where optimal agent selection depends on evolving task progress, remaining difficulty, and cost constraints.
AI.method: ProgRouter introduces: (1) a multi-view task progress scorer combining coarse workflow outcome regimes with fine-grained signals on subtask completion, progress trends, and state quality; (2) a dual-path task progress predictor and adaptive meta-gating mechanism to estimate progress gain for candidate LLMs; (3) online step-wise routing decisions balancing progress gain, time budgets, and long-term cost efficiency.
AI.result: Experiments on HumanEval Plus, MBPP, MATH-500, and ASQA (covering code generation, mathematical reasoning, and retrieval-augmented QA) show ProgRouter reduces operating costs relative to key baselines while maintaining strong task-solving performance.
AI.conclusion: ProgRouter effectively addresses the cost-efficiency challenge in multi-agent LLM workflows through adaptive online routing that considers task progress, enabling substantial cost savings without compromising task-solving quality across diverse domains.

title: Same-Player Verification for Account Consistency in Counter-Strike 2
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: In competitive first-person shooter (FPS) games such as Counter-Strike 2 (CS2), account-integrity review often asks whether an account's recent behavior remains consistent with its historical operator. This consistency question arises in cases such as temporary substitution, rank boosting, and high-skill players using lower-ranked accounts, where manual review requires comparing a current match against multiple historical matches. We formulate this review task as same-player verification: we encode the behavioral trajectory of a single player in a match replay (demo) as a demo-player behavioral fingerprint, and train a model to judge whether two behavioral observations come from the same real player. Grounded in CS2 game understanding, the fingerprints cover crosshair control, movement-stop-fire coordination, economy/buy, combat/engagement, and temporal rhythm. From 1,330 CS2 demos we extract 13,300 demo-player observations, and sample 663,590 same/different pairs from an 88.4M candidate-pair space for supervised training and evaluation. The final pairwise model reaches an average ROC AUC of 0.931 and achieves 0.722 different-player recall at 95% precision. Feature analysis shows that the strongest identity signals come from low-level operations, especially crosshair control, firing rhythm, and movement-stop-fire coordination, indicating that stable low-level mechanical habits are more informative for this verification task than single-match performance outcomes. In the account-history aggregation evaluation, increasing history depth raises AUC from the K=1 single-pair baseline of 0.931 to 0.986 at K=10. These results show that CS2 demo behavior can support supervised same-player verification and account-level identity-consistency modeling through multi-demo history aggregation.

AI.tldr: A supervised learning approach for same-player verification in Counter-Strike 2 that uses behavioral fingerprints from demo replays to determine if two gameplay observations come from the same real player.
AI.motivation: Account-integrity review in competitive FPS games requires determining if an account's recent behavior is consistent with its historical operator, which arises in cases like temporary substitution, rank boosting, or skilled players using lower-ranked accounts.
AI.method: Encode behavioral trajectories from CS2 demo replays as demo-player behavioral fingerprints covering crosshair control, movement-stop-fire coordination, economy/buy patterns, combat/engagement styles, and temporal rhythm. Train a pairwise model on 663,590 same/different player pairs sampled from 13,300 demo-player observations.
AI.result: Pairwise model achieves ROC AUC of 0.931 with 0.722 different-player recall at 95% precision. Feature analysis shows strongest identity signals from low-level operations: crosshair control, firing rhythm, and movement-stop-fire coordination. Account-history aggregation improves AUC from 0.931 (K=1) to 0.986 (K=10).
AI.conclusion: CS2 demo behavior supports supervised same-player verification, with low-level mechanical habits being more informative than single-match performance outcomes. Multi-demo history aggregation enables effective account-level identity-consistency modeling for integrity review.

title: Why and When Neural Networks Improve Local Approximation in Optimization
comment: 30 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Supplementary material (6 pages) included as an ancillary file. Code and raw results: https://github.com/chengkuobian/neural-surrogates-dfo
summary: Published experience with neural surrogates in derivative-free optimisation is contradictory: the same family of models that cuts the evaluation count of one solver leaves another unchanged, or makes it worse. We show that the contradiction dissolves once three factors are stated, and that these, rather than the fit accuracy a training curve reports, are what delimit when a learned local model pays. Role: a surrogate that proposes candidates the true objective must still approve helps, while one that replaces a gradient the solver depends on hurts. Radius: a model fitted to an optimisation path is reliable only inside a bounded neighbourhood, and its error neither vanishes as that neighbourhood shrinks nor survives its growth. Room: a surrogate can only accelerate progress the base method is still able to make. We formalise radius-aware local generalisation, relate it to the classical fully linear condition, and test each factor with the surrogate class, training pipeline and base method held fixed. Over 117 benchmark instances safeguarded assistance raises the instances solved to high accuracy from 67 to 84 while gradient replacement lowers them to 65; removing the gradient term from the training loss cuts surrogate acceptance from 0.703 to 0.148; and 1000 paired comparisons over ten noise levels show no noise threshold, only a base method that stops early. The same factors bound the gain: a model-based trust-region solver, which leaves little room, drops from 88 to 86 when the identical surrogate is attached, and released interpolation software stays ahead at 103, and on a Monte-Carlo inventory model repairing the acceptance interface is worth 10.40 cost units against 0.00 for the surrogate.

AI.tldr: Neural surrogates in derivative-free optimization help only when they assist rather than replace gradient computations, operate within bounded neighborhoods, and when the base solver has room for acceleration.
AI.motivation: To resolve contradictory results about neural surrogates in derivative-free optimization by identifying the key factors that determine when learned local models are beneficial rather than relying on training accuracy metrics.
AI.method: Formalizes radius-aware local generalization, relates it to classical fully linear conditions, and systematically tests three factors (role, radius, room) while keeping surrogate class, training pipeline, and base method fixed across 117 benchmark instances.
AI.result: Safeguarded assistance increased solved instances from 67 to 84, while gradient replacement decreased them to 65; removing gradient terms from training cut surrogate acceptance from 0.703 to 0.148; no noise threshold was found, only base methods stopping early; model-based solvers with little room dropped from 88 to 86 with identical surrogates.
AI.conclusion: Three factors (role: assist vs replace, radius: bounded reliability, room: base method's acceleration potential) delimit when neural surrogates pay off in derivative-free optimization, not just surrogate fit accuracy, explaining previously contradictory results.

title: Semantic Graph Unification for Industrial Digital Threads: Bridging 11 Heterogeneous Manufacturing Systems Through Ontology-Driven Knowledge Graphs
summary: Modern manufacturing enterprises operate heterogeneous systems -- ERP, MES, PLM, SCADA, QMS, SCM -- each with its own data model and API. The resulting silos prevent holistic analysis, delay root-cause investigation, and obstruct Industry 4.0 traceability. Point-to-point integration scales as O(n^2) and accumulates brittle dependencies. This paper presents an open framework for semantic graph unification of industrial digital threads. An ontology-driven RDF knowledge graph unifies data from 11 simulated sources across nine domains through a five-stage ETL pipeline with automated entity resolution spanning 97 owl:sameAs identity links. The ontology encompasses 78 RDFS classes, 108 object properties, and 243 data properties, drawing on ISA-95, OPC UA, eClass, the Asset Administration Shell, RAMI 4.0, and additional standards. An automated discovery engine applies nine strategy categories -- cross-station correlation, alarm coverage, ECN impact, CUSUM/EWMA drift detection -- to surface insights spanning system boundaries. The primary empirical result: blocking 24 cross-system tools reduces recall from 1.00 to 0.31 (F1 from 1.00 to 0.48), showing that 69% of discoverable signals require cross-system graph joins. Leave-one-out ablation confirms six of nine strategies contribute unique signals. Verification against a 65-signal manifest (16 positive, 49 null) yields F1 = 1.00 (95% Clopper-Pearson CI [0.79, 1.00]); as the manifest was author-constructed, this constitutes verification not independent validation. The graph is exposed to LLM agents via 287 Model Context Protocol tools as a SPARQL-native semantic layer. Five industry templates (aerospace, CPG, pharma, medical devices, turbine blades) demonstrate schema stability across manufacturing verticals.

AI.tldr: A semantic graph framework unifies heterogeneous manufacturing systems using RDF knowledge graphs with automated discovery engines, reducing integration complexity from O(n²) to O(n) and enabling cross-system insights.
AI.motivation: Modern manufacturing enterprises face data silos from heterogeneous systems (ERP, MES, PLM, etc.), preventing holistic analysis, delaying root-cause investigations, and obstructing Industry 4.0 traceability, with point-to-point integration scaling poorly as O(n²).
AI.method: An ontology-driven RDF knowledge graph unifies data from 11 simulated sources using a five-stage ETL pipeline with automated entity resolution. The framework includes an automated discovery engine applying nine strategy categories for cross-system insights.
AI.result: Blocking cross-system joins reduces signal recall from 1.00 to 0.31 (F1 from 1.00 to 0.48), showing 69% of discoverable signals require cross-system graph joins. The framework achieves F1 = 1.00 on verification against a 65-signal manifest and exposes graphs to LLM agents via Model Context Protocol tools.
AI.conclusion: The semantic graph framework successfully addresses manufacturing data integration challenges by providing unified semantic access, enabling cross-system insights that would otherwise be missed in siloed systems, with demonstrated applicability across multiple industry verticals.

title: Physics-Informed Error Field Learning: A Post-Training Optimization Framework for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as an important class of numerical methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, during the late-stage optimization process, further parameter updates often yield diminishing accuracy improvements while increasing computational costs. To address this issue, this paper proposes a Physics-Informed Error Field Learning (PIEFL) framework for PINNs. Unlike conventional approaches that continuously approximate the solution field using a single network, PIEFL introduces an auxiliary error network after the primary network achieves satisfactory accuracy and shifts the learning objective from the solution field to the error field. By deriving error control equations under physical constraints, the error network learns the discrepancy between the current approximation and the exact solution, and the learned error correction is combined with the primary prediction to improve solution accuracy. The proposed framework avoids continuous optimization of the entire solution space and focuses computational resources on correcting existing prediction errors. Moreover, PIEFL requires no modification to the primary network architecture, making it compatible with existing PINN models and applicable as a general post-training optimization strategy. Numerical experiments on representative PDEs demonstrate that PIEFL achieves higher solution accuracy under the same computational budget, validating its effectiveness in improving the performance of PINNs.

AI.tldr: Proposes Physics-Informed Error Field Learning (PIEFL), a framework that adds an auxiliary error network to existing PINNs to correct prediction errors rather than continuously optimizing the entire solution space, improving accuracy with the same computational budget.
AI.motivation: PINNs suffer from diminishing accuracy improvements during late-stage optimization while computational costs increase. The problem is that conventional PINNs continuously approximate the entire solution field using a single network, leading to inefficient use of computational resources when trying to refine already satisfactory approximations.
AI.method: PIEFL introduces an auxiliary error network after the primary PINN achieves satisfactory accuracy. Instead of continuing to optimize the solution field, the framework shifts focus to learning the error field - the discrepancy between current approximation and exact solution. Derives error control equations under physical constraints to train the error network, which then provides correction terms that combine with primary predictions to improve accuracy.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on representative PDEs demonstrate that PIEFL achieves higher solution accuracy under the same computational budget compared to conventional PINN approaches. The framework effectively improves PINN performance without modifying the original network architecture.
AI.conclusion: PIEFL provides an effective post-training optimization strategy for PINNs by focusing computational resources on error correction rather than continuous whole-solution optimization. The framework is compatible with existing PINN models and offers a practical approach to overcome the diminishing returns problem in late-stage PINN optimization.

title: post-graph-rag: A PostgreSQL-Native Graph RAG Engine
summary:
Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation connects facts that no single passage states, but current implementations pay for that three times: in infrastructure, requiring a vector store, graph database and document store to be kept consistent; in graph quality, because an extraction pipeline that never refuses output fills the graph with edges that assert nothing; and over time, because a graph that only accumulates treats superseded and current facts alike.
  post-graph-rag is an open-source engine addressing all three. Text chunks with embeddings, a canonical entity graph and community summaries live in one PostgreSQL database, with pgvector for search and edge tables for traversal. Extraction-time invariants run before anything is written: vague predicates, pronominal names and bare quantities are rejected; predicates are normalised onto an optional vocabulary; entities resolve to one vertex per canonical name via model-supplied aliases; and denied relations keep the positive predicate under a negation flag. A temporal layer lets relations carry a validity period from the prose, lets a later document supersede an earlier incompatible assertion from document order alone, and answers as-of queries.
  Against LightRAG on three corpora under identical extraction and embedding models, post-graph-rag builds a denser graph everywhere, up to $2.4\times$ the relations per entity, and a more queryable one: distinct edge labels run at 0.46 to 0.58 per relation, 0.11 under a controlled vocabulary, against 0.77 to 1.33. It answers comparably with lower query latency, and supports temporal evolution the baseline lacks: 13 and 8 relationships superseded on a novel sequence and a decade of filings, against zero. These are engineering measurements, not a benchmark result.
  Code: https://github.com/crajah/post-graph-rag, https://github.com/crajah/post-graph

AI.tldr: post-graph-rag is an open-source RAG engine that integrates vector embeddings, entity graphs, and document storage in one PostgreSQL database with temporal capabilities, addressing infrastructure complexity, graph quality issues, and temporal evolution problems in current graph-based RAG systems.
AI.motivation: Current graph-based retrieval-augmented generation systems face three main problems: 1) Infrastructure complexity requiring separate vector stores, graph databases, and document stores that must be kept consistent, 2) Poor graph quality because extraction pipelines don't filter uninformative edges, and 3) Inability to handle temporal evolution, treating superseded and current facts alike.
AI.method: post-graph-rag integrates text chunks with embeddings, canonical entity graph, and community summaries in a single PostgreSQL database using pgvector for search and edge tables for traversal. It implements extraction-time invariants: rejects vague predicates and pronominal names, normalizes predicates onto optional vocabulary, resolves entities to canonical names via model-supplied aliases, and handles negation. It includes a temporal layer with validity periods and as-of query support.
AI.result: Compared to LightRAG on three corpora, post-graph-rag builds denser graphs (up to 2.4× relations per entity) with more queryable structure (0.46-0.58 distinct edge labels per relation vs 0.77-1.33). It answers comparably with lower query latency and supports temporal evolution, superseding 13 and 8 relationships on different datasets while baseline supersedes none.
AI.conclusion: post-graph-rag successfully addresses the three major limitations of current graph-based RAG systems through unified database architecture, quality-focused extraction invariants, and temporal layer support, demonstrating practical improvements in graph quality, queryability, and temporal handling while reducing infrastructure complexity.

title: Resource-Efficient Pruning for Transformer via Low-Rank Importance Estimation
summary: With the rapid development of large-scale pre-trained language models based on Transformer architectures, their high computational and memory costs have become a major obstacle to deployment, especially in resource-constrained environments. Traditional pruning methods typically depend on full gradient-based importance estimation, and they necessitate prior finetuning of the model to achieve satisfactory performance. This process often results in intolerable resource consumption. This paper proposes REP-LIE, a new approach to enable resource-efficient pruning during the process of finetuning. REP-LIE leverages the gradients of LoRA low-rank matrices to estimate the importance of weights without requiring full gradient computation. To address the inherent randomness in importance estimation, a stability score is introduced, serving as the basis for iterative pruning of unimportant model parameters. The pruned model is further finetuned through lightweight updates, eliminating the need for full-parameter optimization in the process of finetuning. Extensive experiments on both medium-scale encoder models and large-scale generative models (LLaMA-7B and Mistral-7B) demonstrate that REP-LIE still achieves competitive performance compared to existing approaches.

AI.tldr: REP-LIE enables resource-efficient pruning during finetuning by using LoRA gradient-based importance estimation with stability scores, eliminating full gradient computation and full-parameter optimization.
AI.motivation: Large-scale pre-trained language models have high computational and memory costs that hinder deployment in resource-constrained environments. Traditional pruning methods require full gradient-based importance estimation and prior finetuning, resulting in intolerable resource consumption.
AI.method: REP-LIE leverages gradients of LoRA low-rank matrices to estimate weight importance without full gradient computation, introduces stability scores to address estimation randomness, performs iterative pruning of unimportant parameters, and finetunes through lightweight updates without full-parameter optimization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on medium-scale encoder models and large-scale generative models (LLaMA-7B and Mistral-7B) show that REP-LIE achieves competitive performance compared to existing approaches while being more resource-efficient.
AI.conclusion: REP-LIE provides an effective and resource-efficient approach for pruning large language models during finetuning, addressing the computational and memory challenges of traditional pruning methods while maintaining competitive model performance.

title: FrontierChallenge: Evaluating Scientific Workflow Completion
summary: Scientific agents increasingly analyze data, execute code, and produce research artifacts, yet most benchmarks emphasize final answers, isolated programs, or a single domain. We introduce FrontierChallenge, a cross-domain benchmark comprising 300 end-to-end scientific workflows. In this paper, we release and evaluate 97 of these tasks, spanning quantum chemistry, molecular dynamics, materials characterization, analytical chemistry, life science, and electrochemistry/environment. Each task provides fixed inputs and specifies a bundle of required scientific deliverables. We evaluate twelve frontier models with three agent scaffolds. Pass Rate measures the fraction of tasks satisfying the full-completion criterion, while Avg. Score captures partial progress. Each of the best-performing configurations completed only 20 of the 97 released tasks, yielding a Pass Rate of 20.6%. Partial progress translated especially poorly into complete delivery in analytical chemistry and electrochemistry/environment: Avg. Scores reached 87.6 and 94.9, but the highest Pass Rates were only 4% and 0%. Among non-passing Claude Code trajectories, 75.5% still ended with language claiming completion. These findings show that neither high partial scores nor confident claims of completion reliably indicate that a scientific task has been fully delivered, highlighting the need to evaluate end-to-end workflow execution and the completeness of scientific deliverables together.

AI.tldr: FrontierChallenge is a cross-domain benchmark of 300 scientific workflows evaluating AI agents on end-to-end scientific tasks, revealing that high partial scores and confident completion claims don't reliably indicate successful task completion.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks focus on final answers, isolated programs, or single domains, lacking comprehensive evaluation of AI agents' ability to execute complete end-to-end scientific workflows across multiple domains.
AI.method: Introduced FrontierChallenge with 300 end-to-end scientific workflows (released 97 tasks), spanning quantum chemistry, molecular dynamics, materials characterization, analytical chemistry, life science, and electrochemistry/environment. Evaluated 12 frontier models with 3 agent scaffolds using Pass Rate (full completion) and Avg. Score (partial progress).
AI.result: Best-performing configurations completed only 20/97 tasks (20.6% Pass Rate). High Avg. Scores in analytical chemistry (87.6) and electrochemistry/environment (94.9) contrasted with low Pass Rates (4% and 0%). 75.5% of non-passing Claude Code trajectories still claimed completion.
AI.conclusion: High partial scores and confident completion claims don't reliably indicate full task completion, highlighting the need for benchmarks that evaluate both end-to-end workflow execution and completeness of scientific deliverables.

title: Clearing the Underbrush: AI-Enhanced RF Interference Suppression
comment: 7 pages, 10 figures, Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Military Communications Conference (MILCOM)
summary: AI-based structured interference rejection has grown more popular because deep learning approaches can outperform traditional methods by jointly considering the signal of interest (SOI) and the signal mixture (SOI plus interference). This work builds on a previous AI-enabled approach utilizing autoregressive transformer-based models by adding a Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ) tokenizer layer which aims to improve the interference rejection performance while keeping overall latency to a minimum. Additionally, we experiment with other inference optimization techniques with the goal of speeding up inference without much accuracy loss. We explore this space with an experiment where the SOI is a digitally modulated radio frequency (RF) signal and the structured interference is a digital television signal, an extremely common type of Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing (OFDM) transmission. Our results achieve low latency and increased interference rejection over traditional techniques and prior work with other AI-enabled methods. We demonstrate the benefits of the AI-enabled approaches via audio metrics such as Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ). Additionally, we explore a variety of applications and detail how our interference rejection algorithm may be used in operationally-relevant scenarios.

AI.tldr: An AI-based interference rejection method using transformer models with Finite Scalar Quantization tokenizer to improve performance while maintaining low latency, tested on RF signals with OFDM interference.
AI.motivation: AI-based structured interference rejection can outperform traditional methods by jointly considering signal of interest and interference. Need to improve performance while keeping latency low for practical applications.
AI.method: Builds on autoregressive transformer-based models by adding a Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ) tokenizer layer. Also experiments with inference optimization techniques. Tested on digitally modulated RF signals with OFDM interference (digital TV signals).
AI.result: Achieved low latency and increased interference rejection over traditional techniques and prior AI methods. Demonstrated benefits via audio metrics like PESQ. Explored operational applications.
AI.conclusion: The proposed AI-enabled approach with FSQ tokenizer successfully improves interference rejection performance while maintaining low latency, making it suitable for operationally-relevant scenarios with RF signals and OFDM interference.

title: Solving Robust POMDPs with Omega-regular Objectives via Partially Observable Stochastic Games
summary: Robust POMDPs (RPOMDPs) generalize classical POMDPs to the setting where exact transition probabilities are not known -- rather, they are only known to belong to some uncertainty set of values. In this work, we study the problem of solving RPOMDPs with general omega-regular objectives, which subsume a broad class of objectives such as reachability, safety, and linear temporal logic (LTL) objectives. We show that, for (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets, the problem of solving RPOMDPs under omega-regular objectives can be reduced to solving partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) under omega-regular objectives. Moreover, we show for the first time that reductions can be constructed in both directions, establishing the semantic equivalence between (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets and POSGs. This allows us to derive a range of new computational complexity results, including both upper and lower complexity bounds, on solving RPOMDPs with different omega-regular objectives. As a corollary, we also derive new computational complexity results for RMDPs.

AI.tldr: RPOMDPs with omega-regular objectives can be reduced to POSGs with the same objectives, establishing semantic equivalence and enabling new complexity results.
AI.motivation: Robust POMDPs (RPOMDPs) extend classical POMDPs to handle uncertainty in transition probabilities, where probabilities are only known to belong to an uncertainty set. This work aims to solve RPOMDPs with general omega-regular objectives (which include reachability, safety, and LTL) and establish computational complexity results.
AI.method: The authors show that for (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets, the problem can be reduced to solving partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) under omega-regular objectives. They demonstrate that reductions can be constructed in both directions, establishing semantic equivalence between these two frameworks.
AI.result: The paper establishes semantic equivalence between (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets and POSGs. This equivalence enables the derivation of new computational complexity results for solving RPOMDPs with different omega-regular objectives, including both upper and lower bounds.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a fundamental connection between RPOMDPs and POSGs, offering a reduction-based framework for solving RPOMDPs with omega-regular objectives and establishing comprehensive computational complexity results for this important class of problems.

title: MSR-IVA: Masked Structural Residual Independent Vector Analysis for State-Aware Fusion of Structural MRI and Dynamic Functional Network Connectivity
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Workshop on Machine Learning for Signal Processing (MLSP 2026), Atlanta, GA, USA
summary: Multimodal fusion of structural MRI (sMRI) and dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) can reveal how brain structure relates to changing functional states. When the same structural latent representation is coupled with multiple states, applying independent vector analysis (IVA) separately to each state can produce unrelated structural decompositions, while forcing identical decompositions may suppress state-specific relationships. In addition, not every subject expresses every dynamic state. We propose masked structural residual IVA (MSR-IVA), a state-aware framework that combines a shared structural representation with state-specific residual adaptations and masks for incomplete state expression. On an Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort, MSR-IVA improved matched source coupling by 6.5% and reduced unmatched dependence by 15.7% relative to the independent pairwise IVA baseline. Among subjects expressing both states, mean absolute cross-state structural source correlation was 0.9177 for MSR-IVA versus 0.2978 for no sharing, demonstrating controlled structural sharing that preserves source correspondence while allowing state-specific adaptation.

AI.tldr: MSR-IVA: A multimodal fusion method that combines shared structural MRI representations with state-specific adaptations and masking for incomplete dynamic state expression, improving source coupling in brain network analysis.
AI.motivation: Current methods for fusing structural MRI (sMRI) with dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) have limitations: independent analysis of each state produces unrelated structural decompositions, while forcing identical decompositions suppresses state-specific relationships. Additionally, not all subjects express every dynamic state.
AI.method: Masked Structural Residual IVA (MSR-IVA) - a state-aware framework that combines: 1) a shared structural representation across states, 2) state-specific residual adaptations to capture state-dependent relationships, and 3) masking to handle incomplete state expression across subjects.
AI.result: On Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data: improved matched source coupling by 6.5%, reduced unmatched dependence by 15.7% compared to independent pairwise IVA baseline. For subjects expressing both states, mean absolute cross-state structural source correlation was 0.9177 for MSR-IVA vs 0.2978 for no sharing.
AI.conclusion: MSR-IVA successfully achieves controlled structural sharing that preserves source correspondence while allowing state-specific adaptation, addressing limitations of existing multimodal fusion approaches for sMRI and dFNC analysis.

title: CVE-SAI: Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing for Risk-Controlled E-commerce Search
summary: Multimodal product models can complete missing e-commerce attributes, yet current methods still optimize attribute-answer accuracy without verifying visual support, conflate transient prediction with persistent index admission, and lack explicit risk control over factually incorrect or visually unsupported values. We address these gaps with Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing (CVE-SAI), which first infers and freezes an ontology-constrained candidate from the primary image and attribute question without catalog text, and then decides whether that candidate should enter the index. Focus-Zone Distortion (FZD) constructs an attribute-specific visual-dependence proxy through a controlled counterfactual intervention, and Evidence-Guided Attention Redistribution (EGAR) uses the proxy to refine ontology-constrained scoring. The canonical candidate is frozen before evidence necessity, evidence retention, nuisance-transformation stability, and candidate-specific catalog-text conflict audits; catalog text can only tighten admission and cannot revise the candidate. Independent family-level calibration selects one policy with a simultaneous one-sided finite-sample bound under a 5% unsafe-admission budget. Experiments on five visual attributes derived from Amazon Berkeley Objects show that CVE-SAI improves attribute inference and evidence localization, achieves the highest certified admission coverage under the shared risk protocol, and yields the strongest controlled retrieval performance with the lowest unsafe auto-induced exposure among automatic-admission systems. Separating inference from admission therefore enables visually supported attribute completion to improve retrieval while limiting persistent index contamination.

AI.tldr: CVE-SAI introduces a selective attribute indexing system for e-commerce that separates attribute inference from admission decisions, using visual evidence guidance and risk controls to prevent unsupported attributes from contaminating product indexes.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal product models optimize for attribute-answer accuracy without verifying visual support, conflate prediction with persistent index admission, and lack explicit risk control over factually incorrect or visually unsupported attribute values.
AI.method: CVE-SAI (Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing) uses a two-stage approach: 1) infers and freezes an ontology-constrained candidate from primary image and attribute question without catalog text, 2) decides whether candidate enters index using Focus-Zone Distortion (FZD) for visual-dependence proxy and Evidence-Guided Attention Redistribution (EGAR) for refined scoring. Includes multiple audits and independent family-level calibration with finite-sample bounds.
AI.result: Experiments on five visual attributes from Amazon Berkeley Objects show CVE-SAI improves attribute inference and evidence localization, achieves highest certified admission coverage under shared risk protocol, yields strongest controlled retrieval performance with lowest unsafe auto-induced exposure among automatic-admission systems.
AI.conclusion: Separating inference from admission enables visually supported attribute completion to improve retrieval while limiting persistent index contamination, establishing a framework for safer attribute indexing in e-commerce applications.

title: D$^3$-MOPD: Adaptive Dynamic Domain ScheDuling for Efficient Multi-Teacher Distillation
summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) distills several domain-expert teachers into a single student by minimizing per-domain reverse-KL divergence on the student's own rollouts. Existing approaches typically fix the per-domain data mixture before training, overlooking the fact that different domains converge at substantially different rates: some plateau early while others continue to improve throughout the training budget. A fixed mixture therefore wastes compute on fast-converging domains and undertrains slower-converging ones. To address this, we propose D$^3$-MOPD (Dynamic Domain ScheDuling for MOPD), a zero-overhead scheduler that repurposes the per-domain reverse-KL signal already produced during training to adapt the domain mixture online. Running asynchronously outside the training process, an off-process watcher periodically tracks each domain's KL trajectory, estimates remaining headroom and current improvement rate, and accordingly adjusts the domain sampling ratios without altering the core training loop. Our D$^3$-MOPD scales naturally to arbitrary numbers of domains, and the expected benefit grows as more domains introduce more diverse convergence patterns for the scheduler to exploit. On a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B student distilled from four domain-expert teachers, D$^3$-MOPD closes 97% of the average student-to-teacher performance gap, compared with 63% for vanilla MOPD, reaches the same peak performance with an approximately 3$\times$ reduction in rollout steps, and surpasses the specialist teachers on three of seven benchmarks.

AI.tldr: D³-MOPD dynamically adjusts domain sampling ratios during multi-teacher distillation based on each domain's convergence progress, achieving better performance with 3x fewer rollout steps.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-teacher distillation uses fixed domain data mixtures, wasting compute on fast-converging domains while undertraining slower ones due to their different convergence rates.
AI.method: Proposes D³-MOPD: a zero-overhead scheduler that tracks each domain's KL trajectory during training, estimates remaining headroom and improvement rate, and dynamically adjusts domain sampling ratios without modifying the core training loop.
AI.result: On a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B student distilled from four teachers, D³-MOPD closes 97% of the student-to-teacher gap (vs 63% for vanilla MOPD), achieves same peak performance with ~3x fewer rollout steps, and surpasses specialist teachers on 3 of 7 benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic domain scheduling during multi-teacher distillation is crucial for efficient training and achieves superior performance by intelligently allocating compute to domains based on their convergence progress.

title: Retrieve, Match, Escalate: Accurate and Scalable Product Linking with VLM-Distilled Cross-Encoders and Agentic VLMs
summary: Product linking, the entity-resolution task of mapping merchant product records to canonical catalog products, consolidates fragmented listings so downstream search, recommendation, and advertising see one clean entry per product. At marketplace scale, billions of noisy, multi-category records must be resolved against tens of millions of canonical products, where scoring every candidate with a single model is either too weak for the hard cases or too costly for the easy ones. We present a production retrieve-then-match cascade that spends computation in proportion to difficulty: retrieval surfaces plausible matches, a lightweight text cross-encoder auto-resolves the high-confidence majority, and an agentic multimodal vision-language model settles the ambiguous remainder by inspecting product images and issuing web searches for evidence that is in neither record. The cross-encoder is distilled from millions of dual-VLM-consensus labels, retiring human annotation from the training set, and is calibrated to auto-accept links at a 98% precision bar validated against a smaller operator-certified audit. The agent is a self-hosted open-weight model that reaches a closed frontier VLM's precision at a four-point recall cost (88% versus 92%) for roughly one-seventh the per-pair cost, with no fine-tuning. Per-pair cost spans nearly five orders of magnitude from the cheap cross-encoder to the frontier VLM, so escalating only the hard tail to the agent raises end-to-end link coverage from the cheap stage's 68% to 77%.

AI.tldr: A cascade system for product linking that uses retrieval, lightweight cross-encoder, and multimodal agent to efficiently resolve billions of product records with compute proportional to difficulty.
AI.motivation: At marketplace scale, billions of noisy product records need to be mapped to millions of canonical products. A single model approach is either too weak for hard cases or too costly for easy ones, requiring a more efficient solution.
AI.method: Three-stage retrieve-then-match cascade: 1) retrieval surfaces plausible matches, 2) lightweight text cross-encoder auto-resolves high-confidence majority, 3) agentic multimodal vision-language model settles ambiguous cases using product images and web searches. Cross-encoder is distilled from VLM consensus labels and calibrated for auto-acceptance.
AI.result: System achieves 98% precision for auto-accepted links. The self-hosted open-weight agent matches frontier VLM precision at 88% recall vs 92% (4-point cost) at 1/7th the cost. End-to-end coverage increases from 68% (cheap stage) to 77% by escalating hard cases to agent.
AI.conclusion: The cascade approach successfully addresses marketplace-scale product linking by spending computation proportional to difficulty, achieving high precision and coverage while controlling costs through intelligent escalation of hard cases to multimodal agents.

title: Rollout-Decoded Reconstruction for Long-Horizon Prediction in Latent World Models
summary: A latent world model trains its decoder on latents anchored to observations, then deploys it on the model's own free-running rollout, hundreds of steps past the last observation. Rollout-Decoded Reconstruction (RDR) closes this gap with a single loss term that free-runs the model during training exactly as evaluation will, decodes every rollout latent, and penalizes reconstruction error against ground truth. The term adds no parameters, costs training-time compute only, and reduces to the standard objective at weight zero, so every comparison in this paper is a one-flag A/B. On the chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, RDR raises valid prediction time (the time to first crossing of normalized error 0.5) from $3.87 \pm 0.23$ to $6.97 \pm 0.42$ time units at an identical 193,568 parameters, a $1.80\times$ improvement confirmed on seeds never used in selection and holding in 10 of 10 preregistered configurations at ratios of 1.71-2.50$\times$. The results come from a single system; a sweep in which the advantage grows with latent width is descriptive, and control experiments on two classic tasks are preliminary.

AI.tldr: RDR (Rollout-Decoded Reconstruction) is a training method that closes the gap between training and evaluation in latent world models by decoding rollout latents during training and penalizing reconstruction error against ground truth, leading to significantly improved prediction times without adding parameters.
AI.motivation: There's a gap between how latent world models are trained (decoding latents anchored to observations) and how they're deployed (free-running rollouts hundreds of steps past the last observation). This training-evaluation mismatch limits model performance during actual deployment.
AI.method: RDR adds a single loss term that free-runs the model during training exactly as in evaluation, decodes every rollout latent, and penalizes reconstruction error against ground truth. The method adds no parameters, costs only training-time compute, and reduces to the standard objective at weight zero.
AI.result: On the chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, RDR raised valid prediction time from 3.87±0.23 to 6.97±0.42 time units (1.80× improvement) at identical 193,568 parameters. Results held on unseen seeds and 10/10 preregistered configurations with improvement ratios of 1.71-2.50×.
AI.conclusion: RDR effectively closes the training-evaluation gap in latent world models, significantly improving long-term prediction performance without adding model parameters. The advantage appears to grow with latent width, suggesting promising scalability.

title: LifePlanner: Evaluating LLM Agents for Geo-spatial Planning with Social Media Data
summary: Geo-spatial planning, like trip design, is a realistic testbed for LLM agents because it requires grounded tool use, noisy evidence retrieval, and multi-constraint reasoning. Most benchmarks, however, only provide clean geospatial data and tools, missing the open-ended social signals that people use in daily planning. We introduce LifePlanner, a benchmark that enriches map data with large-scale local social media posts and provides access through an MCP toolset. LifePlanner provides an evaluation suite spanning four task categories and three difficulty levels. Experiments show frontier LLMs perform well on simple retrieval but degrade sharply on complex planning, with the Pass Rate dropping to 40.2%. Results show that failures mainly stem from incomplete evidence acquisition from such a large multimodal database, imprecise tool use, and weak constraint integration rather than model size or reasoning length, suggesting that future progress requires effective grounded planning instead of scaling alone.

AI.tldr: LifePlanner is a new benchmark that tests LLM agents on geo-spatial planning tasks by combining clean map data with noisy social media posts, revealing that current frontier models struggle with complex planning despite good performance on simple retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM agents in geo-spatial planning (like trip design) only provide clean geospatial data and tools, missing the open-ended social signals that people actually use in daily planning, creating an unrealistic test environment.
AI.method: The authors introduce LifePlanner, a benchmark that enriches standard map data with large-scale local social media posts and provides access through an MCP (Model Context Protocol) toolset, with an evaluation suite covering four task categories and three difficulty levels.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs perform well on simple retrieval tasks but degrade sharply on complex planning, with Pass Rate dropping to 40.2%. Failures stem from incomplete evidence acquisition from large multimodal databases, imprecise tool use, and weak constraint integration rather than model size or reasoning length limitations.
AI.conclusion: Future progress in LLM agents for realistic planning tasks requires effective grounded planning capabilities rather than simply scaling model size or reasoning length, highlighting the need for better integration of multimodal evidence and constraint reasoning.

title: On the Representational Geometry of Dynamic Programs
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures; submitted to NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (Extended Abstract Track)
summary: Standard neural architectures often fail to generalize to longer inputs for dynamic programming (DP) targets. We investigate what makes this hard geometrically. Every finite min-plus DP is a shortest path on a DAG, which is equivalently a tropical polynomial whose extended Newton polyhedron encodes the decision boundary of which path wins. We prove these three descriptions (graph, polynomial, polyhedron) form isomorphic semirings at two levels --- formal polynomials and their computed functions --- connected by operations that characterize all structural redundancies. We then address the length-generalization question geometrically: does the decision boundary at length $T$ decide the boundary at $T+1$? We present two structural negatives. The semiring's two native ways to reduce dimension (setting a variable to each identity) are neither injective nor always closed within the DP. Series and parallel composition fail to construct all DAG topologies from smaller sub-DAGs, and even all terminal-only operations do not capture all DP compositions.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why neural networks fail to generalize to longer inputs for dynamic programming tasks by analyzing DP problems as isomorphic semiring structures (graph, polynomial, polyhedron) and showing structural limitations in length generalization.
AI.motivation: Standard neural architectures often fail to generalize to longer inputs for dynamic programming targets, which is a significant limitation in applying neural methods to sequential decision problems.
AI.method: The authors analyze dynamic programming problems through three isomorphic descriptions: as shortest paths on DAGs, as tropical polynomials, and via extended Newton polyhedra that encode decision boundaries. They prove these form isomorphic semirings and examine structural properties of dimension reduction and composition operations.
AI.result: The paper presents two structural negative results: (1) The semiring's native dimension reduction operations (setting variables to identities) are neither injective nor always closed within DP, and (2) Series and parallel composition fail to construct all DAG topologies from smaller sub-DAGs, and terminal-only operations don't capture all DP compositions.
AI.conclusion: The geometric analysis reveals fundamental structural limitations in how dynamic programming problems scale with input length, explaining why neural networks struggle with length generalization for DP targets and providing insights into the inherent complexity of these problems.

title: SimVerity: When Does Simulated Agent Success Survive Physical Deployment?
comment: Submitted to the Main Technical Track of AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-27); currently under review
summary: Simulated evaluation is widely used to benchmark AI agents, yet how much evidence a simulated pass provides about physical deployment has not been systematically quantified. We present SimVerity, a verdict-transfer assurance framework: it replays matched scenarios on target smart home deployments and cross-validates agent execution against independently qualified physical witnesses. Our evaluation highlights that deployment success is a real-world process, not a static property in simulation: completion, reported state, observable effect, and settled outcome diverged within the same execution. Although an advanced simulator cleared all 240 light trials, a camera caught 42 sub-second failures invisible to settled-state checks. False clearance was predictable: a risk profile learned from measured trials and locked before evaluation predicted failures on a path it never physically measured, beating a property-blind baseline in all eleven held-out sessions across two cohorts. Agent auditability was also measurable: switching one agent loop's model-client/serving configuration raised its scenario-matching share from 52-88% to 100%. Finally, a second qualified simulator added no independent cross-check: it never disagreed on any overlapping case, and only physical measurement exposed their shared blind spots. SimVerity turns verdict transfer into an explicit decision: clear, abstain, or escalate before deployment.

AI.tldr: SimVerity is a framework that quantifies how much evidence from simulated AI agent testing transfers to real-world physical deployment by cross-validating agent execution against physical witnesses in smart home environments.
AI.motivation: Current simulated evaluation of AI agents lacks systematic quantification of how well simulation results transfer to physical deployment, creating uncertainty about real-world performance despite successful simulated tests.
AI.method: The SimVerity framework replays matched scenarios on target smart home deployments and cross-validates agent execution against independently qualified physical witnesses. It learns a risk profile from measured trials to predict failures and measures agent auditability through configuration changes.
AI.result: Simulation success doesn't guarantee physical deployment: despite clearing all 240 light trials in simulation, cameras caught 42 sub-second failures. The learned risk profile predicted failures on unmeasured paths, beating baseline in all 11 held-out sessions. Configuration changes improved scenario-matching from 52-88% to 100%. Additional simulators didn't provide independent cross-checking.
AI.conclusion: Deployment success is a real-world process with multiple failure modes beyond simulation checks. SimVerity transforms verdict transfer into an explicit decision framework (clear, abstain, or escalate) based on systematic physical validation before deployment.

title: DeMMO: Longitudinal and Cross-Disease Modelling of Digital Mobility Outcomes via Multi-Task Learning
comment: 24 pages, 5 figures, and 7 tables. Implementation code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/menghui-zhou/DeMMO
summary: Digital mobility outcomes (DMOs) derived from wearable sensors characterise mobility in daily life and offer a promising means of monitoring disease progression. Yet most DMO studies examine one disease at one visit; they do not model how multivariate DMO relationships with multiple clinical outcomes evolve jointly across diseases. Technically, existing temporal multi-task frameworks can model progression within an individual disease, but they do not jointly model multiple prediction outcomes across diseases, particularly when disease cohorts do not share participants. To address these gaps, we propose DeMMO, an interpretable framework for longitudinal, multi-disease, and multi-outcome learning. DeMMO represents each disease-outcome objective by a longitudinal DMO coefficient matrix and combines temporal regularisation with stable and visit-specific feature selection. Its central technical contribution is an automatic cross-disease and cross-outcome relation-learning mechanism that learns signed relations directly from these longitudinal mappings, enabling selective information sharing without paired participants. We evaluate DeMMO on the recently released, large-scale, multicentre Mobilise-D dataset, which provides a new opportunity to study 24 harmonised real-world DMOs over five visits across multiple mobility-limiting conditions. Against nine strong linear, longitudinal, and deep-regression baselines, DeMMO achieves the best overall and outcome-specific prediction performance, with significant improvements over the strongest baselines. Stability selection further identifies reliable longitudinal DMO patterns for subsequent clinical validation and disease monitoring. The implementation code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/menghui-zhou/DeMMO.

AI.tldr: DeMMO is an interpretable framework for longitudinal, multi-disease, multi-outcome learning that models how digital mobility outcomes relate to clinical measures across different diseases without requiring shared participants.
AI.motivation: Current digital mobility outcome studies typically examine one disease at one visit and fail to model how multivariate DMO relationships with multiple clinical outcomes evolve jointly across diseases. Existing temporal multi-task frameworks can't jointly model multiple prediction outcomes across diseases, especially when disease cohorts don't share participants.
AI.method: DeMMO represents each disease-outcome objective by a longitudinal DMO coefficient matrix and combines temporal regularization with stable and visit-specific feature selection. Its key innovation is an automatic cross-disease and cross-outcome relation-learning mechanism that learns signed relations directly from these longitudinal mappings, enabling selective information sharing without paired participants.
AI.result: On the large-scale Mobilise-D dataset with 24 harmonized DMOs over five visits across multiple mobility-limiting conditions, DeMMO achieved the best overall and outcome-specific prediction performance against nine strong linear, longitudinal, and deep-regression baselines, with significant improvements over the strongest baselines.
AI.conclusion: DeMMO provides an effective framework for joint longitudinal modeling of multiple diseases and outcomes, identifies reliable longitudinal DMO patterns for clinical validation and disease monitoring, and enables information sharing across diseases without requiring shared participants.

title: Auto-Policy, not Auto-Skill: Compiled Agent Skills for the Physical World
comment: Presented at the 1st Workshop on Agent Skills (Agent Skills '26), ACM CAIS 2026, San Jose, May 26, 2026
summary: Self-evolving Skill harnesses (AutoSkills, Hermes Agent) generate more advisory orchestration automatically; their reported gains are efficiency, not safety. This misses the actual gap: a Skill describes how an agent should behave; a Policy decides which behavior is allowed to become an action. Today's format covers the first with markdown and scripts; the second is left to the model. Generating more Skills scales the gap, not the safety, especially when a wrong invocation can unlock a door or move money. Two adjacent attacks are documented: malicious skills compromising cloud software, and jailbroken LLM-controlled robots causing physical harm. Their intersection, malicious agent skills causing physical harm, follows directly but has not been reported. We name this class Borrowed Authority: Skills format gives the receiving agent no typed way to reject an inter-agent permission claim, so a malicious or misused Skill can drive actuation by attaching one. We propose Edge Skillguard, a typed authority layer that lives inside the Skill artifact rather than between tools as workflow engines do, with guards over world state and sensor evidence. On a live edge control-plane testbed, the guards reject 60/60 borrowed-authority requests across five attack variants without blocking benign requests, and the result holds at 5x scale and across hosts over a Tailscale mesh. These results suggest that high-risk Skills should co-package typed invocation policy with procedural knowledge, so that physical actions depend on machine-checkable evidence rather than peer-agent claims.

AI.tldr: Edge Skillguard is a typed authority layer embedded in Skill artifacts that prevents malicious agent skills from causing physical harm by requiring machine-checkable evidence for critical actions, blocking 60/60 borrowed-authority attacks in live testing.
AI.motivation: Current agent orchestration systems (AutoSkills, Hermes Agent) focus on efficiency but ignore the critical safety gap: Skills describe behavior while Policy decides what's allowed. This creates a "Borrowed Authority" vulnerability where malicious skills can cause physical harm by exploiting the lack of typed permission rejection in inter-agent communication.
AI.method: Edge Skillguard proposes embedding a typed authority layer inside Skill artifacts (rather than between tools like workflow engines). It includes guards over world state and sensor evidence to verify authority claims before allowing actuation.
AI.result: On a live edge control-plane testbed, Edge Skillguard successfully rejected 60/60 borrowed-authority requests across five attack variants without blocking benign requests. The results held at 5x scale and across hosts over a Tailscale mesh.
AI.conclusion: High-risk Skills should co-package typed invocation policy with procedural knowledge, ensuring physical actions depend on machine-checkable evidence rather than peer-agent claims, thus preventing the "Borrowed Authority" class of attacks.

title: NVExplain: Explaining Time Series Forecasting with Latent Trajectory Analysis and Structure-Preserving Surrogates
summary: Time series forecasting models are widely used in high-stakes settings, yet their predictions remain difficult to interpret because existing post-hoc methods often ignore temporal dependence and fail to provide horizon-specific explanations. We propose a model-agnostic explainability framework that explains forecasting predictions by attributing each forecast horizon to temporally relevant historical lags. The framework models forecasting as a latent trajectory and introduces semantic flow to quantify how information evolves across time in the model's internal representations. By aggregating semantic flow, it constructs a lag-horizon attribution matrix that captures horizon-resolved temporal influence. To improve explainability, we further generate structure-preserving perturbations and fit sparse local surrogate models, producing human-readable and temporally coherent explanations. We evaluate the method using faithfulness and stability diagnostics across multiple benchmark datasets. Results show that the semantic-flow variant achieves competitive or superior faithfulness compared to standard post-hoc baselines, while being substantially more computationally efficient. Stability analysis further demonstrates that the explanations are robust and identifies regimes where interpretation should be applied with caution.

AI.tldr: A model-agnostic explainability framework for time series forecasting that explains predictions by attributing forecast horizons to relevant historical lags using semantic flow analysis.
AI.motivation: Current time series forecasting models lack interpretability because existing post-hoc explanation methods ignore temporal dependence and fail to provide horizon-specific explanations, which is problematic in high-stakes applications.
AI.method: The framework models forecasting as a latent trajectory and introduces semantic flow to quantify information evolution across time in model representations. It aggregates semantic flow to create lag-horizon attribution matrices, generates structure-preserving perturbations, and fits sparse local surrogate models for human-readable explanations.
AI.result: The semantic-flow variant achieves competitive or superior faithfulness compared to standard post-hoc baselines while being substantially more computationally efficient. Stability analysis shows explanations are robust but identifies regimes requiring cautious interpretation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully addresses key limitations of existing methods by providing horizon-resolved, temporally coherent explanations for time series forecasting models while maintaining computational efficiency and robustness.

title: PhysElite: How Far Are LLMs from Solving Olympiad-Level Physics Problems?
summary: Understanding how (multimodal) large language models perform on physics problems requires benchmarks that reflect the difficulty and breadth of expert-level physical reasoning. Existing physics benchmarks remain limited in the following two important ways: (1) short of high-difficulty datasets, and (2) lack of comprehensive coverage of visual forms, knowledge points, and step-by-step solution processes. As a result, model performance on current datasets may not be fully representative of their ability to solve complex physics problems. To address these issues, we present PhysElite, a large-scale bilingual multimodal benchmark for Olympiad-level physics reasoning. PhysElite contains 11,586 Olympiad-tier problems. For each problem, we provide corresponding visual diagrams, step-by-step bilingual Chinese-English solution derivations, and the final answer. We benchmark 18 open-source and closed-source MLLMs, and find that even the strongest model reaches only 33.7% answer accuracy. We additionally conduct step-level process evaluation to diagnose where models fail in the reasoning chain. Our datasets are released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/physelite/PhysElite.

AI.tldr: PhysElite is a new multimodal benchmark for Olympiad-level physics reasoning with 11,586 problems, bilingual solutions, and visual diagrams, revealing that even top models only achieve 33.7% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current physics benchmarks are limited in difficulty and breadth, lacking high-difficulty datasets and comprehensive coverage of visual forms, knowledge points, and step-by-step solutions, making model performance on existing datasets unrepresentative of their ability to solve complex physics problems.
AI.method: Created PhysElite - a large-scale bilingual multimodal benchmark with 11,586 Olympiad-tier physics problems, each with visual diagrams, step-by-step bilingual Chinese-English solution derivations, and final answers. Benchmarked 18 open-source and closed-source multimodal large language models (MLLMs).
AI.result: Even the strongest model reached only 33.7% answer accuracy, indicating significant limitations in handling complex physics reasoning. Additional step-level process evaluation was conducted to diagnose where models fail in the reasoning chain.
AI.conclusion: PhysElite provides a more comprehensive and challenging benchmark for evaluating multimodal LLMs on expert-level physics reasoning, revealing substantial gaps in current models' capabilities and enabling better diagnosis of reasoning failures.

title: The Frame Kernel Method for Multiscale Operator Learning
summary: We present a natively multiscale operator learning method for the surrogate modeling of (numerical solvers for) multiscale partial differential equations (PDEs). The primary novelty of our method lies in a novel multiscale kernel frame function approximation technique. Leveraging this new kernel frame technique, we cast the operator learning problem as one of learning frame coefficients of output functions as a function of frame coefficients of input functions. The generalization step then automatically allows for a multiscale decomposition of the output functions. Our method is applicable to both tensor-product grids and point clouds. We present interpolation proofs, error estimates, and numerical convergence rates for our frame approximation. We the demonstrate the applicability of our method for the surrogate modeling of inherently multiscale PDEs. The new multiscale frame kernel method is significantly more accurate than popular neural operators on challenging problems from the literature, while simultaneously admitting an a posteriori multiscale decomposition upon generalization.

AI.tldr: A novel multiscale operator learning method using kernel frame approximation for surrogate modeling of multiscale PDEs, outperforming neural operators with built-in multiscale decomposition.
AI.motivation: Need for accurate surrogate modeling of multiscale PDEs and numerical solvers, overcoming limitations of existing neural operators that lack native multiscale capabilities and explicit decomposition.
AI.method: Develops a novel multiscale kernel frame function approximation technique that casts operator learning as learning frame coefficients mapping input to output functions, enabling automatic multiscale decomposition of outputs.
AI.result: The method shows significantly higher accuracy than popular neural operators on challenging multiscale PDE problems, with theoretical interpolation proofs, error estimates, and numerical convergence rates.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multiscale kernel frame method provides superior accuracy for multiscale PDE surrogate modeling while offering the unique advantage of a posteriori multiscale decomposition during generalization.

title: Towards Reliable, Generalizable, and Specific In-Context Knowledge Editing via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
comment: Our work proposes a multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm that optimizes prompt construction for reliable, generalizable, and specific in-context knowledge-editing
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful but limited by static parametric knowledge that becomes outdated once pretraining ends. Knowledge editing addresses this problem by updating model behavior on target facts without full retraining. In particular, in-context knowledge editing has gained attention because it is training-free and readily applicable to black-box LLMs. Recent reinforcement learning (RL)-based approaches improve over fixed retrieval strategies by adapting prompt construction to the quantity-quality trade-off. Despite initial success, they fail to model the prompt as a structured entity under the distinct and often competing objectives of reliability, generality, and specificity. Previous methods largely optimize a single objective and make decisions over only part of the prompt construction process, thereby overlooking both the balance of different objectives and the global organization of demonstrations. We propose Multi-Objective In-context Knowledge Editing (MO-IKE), a multi-objective RL algorithm that formulates prompt construction for in-context knowledge editing as a Constrained Markov Decision Process. MO-IKE trains a dynamic retriever to optimize competing objectives in knowledge editing, enabling more balanced and globally coherent prompt construction. On Llama-3.2, MO-IKE improves edit success (reliability) from 85.0% to 92.0%, paraphrase consistency (generality) from 77% to 79%, while increasing retention rate (specificity) by 23.0% compared to prior RL-based methods.

AI.tldr: MO-IKE is a multi-objective RL algorithm for in-context knowledge editing that optimizes competing objectives (reliability, generality, specificity) to construct better prompts than previous single-objective approaches.
AI.motivation: LLMs have static parametric knowledge that becomes outdated, and current in-context knowledge editing methods using reinforcement learning fail to properly model prompts as structured entities under competing objectives, optimizing only single objectives rather than balancing reliability, generality, and specificity.
AI.method: Multi-Objective In-context Knowledge Editing (MO-IKE) formulates prompt construction as a Constrained Markov Decision Process and trains a dynamic retriever using multi-objective reinforcement learning to optimize competing objectives simultaneously.
AI.result: On Llama-3.2, MO-IKE improves edit success (reliability) from 85.0% to 92.0%, paraphrase consistency (generality) from 77% to 79%, while increasing retention rate (specificity) by 23.0% compared to prior RL-based methods.
AI.conclusion: MO-IKE demonstrates that modeling prompt construction as a multi-objective optimization problem leads to more balanced and globally coherent prompt construction for in-context knowledge editing, significantly improving performance across all key metrics.

title: The Von-Neumann State-Space Transformer for neural decoding
summary: Cortical computation is strikingly low-dimensional: a handful of latent variables, carried in a neural population's activity, steer the higher-dimensional responses of individual neurons. Our aim is sample efficiency-models that decode well from limited data and at small parameter budgets. In a standard Transformer layer, the feed-forward block applies the same operator to every token. We suggest a von-Neumann inspired hypothesis of efficient computation as an alternative for neural decoding: a controller decodes an instruction and then executes a token-specific operator; the usual realization-a soft mixture of experts-only blends their outputs, not operators. We introduce a von-Neumann State-Space Transformer (VN-SST), a memory-augmented Transformer whose feed-forward block is a low-rank instruction bank: a shared base operator plus a small set of learned low-rank instructions, from which a per-token code synthesizes the weight matrix actually used at that token. The code is read from a low- dimensional projection of a carried state-space memory, so a slow latent trajectory acts as an instruction pointer-mirroring how low-dimensional dynamics may route cortical computation. On three motor-cortex neural-decoding benchmarks, VN-SST is far more data-efficient than a modern Transformer, each jointly predicting spikes and decoding behavior. This model wins by a wide margin on the scarcest benchmark, leads on the other two, and turns longer context into rising rather than falling accuracy. We evaluated that the network compresses a large instruction bank to a few bits per token, so program capacity acts as a control channel, not an accuracy lever. The same model is also more parameter-efficient on two small text benchmarks used for language modeling (LLMs), suggesting a generic mechanism.

AI.tldr: A novel Transformer architecture (VN-SST) with von-Neumann inspired low-rank instruction banks dramatically improves data efficiency for neural decoding and parameter efficiency for language modeling.
AI.motivation: To create models that decode effectively from limited data with small parameter budgets, inspired by cortical computation where low-dimensional latent variables steer high-dimensional neural responses and von-Neumann architecture principles.
AI.method: Developed von-Neumann State-Space Transformer (VN-SST) with memory-augmented feed-forward blocks using low-rank instruction banks: a shared base operator plus learned low-rank instructions, with per-token code synthesis from low-dimensional state-space memory projections.
AI.result: VN-SST significantly outperforms modern Transformers on three motor-cortex neural-decoding benchmarks, especially on scarce data, with rising accuracy for longer context. Also shows superior parameter efficiency on two small text language modeling benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The von-Neumann inspired approach of using low-dimensional state memory as an instruction pointer provides a generic mechanism for both neural decoding and language modeling that improves data and parameter efficiency while mirroring cortical computation principles.

title: FuzzingBrain-Bench V1: Evaluating Open-Ended Bug Discovery by LLMs
comment: 21 pages, 12 figures, 7 tables. Ze Sheng and Aleksandar Kezic contributed equally. Benchmark corpus and harnesses: https://github.com/fuzzingbrain/FuzzingBrain-Bench Counts verified against the built PDF and sources: 21 pages, 12 figure environments, 7 tables
summary:
Evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to discover software bugs is increasingly important. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate this capability by asking the model to generate a proof-of-concept input that triggers a predefined target vulnerability. However, this setup may overlook valid crashes discovered by the model when they do not match the predefined target. As a result, the evaluation may not reflect the model's real capability.
  We present FuzzingBrain-Bench, a benchmark for assessing AI models' ability to discover bugs in open-source software. Models are given an open-source project and a sanitizer-instrumented harness in a self-contained Docker image. Their goal is to generate inputs that trigger as many distinct crashes as possible through the harness. A model's performance on each challenge is scored based on the number of distinct crash signatures it produces, capped at a predefined maximum and weighted by a difficulty coefficient.
  FuzzingBrain-Bench V1 consists of 77 challenges drawn from 43 open-source projects, with 36 C, 32 C++, and 9 Java/JVM challenges. We evaluate Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Claude Opus 4.8 on the full benchmark. Claude Opus 4.8 performs best, triggering crashes in 60 of 77 challenges and achieving a score of 196 out of 579. None of the three models triggers a crash in 13 challenges. The FuzzingBrain-Bench corpus and harnesses are publicly available at https://github.com/fuzzingbrain/FuzzingBrain-Bench.

AI.tldr: FuzzingBrain-Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to discover software bugs by generating inputs that trigger distinct crashes in open-source projects, moving beyond predefined vulnerability matching.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate LLM bug-finding ability by asking models to generate inputs for predefined vulnerabilities, but this overlooks valid crashes that don't match the target, potentially misrepresenting real capabilities.
AI.method: Models are provided with open-source projects and sanitizer-instrumented harnesses in Docker containers, then evaluated based on the number of distinct crash signatures they can trigger, with scores capped at a maximum and weighted by difficulty.
AI.result: FuzzingBrain-Bench V1 has 77 challenges from 43 projects (36 C, 32 C++, 9 Java/JVM). Claude Opus 4.8 performed best, triggering crashes in 60/77 challenges with a score of 196/579, while all three models failed on 13 challenges.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides a more realistic evaluation of LLMs' bug-finding capabilities by focusing on crash discovery rather than predefined vulnerability matching, with publicly available corpus and harnesses for community use.

title: Understanding the Energy Scaling of Large Language Model Inference Across Context Lengths and Attention Architectures
summary: The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) has raised increasing concerns about the energy consumption and environmental impact of inference. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of decode-phase energy consumption across representative open-source LLMs employing Multi-Head Attention (MHA), Grouped Query Attention (GQA), and Grouped Query Attention with Sliding Window Attention (SWA) to characterize how attention architecture influences decode-phase energy consumption under varying inference workloads. We evaluate four models across different context lengths, batch sizes, and generation workloads while measuring GPU energy using NVIDIA hardware counters. We examine the effects of context length, attention mechanism, Key-Value (KV) cache growth, and batching on decode-phase energy consumption. Results show that attention mechanism is the primary factor governing how decode energy scales with context length. MHA models exhibit substantially steeper energy growth than GQA models, whereas GQA with SWA maintains nearly constant energy consumption. We further show that model size primarily determines absolute energy consumption, while batching reduces both energy per generated token and request latency by up to 87%. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting energy-efficient LLM architectures and inference configurations.

AI.tldr: Systematic empirical study showing how different attention mechanisms (MHA, GQA, SWA) affect decode-phase energy consumption in LLMs, with GQA+SWA achieving near-constant energy scaling.
AI.motivation: Growing concerns about energy consumption and environmental impact of LLM inference require understanding how attention architectures influence decode-phase energy consumption under varying workloads.
