AI.method: The authors conducted 150 seed-replicated regularized maximum-likelihood fits on WikiArt data (27 styles, 81,446 paintings with frozen CLIP ViT-B/16 features), varying embedding dimension, curvature, and regularizer strength. They compared Euclidean R^d vs. Poincaré ball B^d_c manifolds and evaluated using three reference-tree definitions (hand-built lineage, CLIP-derived, and DINOv2-derived).
AI.result: Poincaré prototypes preserve the topology of the nearest-neighbor graph in latent space substantially better than Euclidean prototypes (sibling recall@5 +8.7 percentage points, cousin recall +15.2 percentage points). Euclidean prototypes performed similarly to logistic regression on raw encoder features, while only hyperbolic fits improved on k-NN encoder baselines. Global tree-fidelity comparisons were unstable across reference trees.
AI.conclusion: The study provides an empirical separation between Euclidean and hyperbolic latent geometries for class-structured regularizers in hierarchical classification. While hyperbolic embeddings better preserve topological relationships, global tree-fidelity comparisons show mixed results, suggesting context-dependent advantages for different manifolds.

title: Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning
comment: 82 pages, 15 figures. Code, prompts, and evaluation data are available at https://github.com/paulrosu11/training-auditing-agents-public
summary: Alignment auditing of frontier models increasingly relies on LLM auditors to surface undesirable behaviors at scale, but current automated auditors can struggle with coherent investigation and audit realism. In this work, we improve LLM auditors with reinforcement learning. In our best training environment, the policy investigates target models that potentially possess hidden behaviors planted via their system prompt. An LLM judge, which knows whether the target has a hidden behavior, holistically compares the policy's investigation to a reference investigation to determine the reward. With systematic ablations, we find that pairwise rewards yield more robust training compared to pointwise rewards, and that adding targets without planted behaviors helps maintain a low false positive rate. Training improves investigation quality against targets with planted behaviors, the rate of concerning behaviors surfaced in unmodified production models, and audit realism, while false-positive rates stay below 1%. Furthermore, auditing capabilities generalize across scaffolds: performance on AuditBench's adversarially fine-tuned targets substantially improves [Sheshadri et al., 2026].

AI.tldr: Training LLM auditors with reinforcement learning improves their ability to investigate and surface hidden behaviors in frontier models while maintaining low false positive rates.
AI.motivation: Current automated LLM auditors struggle with coherent investigation and audit realism when alignment auditing frontier models at scale, creating a need for more effective auditing methods.
AI.method: Reinforcement learning is used to train LLM auditors in an environment where policies investigate target models with potential hidden behaviors planted via system prompts. An LLM judge, aware of whether targets have hidden behaviors, compares the policy's investigation to reference investigations using pairwise rewards (better than pointwise), and targets without planted behaviors are included to maintain low false positive rates.
AI.result: The trained auditors show improved investigation quality against targets with planted behaviors, increased detection of concerning behaviors in unmodified production models, better audit realism, while maintaining false positive rates below 1%. Capabilities generalize across different audit scaffolds, with substantial performance improvement on AuditBench's adversarially fine-tuned targets.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning effectively enhances LLM auditors for alignment auditing of frontier models, improving their ability to surface hidden behaviors while maintaining reliability and generalizability across different audit scenarios.

title: Learning Mixtures of Plackett-Luce Models for Multi-Objective Alignment
summary: We consider the problem of learning a mixture of $k$ Plackett-Luce models given multi-way ranking responses from annotators that may represent heterogeneous underlying preferences. This problem has many applications in AI alignment and preference optimization. Prior work has studied mixtures of Bradley-Terry models from pairwise comparisons. However, uncovering mixture models is theoretically unidentifiable when $k$ exceeds $m/2$, where $m$ is the length of a ranking. We propose an efficient implementation to address this limitation, which involves first augmenting the rankings to a larger size by generating new responses from a base language model, followed by a gradient-based estimation to reduce inference cost in the input embedding space. Based on this procedure, we then design an expectation-maximization algorithm with these two steps to fit a mixture of Plackett-Luce models, called MoPLEx. Extensive experiments are conducted to verify this approach. First, we show that the gradient-based approximation estimates true probabilities with less than 5% error on models with up to 34 billion parameters. Second, we show that MoPLEx improves clustering and ranking accuracy by an average of 43.7% and 15.2% over baselines using single ranking and mixtures of Bradley-Terry models, on preference optimization datasets. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of MoPLEx for tackling multi-way rankings from heterogeneous preferences through measuring alignment between gradients.

AI.tldr: MoPLEx: An EM algorithm for learning mixtures of Plackett-Luce models from multi-way ranking data with heterogeneous preferences, using gradient-based estimation and data augmentation to overcome theoretical identifiability limits.
AI.motivation: Learning mixture models from multi-way ranking data is important for AI alignment and preference optimization, but existing methods using Bradley-Terry models have theoretical identifiability limitations when number of mixtures exceeds half the ranking length.
AI.method: Two-step approach: 1) Augment rankings by generating new responses from a base language model, 2) Gradient-based estimation to reduce inference cost in embedding space, followed by EM algorithm (MoPLEx) fitting mixture of Plackett-Luce models.
AI.result: Gradient-based approximation estimates probabilities with <5% error on models up to 34B parameters; MoPLEx improves clustering accuracy by 43.7% and ranking accuracy by 15.2% over baselines on preference optimization datasets.
AI.conclusion: MoPLEx effectively handles multi-way rankings from heterogeneous preferences by measuring gradient alignment, overcoming theoretical identifiability limitations of previous methods while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: PonsRAG: A Pons-Inspired RAG Bridging Cognitive Islands for Coordinated Long Narrative Reasoning
summary: Long Narrative Reasoning is an essential capability for processing and reasoning over complex narratives. While retrieval-augmented generation provides a promising framework, existing methods still face two critical challenges: cognitive islanding and cross-layer evidence disconnection. To address these issues, we propose PonsRAG, a coordinated RAG framework inspired by the biological pons. PonsRAG consists of two key components: Triple-Layer Indexing, which organizes documents into a connected knowledge structure to bridge cognitive islands, and Coordinated Reasoning, which retrieves evidence across distinct layers and integrates cross-layer information into a unified context. We evaluate PonsRAG on four long-context narrative benchmarks, and experimental results show that it outperforms the strongest baseline, achieving a 11.56% relative improvement in average accuracy on multi-choice tasks.

AI.tldr: PonsRAG: A coordinated RAG framework inspired by the biological pons that addresses cognitive islanding and cross-layer evidence disconnection in long narrative reasoning through triple-layer indexing and coordinated reasoning mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented generation methods face critical challenges in long narrative reasoning: cognitive islanding (isolated knowledge segments) and cross-layer evidence disconnection (inability to connect information across different abstraction levels).
AI.method: PonsRAG features two key components: 1) Triple-Layer Indexing organizes documents into a connected knowledge structure to bridge cognitive islands, and 2) Coordinated Reasoning retrieves evidence across distinct layers and integrates cross-layer information into a unified context.
AI.result: On four long-context narrative benchmarks, PonsRAG outperforms the strongest baseline with an 11.56% relative improvement in average accuracy on multi-choice tasks.
AI.conclusion: The biological pons-inspired coordinated RAG framework effectively addresses key challenges in long narrative reasoning by bridging cognitive islands and enabling cross-layer evidence integration, demonstrating superior performance over existing methods.

title: LibriBrain100: One Hundred Hours of Broad and Deep MEG Data for Neural Speech Decoding at Scale
comment: 10 content pages + 22 pages for references and appendices (in total: 32 pages, 16 figures, 6 tables)
summary: We introduce LibriBrain100, a large-scale MEG dataset for speech decoding designed from the ground up for reproducible, standardised evaluation. LibriBrain100 more than doubles the size of the original LibriBrain release, resulting in over 100 hours of high-quality MEG acquired while subjects listened to naturalistic continuous speech. With $\sim$80 hours from a single subject, LibriBrain100 sets a new record for deep, within-subject neural data (8$\times$ more than the next comparable dataset and roughly 80$\times$ more than other datasets). To demonstrate the payoff of this depth-first design, we evaluate on a word-classification benchmark---an increasingly well-established stepping stone towards the open challenge of noninvasive brain-to-text decoding. Using an existing decoding model, we achieve state-of-the-art performance---validating both the quality of the recordings and the value of within-subject data at scale. Because collecting 80 hours of data per user is impractical for real-world applications, we also collected $\sim$40 minutes of additional data from each of 32 subjects. Using the same word-classification benchmark, we demonstrate the value of broad multi-subject data: supervised finetuning of a pre-trained model can substantially compensate for limited per-subject data. We provide standard train, validation, and test splits, all reproducible through an open-sourced Python library that supports easy downloading, optional preprocessing, and data loading for common deep learning frameworks. In addition, the dataset and evaluation infrastructure are being released alongside an open machine-learning competition with a public leaderboard for standardised benchmarking. Ultimately, our hope is that LibriBrain100 will accelerate progress towards practical non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, capable of restoring communication to people living with severe paralysis.

AI.tldr: LibriBrain100 is a massive MEG dataset with 100+ hours of neural recordings during speech listening, featuring unprecedented single-subject depth and multi-subject breadth for advancing speech decoding research.
AI.motivation: To accelerate progress in non-invasive brain-computer interfaces for communication restoration by providing a large-scale, standardized MEG dataset that enables reproducible evaluation and benchmarking of speech decoding models.
AI.method: Created LibriBrain100 by expanding the original LibriBrain dataset, collecting over 100 hours of high-quality MEG recordings during continuous speech listening. Features ~80 hours from a single subject (depth-first design) plus ~40 minutes each from 32 additional subjects (breadth component).
AI.result: Demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on word-classification benchmark using existing decoding models, validating both recording quality and value of within-subject data. Showed that supervised fine-tuning with multi-subject data can compensate for limited per-subject data.
AI.conclusion: LibriBrain100 provides unprecedented neural data scale and quality for speech decoding research, with standardized splits, open-source tools, and competition infrastructure to enable reproducible benchmarking and accelerate development of practical non-invasive BCIs.

title: CaSKG: Counterfactual-Causal Skill Graphs for Scalable Agent Skill Retrieval
summary: Reusable skill libraries allow large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedural knowledge across tasks, but they also turn memory access into a challenging retrieval problem. Full-library prompting preserves coverage at high context cost, vector retrieval returns compact neighborhoods but treats skills as independent text, and graph-based retrieval can recover workflow context only when the edges that carry relevance are reliable. We propose CaSKG, a counterfactual-causal skill graph framework that calibrates procedural relations before retrieval. CaSKG first builds a high-recall directed candidate graph from semantic, lexical, input/output, and structural evidence, with repair evidence and an optional LLM judge further refining candidate scores. It then applies direction-conditioned textual counterfactual probes that remove, substitute, and reorder skill pairs, aggregates the evidence with Bayesian smoothing, and publishes a state-filtered weighted graph for task-conditioned expansion. The graph is constructed offline and used without changing the downstream agent policy or task interface. Across six LLM backbones on ALFWorld ID-140 and ScienceWorld U211, CaSKG achieves the highest task score in all twelve combinations of model and benchmark. Relative to Graph-of-Skills (GoS), it improves the six-model macro-average ScienceWorld score from 72.62 to 80.50 and ALFWorld success from 80.01\% to 86.79\%, while reducing mean environment steps on both benchmarks. Qualitative and ablation analyses further show that calibrated edges help retrieval preserve prerequisites, state-changing actions, verification routines, and final completion steps. These results position edge-confidence calibration as an effective route to compact and executable skill retrieval at scale\footnote{Code is available at: https://github.com/ZhiyuanLi218/Caskg }.

AI.tldr: CaSKG is a counterfactual-causal skill graph framework that calibrates procedural relations between skills for better retrieval from reusable skill libraries, outperforming existing methods across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reusable skill libraries for LLM agents create memory access challenges: full-library prompting is context-heavy, vector retrieval treats skills independently ignoring relationships, and graph-based retrieval requires reliable edges. There's a need for calibrated skill relationships to improve retrieval quality.
AI.method: Builds high-recall directed candidate graph using semantic, lexical, input/output, and structural evidence with repair and optional LLM judge scoring. Applies direction-conditioned textual counterfactual probes (removing, substituting, reordering skill pairs) with Bayesian smoothing, then creates state-filtered weighted graph for task-conditioned expansion. Offline construction with downstream agent unchanged.
AI.result: Achieved highest task scores in all 12 combinations of 6 LLM backbones across ALFWorld ID-140 and ScienceWorld U211. Improved macro-average ScienceWorld score from 72.62 to 80.50 and ALFWorld success from 80.01% to 86.79%, while reducing mean environment steps on both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Edge-confidence calibration through counterfactual-causal skill graphs is an effective approach for compact and executable skill retrieval at scale, helping preserve prerequisites, state-changing actions, verification routines, and completion steps in retrieved skill sequences.

title: Representing MAX functions using two-hidden-layer ReLU networks
summary:
We study exact representations of $\mathrm{MAX}_N(x)=\max{x_1,\ldots,x_N}$ using two-hidden-layer ReLU neural networks. This problem has been studied in recent years in an attempt to characterize the exact number of hidden layers required to represent continuous piecewise linear functions. The best lower bound is 2, while the current upper bound is logarithmic in $N$. It remains completely open if the right answer is a constant number of hidden layers (possibly even 2!) or not. In fact, a recent breakthrough was the representation of $\mathrm{MAX}_5$ as a two-hidden-layer ReLU function obtained in [Bakaev et al., 2026], and the case of $\mathrm{MAX}_N$ was stated as open for $N\geq 6$ in that paper.
  Using a careful computer assisted search, we obtain two-hidden-layer ReLU representations of $\mathrm{MAX}_5, \mathrm{MAX}_6, \mathrm{MAX}_7$, and $\mathrm{MAX}_8$. We obtain these by considering rational linear combinations of terms of the form $\max\{\sum_{r=1}^{s}\max(x_{a_r},x_{b_r}),\sum_{r=1}^{s}\max(x_{c_r},x_{d_r})\}$, where $a_r,b_r,c_r,d_r\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Each inner maximum of two coordinates can be computed in a first hidden layer, and the outer maximum of the two side-sums can be computed in a second hidden layer. Consequently, every finite linear combination of these terms has a two-hidden-layer ReLU realization. An identity for $\mathrm{MAX}_N$ in this form therefore gives an exact two-hidden-layer ReLU representation of $\mathrm{MAX}_N$.
  Very recently, two-hidden-layer representations of $\mathrm{MAX}_N$ of the above form were obtained for all $N\leq 10$ in [Ruess et al., 2026]. Our representations are different and were developed independently. While our techniques share most of the high-level ideas presented in [Ruess et al., 2026], there are also some minor differences which may be of interest for future research on this problem.

AI.tldr: Two-hidden-layer ReLU networks can exactly represent MAX_N functions (maximum of N inputs) for N up to 8, matching recent breakthrough results and addressing an open problem in neural network expressivity.
AI.motivation: To determine the minimal number of hidden layers required to represent continuous piecewise linear functions like MAX_N using ReLU neural networks. The problem was open for N≥6 after a breakthrough showing MAX_5 could be represented with two hidden layers.
AI.method: Computer-assisted search for identities of the form MAX_N = max{∑ max(x_aᵣ, x_bᵣ), ∑ max(x_cᵣ, x_dᵣ)}. Each inner maximum of two coordinates is computed in the first hidden layer, and the outer maximum of two sums is computed in the second hidden layer.
AI.result: Successfully obtained two-hidden-layer ReLU representations for MAX_5, MAX_6, MAX_7, and MAX_8. These results match and were developed independently of recent work showing representations for N≤10.
AI.conclusion: Two hidden layers are sufficient to represent MAX_N functions for N up to 8, providing evidence that the minimal depth for such functions might be constant (possibly 2) rather than logarithmic. The approach uses specific mathematical forms that naturally map to two-layer ReLU architectures.

title: Agentic Game Development as a Verifiable Trajectory Data Engine for Scaling World Models
summary: A common strategy for scaling world models is to train on more crawled video with more compute. We argue that this strategy is inefficient: scaling world models also requires a recursive data engine that offers grounded reward signals. The success of code agents illustrates why this matters. As code is executable, compilers and runtimes can provide high-quality rewards for Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training of LLMs. By contrast, spatial generation still relies largely on fuzzy proxies such as CLIP scores. These signals are fuzzy and biased, making them hard to support RL post-training. Compared with these, game development provides a missing reward environment for spatial world models. A scene encoded by a game engine is an executable world specification: the engine can efficiently check collision, physics, navigability and bounded playability, while the developer provides the global verification signal by judging whether the scene should be accepted. Game development also provides real-world long-horizon trajectory data for RL post-training. We therefore propose Reinforcement Learning with Human-Engine Verification (RLHEV), a post-training paradigm that combines dense engine signals with implicit human acceptance feedback from the development process.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RLHEV, a reinforcement learning post-training paradigm that uses game development environments for grounded reward signals, combining dense engine verification with human acceptance feedback to train better spatial world models.
AI.motivation: Current scaling strategies for world models rely on more video data and compute, which is inefficient. Spatial generation lacks executable reward environments like those available in code (compilers/runtimes), and current proxies like CLIP scores are fuzzy and biased, making RL post-training difficult.
AI.method: Reinforcement Learning with Human-Engine Verification (RLHEV) leverages game development environments where game engines provide dense verification signals (collision, physics, navigability) and developers provide implicit acceptance feedback during the development process.
AI.result: Not specified in the abstract (requires reading full paper), but the method promises to provide the missing reward environment needed for effective RL post-training of spatial world models.
AI.conclusion: Game development offers an ideal executable environment for training spatial world models, combining precise engine verification with human judgment, creating a more effective foundation for RL post-training than current fuzzy proxy signals.

title: Trust the Mass: Forced Weights in KV-Cache Eviction
summary: Every deployed sparse-attention or KV-cache-eviction rule keeps a subset of the keys, discards the rest, and renormalizes the attention weights over the kept set. Enumerating the exact best subset under that constraint on $168{,}192$ attention rows from five models shows that keeping the largest weights is already near-optimal, since the best subset closes only a median $2$ to $5\%$ of the remaining gap to full attention. If selection closes this little, published margins between eviction methods must come from elsewhere, so we measure the bytes each method holds. In the shared evaluation pipeline, the strongest query-agnostic methods hold the full cache because their per-head selections are stored as masks, and only ragged per-head storage frees that memory. Enforcing a nominal budget on one fixed selection costs $14$ to $62$ benchmark points. We trace an $87.6$-point retrieval margin to rankings computed while the question is visible. ContourKV, a training-free allocator built from the dropped-mass statistic, wins $93$ of $160$ paired comparisons against that state of the art and loses $22$ at the byte count of the budget-enforcing baselines, and it ties the strongest of them.

AI.tldr: Analysis shows that keeping largest attention weights is near-optimal for KV cache eviction, with minimal performance gain from optimal subset selection. Published performance margins come from memory usage differences and question-visible rankings, not selection quality.
AI.motivation: Existing sparse-attention and KV-cache-eviction methods claim performance differences, but the researchers wanted to understand the real source of these margins - whether they come from better selection algorithms or other factors like memory usage.
AI.method: 1) Enumerated exact best subsets for 168,192 attention rows across five models to test if keeping largest weights is optimal. 2) Measured actual bytes held by different methods. 3) Introduced ContourKV, a training-free allocator using dropped-mass statistic.
AI.result: 1) Keeping largest weights is near-optimal, closing only 2-5% of gap to full attention. 2) Published method margins come from memory usage differences, not selection quality. 3) Budget-enforcing baselines lose 14-62 benchmark points. 4) ContourKV wins 93/160 comparisons vs state-of-art, ties strongest baselines.
AI.conclusion: Performance differences between KV-cache methods primarily come from memory overhead and implementation details rather than selection algorithm quality. Simple strategies like keeping largest weights are already near-optimal, challenging the need for complex eviction rules.

title: Using profiles of cognitive capability to assess AI suitability for workplace tasks
summary: Organisations deploying AI face a scoping problem: which tasks can be automated, which should remain with humans, and which are best shared between the two. Aggregate benchmark scores provide little insight into where systems will succeed or fail in practice, while human judgements of model capabilities quickly become outdated. We introduce a pipeline that profiles agents and tasks using a shared set of core cognitive capabilities. Cognitive capability profiling infers an agent's capabilities from performance on a benchmark battery annotated for the cognitive demands of each item. Task requirements weighting elicits from domain experts the relative importance of these same capabilities for their work. As both use a common set of cognitive dimensions, they can be updated independently as models and roles change, and combined to estimate AI suitability at the level of a domain, organisation, role, or individual duty. We validate capability recovery on synthetic agents, profile six AI systems, and elicit task requirements from 410 employees across six occupational domains. AI systems differed more across cognitive dimensions than across model families, while workplace activities converged on a shared cognitive core. The resulting scores provide a comparative scoping tool for identifying promising candidates for piloting and areas where current systems are unlikely to be well suited. We discuss extending the framework to profile human workers alongside AI systems, moving from AI suitability towards human-machine task allocation.

AI.tldr: A cognitive capability profiling framework that matches AI systems with workplace tasks by evaluating both on shared cognitive dimensions, enabling data-driven task allocation decisions.
AI.motivation: Organizations struggle with AI scoping decisions - determining which tasks to automate, keep human, or share. Traditional methods like aggregate benchmark scores are insufficient for practical application, and human judgments quickly become outdated as AI capabilities evolve rapidly.
AI.method: Two-part pipeline: (1) Cognitive capability profiling evaluates AI agents through benchmark batteries annotated for cognitive demands, (2) Task requirements weighting collects expert judgments on cognitive capability importance for specific work tasks. Both use a shared set of cognitive dimensions, enabling independent updates and combination for AI suitability estimation.
AI.result: Validation with synthetic agents, profiling of six AI systems, and task requirement data from 410 employees across six domains showed: AI systems varied more across cognitive dimensions than model families; workplace activities share a common cognitive core; the framework successfully identifies promising automation candidates and unsuitable areas.
AI.conclusion: The cognitive capability profiling approach provides a practical scoping tool for organizations, with potential extension to profile human workers alongside AI systems, enabling systematic human-machine task allocation rather than just AI suitability assessment.

title: Output Dilution: Redundant but Fragile Representations in MoE Models
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures. Code and outputs at https://github.com/deepsteer/deepsteer
summary:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models appear to encode moral content as robustly as dense models, yet prove far more fragile in their encoding. In OLMoE-1B-7B, linear probes recover moral valence from nearly every expert-layer combination, with mean peak-layer accuracy above 90%. But these representations collapse under levels of activation noise that a dense model of matched size easily tolerates, with a 4.2-fold difference in robustness.
  We trace this to output dilution. Because the MoE block averages across active experts before contributing to the residual stream, the feedforward signal reaching downstream layers is nearly two orders of magnitude smaller than in a dense MLP. Moral information, our interest, survives aggregation intact but at a scale trivially overwhelmed by perturbation. Routing itself remains stable under noise while the vulnerability originates entirely in the diluted aggregate.
  Checkpoint trajectories confirm this is architectural, not learned. Experts never specialize and accuracy saturates within the first few thousand steps. In sparse architectures, redundant encoding does not imply robust encoding.

AI.tldr: MoE models encode moral content as well as dense models but are much more fragile to activation noise due to output dilution in the expert averaging process.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates why Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, while appearing to encode moral content robustly (with high linear probe accuracy), prove to be surprisingly fragile compared to dense models of matched size. The researchers want to understand the source of this fragility despite seemingly robust representations.
AI.method: The researchers studied OLMoE-1B-7B models, using linear probes to measure moral valence encoding across expert-layer combinations. They compared robustness to activation noise between MoE and dense models, traced vulnerabilities to output dilution effects in MoE architectures, and analyzed checkpoint trajectories to determine whether the issue is architectural or learned.
AI.result: MoE models achieved >90% mean peak-layer accuracy for moral valence recovery via linear probes, similar to dense models. However, their representations collapsed under activation noise levels that dense models easily tolerated, with a 4.2-fold difference in robustness. This vulnerability stems from output dilution: the MoE block averages across active experts, reducing feedforward signal strength by nearly two orders of magnitude compared to dense MLPs. Routing remains stable under noise, and the issue is architectural rather than learned, as experts never specialize and accuracy saturates early in training.
AI.conclusion: In sparse MoE architectures, redundant encoding does not imply robust encoding. The fundamental vulnerability arises from architectural output dilution in expert averaging, which reduces signal strength to levels easily overwhelmed by perturbations, making MoE models fragile despite their apparent representational capabilities.

title: Narcissus: Program Synthesis Using Context-Aware LLM Approximations
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at programming, but not when the task fixes the target language: prompted with a grammar rare in their training data, their programs usually break the grammar or fail the given specification. Enumerative synthesizers search the space of syntactically correct programs systematically guided by LLMs; the state of the art guides them by approximating LLM proposals into rule frequencies, which loses where each construct belongs and prunes every rule the proposals miss, exactly when the proposals are wrong. We present Narcissus, a synthesizer that keeps the proposals as syntax trees and scores each expansion of a candidate program in its context: does a proposal with the same surrounding structure continue the same way, and does the expansion rebuild a fragment the proposals repeat? A regularization term keeps every rule reachable, so wrong proposals delay the solution but cannot hide it. Across five domains and two search backends, Narcissus beats static guidance at every budget and consistently outperforms re-prompting the LLM to fix its own proposals; it reaches proposal-like programs an order of magnitude sooner and solves $40\%$ of ARC tasks where the raw proposals solve $13\%$, all without a single LLM call during search.

AI.tldr: Narcissus is a program synthesis system that uses LLM-generated proposals as syntax trees to guide enumerative search, significantly outperforming existing methods without needing LLM calls during search.
AI.motivation: While LLMs are good at programming, they struggle when tasks require producing programs in grammars that are rare in their training data. LLM-generated programs often break grammar rules or fail specifications. Existing enumerative synthesizers guided by LLMs lose important structural information by approximating proposals as rule frequencies.
AI.method: Narcissus keeps LLM proposals as syntax trees instead of converting them to rule frequencies. It scores each expansion of a candidate program based on whether proposals with the same surrounding structure continue the same way, and whether the expansion rebuilds fragments that proposals repeat. A regularization term ensures every rule remains reachable.
AI.result: Narcissus beats static guidance at every budget and consistently outperforms re-prompting the LLM to fix its own proposals. It reaches proposal-like programs an order of magnitude sooner and solves 40% of ARC tasks where raw proposals solve only 13%, all without any LLM calls during search.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining proposals as syntax trees provides better guidance for enumerative synthesis than approximating them as rule frequencies. This approach enables effective use of LLM knowledge for programming in unfamiliar grammars while overcoming LLM limitations, achieving significant performance improvements across multiple domains.

title: Long-Term Behavioral Evaluation for Trusted Collaborator Selection via Bidirectional Mamba
summary: Effective selection of trustworthy collaborators is crucial to ensuring the successful completion of collaborative tasks, which requires accurate assessments of both long-term device behavior and short-term collaborative dynamics. Consistent device behavior patterns, which are learned from historical collaborations, can be used to predict their reliability in future collaborations. However, accurately assessing device behavior based on historical collaborations remains challenging. First, behavior assessment from limited historical collaborations captures only instantaneous past behavior, failing to represent the devices' true behavior. Second, due to the temporal dependencies of device behavior, a unidirectional evaluation that relies only on earlier collaborations loses the opportunity to learn from subsequent collaborations. Addressing these challenges requires evaluating device behavior based on long-term collaborations while considering both forward and backward temporal dependencies. To this end, this work proposes a bidirectional Mamba-enabled model (BM) for long-term behavioral evaluation. For each short time slot, a graph is constructed among devices based on historical collaborations, and device behavioral features within the slot are then aggregated accordingly. Subsequently, a bidirectional Mamba model integrates these short-term representations across all time intervals, producing a stable and reliable long-term behavior evaluation for each device. Experimental results demonstrate that BM achieves higher evaluation accuracy than baseline methods, thereby enabling the selection of collaborators that maximize the value of task completion.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a bidirectional Mamba-enabled model (BM) that uses both forward and backward temporal dependencies from historical collaboration data to accurately evaluate long-term device behavior for reliable collaborator selection.
AI.motivation: Accurate assessment of device behavior is crucial for selecting trustworthy collaborators in collaborative tasks. Current methods have limitations: they capture only instantaneous past behavior from limited historical data, failing to represent true device behavior, and unidirectional evaluations based only on earlier collaborations miss learning opportunities from subsequent collaborations.
AI.method: The bidirectional Mamba-enabled model (BM) constructs graphs among devices for each short time slot based on historical collaborations, aggregates device behavioral features within each slot, then uses a bidirectional Mamba model to integrate these short-term representations across all time intervals to produce stable long-term behavior evaluations.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that BM achieves higher evaluation accuracy than baseline methods, enabling the selection of collaborators that maximize the value of task completion.
AI.conclusion: The proposed bidirectional Mamba-enabled model effectively addresses the challenges of long-term device behavior evaluation by considering both forward and backward temporal dependencies, leading to more reliable collaborator selection for successful collaborative task completion.

title: ToST: A Tree-of-Thought Socratic Teaching Framework for Multi-Path Guidance and Parallel Thinking
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong problem-solving abilities, positioning them as promising agents for Socratic teaching to guide students through step-by-step heuristic questioning. However, existing approaches typically adopt a one-problem-one-solution paradigm, restricting the teaching guidance to a single linear reasoning path. This design limits instructional flexibility, weakens error recovery, and restricts students' ability to engage in parallel thinking to explore multiple valid solutions. To overcome these, we propose ToST, a Tree-of-Thought Socratic Teaching framework that explicitly supports multi-path guidance under a one-problem-multiple-solutions paradigm. ToST employs Parallel Sowing, a parallel-thinking-oriented questioning strategy to encourage students to approach problems from diverse perspectives, and a Multi-Path Adaptive Guidance mechanism to provide more robust and non-linear instructions across alternative solution trajectories. Concurrently, to fill the void in systematically evaluating such non-linear instructional capabilities, we advance the task of multi-path Socratic guidance by establishing MPSG-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark that includes a dataset of 31K multi-path teaching dialogues and a five-dimensional evaluation framework grounded in the SOLO (Structure of Observed Learning Outcomes) theory to assess parallel-thinking guidance. Experimental results demonstrate that ToST significantly enhances guidance success rates while empowering students to navigate and explore multiple solution paths more effectively under both automatic and human metrics.

AI.tldr: ToST is a Tree-of-Thought Socratic Teaching framework that enables multi-path guidance for students, moving beyond single-solution teaching approaches to support parallel thinking and multiple valid solutions through parallel questioning and adaptive guidance mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based Socratic teaching approaches use a one-problem-one-solution paradigm, which limits instructional flexibility, weakens error recovery, and restricts students' ability to engage in parallel thinking to explore multiple valid solutions.
AI.method: Proposes ToST framework with Parallel Sowing questioning strategy to encourage diverse perspectives and Multi-Path Adaptive Guidance mechanism for robust non-linear instructions. Also introduces MPSG-Bench benchmark with 31K multi-path teaching dialogues and five-dimensional evaluation framework based on SOLO theory.
AI.result: Experimental results show ToST significantly enhances guidance success rates while empowering students to navigate and explore multiple solution paths more effectively under both automatic and human metrics.
AI.conclusion: ToST framework successfully addresses limitations of single-path Socratic teaching by supporting multi-path guidance, enabling more flexible, robust instruction that better develops students' parallel thinking and problem-solving capabilities.

title: ShuttleArena: Interpretable Self-Play in Physics-Based Badminton
summary: Badminton is a compact but challenging domain for game AI: a player must choose a physically feasible shuttle trajectory, anticipate the opponent's interception, and recover to a court position whose value depends on the opponent's next response. The central challenge is that shot selection and recovery are not separable: the best recovery depends on the shot-induced opponent response, while the value of the shot depends on whether the hitter can cover the reply. This paper presents ShuttleArena, a physics-based singles badminton self-play environment that couples continuous shuttle flight, player interception, structured shot generation, and post-shot recovery. The policy uses role-conditioned outputs: a masked interception choice on receiver turns and a factorized hitter action over shot azimuth, shot elevation, shot speed, and recovery target, enabling interpretable tactical probes. Episodes are single rallies rather than full scored games, and training uses Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) self-play against a staged checkpoint opponent pool with sparse terminal rally-outcome rewards and a factor-specific recovery update. Evaluation with frozen checkpoint play, controlled tactical probes, recovery ablations, qualitative rollouts, and a human-data sanity check shows competitive improvement together with interpretable opponent-conditioned changes in shot geometry and recovery behavior. The learned policies produce recognizable badminton-like structure while also reflecting the abstractions of the simulator, and the recovery intervention shows that learned recovery behavior is competitively important. These results suggest that physics-based racket sports are a useful testbed for interactive digital entertainment AI because they require agents to coordinate execution, positioning, and opponent-relative tactical value.

AI.tldr: ShuttleArena: A physics-based badminton self-play environment with role-conditioned policies that learn shot selection and recovery coordination through PPO self-play, producing interpretable badminton-like tactical behavior.
AI.motivation: Badminton presents a challenging AI domain where shot selection and recovery are interdependent - the best recovery depends on opponent response to shots, while shot value depends on whether the hitter can cover the reply. Existing approaches often treat these as separable problems.
AI.method: Created ShuttleArena, a physics-based singles badminton environment with continuous shuttle flight, player interception, structured shot generation, and post-shot recovery. Uses role-conditioned policies: masked interception choice for receiver, factorized hitter action (shot azimuth, elevation, speed, recovery target). Trained with PPO self-play against staged checkpoint opponent pool, using sparse terminal rally-outcome rewards and factor-specific recovery updates.
AI.result: Learned policies show competitive improvement with interpretable opponent-conditioned changes in shot geometry and recovery behavior. Policies produce recognizable badminton-like structure while reflecting simulator abstractions. Recovery intervention demonstrates learned recovery behavior is competitively important.
AI.conclusion: Physics-based racket sports are a useful testbed for interactive digital entertainment AI because they require agents to coordinate execution, positioning, and opponent-relative tactical value. The approach successfully addresses the inseparable shot selection-recovery challenge in badminton.

title: LocalLSTC: A Long Short-Term Control Architecture for Locally Deployed GUI Agents
summary: Modern GUI-agent frameworks achieve strong desktop task performance with frontier API models, yet persistent control information often remains implicit in growing interaction trajectories. At each step, the planner reconstructs the active task stage, accumulated evidence, and runtime feedback before deciding the next action. This dependence becomes more pronounced under weaker local reasoning backbones. Across four representative state-of-the-art frameworks, replacing GPT-5 with Qwen3.5-9B reduces average OSWorld SR-100 from 60.9\% to 37.7\%. Trajectory annotation further identifies at least one control failure in 91.6\% of failed trajectories. To address this problem, we introduce LocalLSTC, a training-free architecture that organizes control by temporal scope, maintaining persistent cross-step state to guide short-term execution commitments. Long-Term Control maintains the active subgoal, subgoal-aligned evidence, and runtime feedback across interactions, while Short-Term Execution realizes bounded commitments for the current step. Long-to-Short Planning forms each commitment from persistent state, and Short-to-Long Control integrates execution outcomes back into that state for progress assessment, recovery, and termination. With Qwen3.6-27B, LocalLSTC reaches 64.7\% SR-100 on OSWorld and 65.3\% on WindowsAgentArena, outperforming the strongest prior local results on both benchmarks. Ablations further support contributions from mechanisms on both sides of execution. These findings identify temporal organization of control information as a distinct architectural dimension for locally deployed GUI agents.

AI.tldr: LocalLSTC: A training-free architecture for GUI agents that organizes control by temporal scope, maintaining persistent state to guide execution and improving performance on desktop tasks.
AI.motivation: Current GUI-agent frameworks with frontier API models show performance degradation when using weaker local reasoning models, as control information remains implicit in interaction trajectories. The dependence on reconstructing task state at each step becomes problematic with less capable models.
AI.method: Introduces LocalLSTC with dual components: Long-Term Control maintains persistent state (active subgoal, evidence, runtime feedback) across interactions, while Short-Term Execution handles bounded commitments for current steps. Long-to-Short Planning forms commitments from persistent state, and Short-to-Long Control integrates execution outcomes back for progress assessment.
AI.result: With Qwen3.6-27B, LocalLSTC achieves 64.7% SR-100 on OSWorld and 65.3% on WindowsAgentArena, outperforming prior local results. Performance drops significantly when replacing GPT-5 with weaker models, highlighting the importance of temporal control organization.
AI.conclusion: Temporal organization of control information is a crucial architectural dimension for locally deployed GUI agents, addressing the implicit control problem in growing interaction trajectories and enabling better performance with weaker reasoning models.

title: Neural-Bayesian Structure Learning for Discrete Choice Modeling
summary: Conventional discrete choice and machine learning models are estimated primarily from observational data and typically treat explanatory covariates as parallel inputs, providing no internal mechanism for determining how related attributes should adjust when one is deliberately changed. This paper proposes Neural-Bayesian Structure Learning (Neural-BSL), a framework coupling differentiable structure learning with random-utility-based discrete choice estimation in a single differentiable procedure. To prevent mutually exclusive choice outcome from distorting the recovered attribute structure, the observed choice is maintained outside the graph as an alternative-specific utility comparison, while the attribute structure and random-utility parameters are learned jointly. The learned structure enters the choice model through structure-weighted attribute interactions and provides the structural basis for propagating interventions through downstream attributes. An intervention is evaluated by updating the intervened attribute, propagating its model-implied downstream changes in topological order, and then recomputing utilities and choice probabilities. This yields both predicted mode-share responses and the associated changes in downstream traveler or trip attributes. We evaluate Neural-BSL using stated-preference data from Seoul and the revealed-preference data from London. Neural-BSL achieves predictive performance comparable to conventional benchmarks while recovering behaviorally coherent dependency structures. Across policy scenarios, propagating interventions through the learned structure changes the predicted redistribution across modes while exposing the downstream traveler and trip adjustments underlying those responses.

AI.tldr: Neural-BSL combines differentiable structure learning with discrete choice models to learn attribute relationships and propagate policy interventions through learned dependency structures.
AI.motivation: Conventional discrete choice and ML models treat covariates as parallel inputs without internal mechanisms to determine how related attributes should adjust when one is deliberately changed, limiting their ability to propagate policy interventions through attribute structures.
AI.method: Proposes Neural-BSL framework coupling differentiable structure learning with random-utility-based discrete choice estimation in a single differentiable procedure. Maintains observed choice outside the graph as alternative-specific utility comparison, learns attribute structure and random-utility parameters jointly, uses structure-weighted attribute interactions.
AI.result: Evaluated on Seoul stated-preference and London revealed-preference data. Achieves predictive performance comparable to conventional benchmarks while recovering behaviorally coherent dependency structures. Propagating interventions through learned structure changes predicted mode redistribution and exposes downstream traveler/trip adjustments.
AI.conclusion: Neural-BSL provides a framework that maintains predictive performance while enabling intervention propagation through learned attribute structures, offering insights into both mode-share responses and underlying traveler/trip attribute adjustments.

title: Choose Your Game Wisely: Measuring Game-Theoretic Structures in Real-World Vehicle Interactions
summary: Game-theoretic models provide principled frameworks for modeling vehicle interactions, but their underlying temporal assumptions have not been systematically examined against real-world driving behavior. In particular, it remains unclear how simultaneous, sequential, and asymmetric interaction structures can be measured from vehicle trajectories. This paper develops a trajectory-based interaction measurement framework to identify interaction events and quantify behavioral change onset, temporal organization, post-onset response dynamics, and ordering stability. The framework uses behavioral deviations to verify candidate interactions. We evaluate the framework on six real-world trajectory datasets, including INTERACTION, highD, inD, rounD, Waymo Open Motion, and nuPlan, covering diverse road geometries, traffic environments, and interaction types. The results show that concurrent and sequential behavioral changes both constitute substantial proportions of observed following, merging, and conflicting interactions. Among sequential interactions, stable ordering is more prevalent than alternating ordering, indicating that persistent asymmetric roles are a common interaction structure. Importantly, temporal precedence does not necessarily coincide with a measurable behavioral response, indicating that temporal ordering alone may not be sufficient to characterize behavioral dependence. These findings show that real-world interactions exhibit concurrent, sequential, and persistently ordered temporal structures. Different game-theoretic formulations are therefore better regarded as complementary modeling abstractions for different interaction regimes rather than as a universal structure governing all vehicle interactions.

AI.tldr: A framework for measuring real-world vehicle interaction temporal structures from trajectories reveals that interactions exhibit concurrent, sequential, and persistently ordered patterns, challenging game-theoretic assumptions.
AI.motivation: Game-theoretic models of vehicle interactions make temporal assumptions that haven't been systematically examined against real-world driving behavior. There's a lack of understanding about how to measure simultaneous, sequential, and asymmetric interaction structures from actual vehicle trajectory data.
AI.method: Developed a trajectory-based interaction measurement framework that identifies interaction events and quantifies: behavioral change onset, temporal organization, post-onset response dynamics, and ordering stability. The framework uses behavioral deviations to verify candidate interactions and was evaluated on six real-world trajectory datasets (INTERACTION, highD, inD, rounD, Waymo Open Motion, nuPlan) covering diverse road geometries and interaction types.
AI.result: Both concurrent and sequential behavioral changes constitute substantial proportions of observed following, merging, and conflicting interactions. Among sequential interactions, stable ordering (persistent asymmetric roles) is more prevalent than alternating ordering. Temporal precedence doesn't necessarily coincide with measurable behavioral responses, indicating temporal ordering alone may not be sufficient to characterize behavioral dependence.
AI.conclusion: Real-world vehicle interactions exhibit concurrent, sequential, and persistently ordered temporal structures. Different game-theoretic formulations should be viewed as complementary modeling abstractions for different interaction regimes rather than as universal structures governing all vehicle interactions.

title: Mitigating LLM sycophancy with RL-based fine-tuning: Bayesian Truth Serum approach
summary: Large language models (LLMs) frequently exhibit \emph{sycophancy}: they adapt their answers to a user's stated beliefs or preferences instead of reporting what they hold to be true, which lowers factual accuracy and can amplify misinformation. This paper proposes a methodology for mitigating sycophancy that employs the Bayesian Truth Serum (BTS), a peer-prediction mechanism, as the reward in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to fine-tune an LLM. BTS pays an answer for being \emph{surprisingly common}, that is, more frequent among respondents than those respondents themselves predicted. We treat a group of responses from a model for one question as those respondents, so the reward is a function of the model's own outputs and fine-tuning needs neither labels nor preference annotations. We prove that in the large-group limit a sycophantic response earns strictly lower expected reward than an honest one. We also prove that if the entire group agrees in advance on a symmetric answering rule, it cannot earn a higher information score than under truthful reporting. On our true/false benchmark the reference model's answer-flip rate under user pressure decreases from 23% to 4%, and its accuracy under that pressure increases from 80% to 93%. Our reward outperforms SMART and is comparable to synthetic-data fine-tuning and to pinpoint tuning, all three of which train on labels. It spends considerably more compute in exchange, which makes it suitable when labeled data is scarce. Peer Truth Serum, which also pays a premium for a rare answer but elicits no prediction report, reproduces the effect. A peer-prediction reward computed inside a single GRPO group therefore reduces sycophancy without labels, and comparing mechanisms suggests that the premium paid for a rarer answer drives the effect.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using Bayesian Truth Serum (BTS) as a reward signal in Group Relative Policy Optimization to reduce sycophancy in LLMs without requiring labeled data.
AI.motivation: LLMs frequently exhibit sycophancy - adapting answers to match user beliefs rather than reporting truth - which lowers factual accuracy and amplifies misinformation. Current methods require labeled data or preference annotations.
AI.method: The approach uses Bayesian Truth Serum (BTS), a peer-prediction mechanism that rewards answers that are "surprisingly common" (more frequent than predicted). This is implemented as the reward function in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), treating model responses as "respondents" and requiring neither labels nor preference annotations.
AI.result: The method reduces answer-flip rate under user pressure from 23% to 4% and increases accuracy under pressure from 80% to 93%. It outperforms SMART and is comparable to synthetic-data fine-tuning and pinpoint tuning, though with higher compute cost. Peer Truth Serum also shows similar effects.
AI.conclusion: A peer-prediction reward computed within a single GRPO group effectively reduces sycophancy without labels. The key mechanism appears to be the premium paid for rarer answers, suggesting this approach is suitable when labeled data is scarce despite higher compute requirements.

title: Repair or Resample? Rethinking Failure Debugging in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
summary: As large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MASs) are increasingly applied to long-horizon complex tasks, their reliability has emerged as the core bottleneck hindering their real-world deployment. Existing MAS debugging and repair methods typically rely on rerunning and resampling the entire execution trajectory. However, a fundamental question remains to be answered: do these methods causally repair MAS failures or merely stochastically repair by leveraging the randomness of LLM sampling? To evaluate the effectiveness of MAS repair methods, we introduce SymTrace, a controlled evaluation framework that records the MAS execution trajectory and establishes intervention anchors. During replay, it effectively reconstructs the execution before the anchor using recorded logs and only regenerates the downstream trajectory, thereby enabling the reliable reproduction of MAS failures. We further construct the dataset SymFail, comprising 536 human-annotated failure trajectories with graph-linked locations, categories, and trace evidence. Based on these foundations, we conduct a large-scale empirical study across three mainstream MAS frameworks. Our findings reveal that existing unguided rerun methods are highly unreliable, exhibiting low failure reproduction and repair rates (only 67.97% and 6.90%, respectively). Building upon these findings, we further explore the effectiveness of a symptom-driven intervention method, which successfully repairs 20.15% of the failed cases (a 191.89% improvement to state-of-the-art repair methods). This study aims to provide actionable insights for MAS debugging and repair research, paving the way for the robust deployment of multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: SymTrace introduces a controlled evaluation framework for debugging LLM-based multi-agent systems by enabling reliable failure reproduction through intervention anchors, revealing current methods are unreliable and proposing symptom-driven repairs.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based multi-agent systems are increasingly applied to complex tasks, their reliability becomes a critical bottleneck. Existing debugging methods rely on rerunning entire trajectories, but it's unclear whether they causally repair failures or just leverage randomness of LLM sampling.
AI.method: Introduces SymTrace framework that records MAS execution trajectories and establishes intervention anchors. During replay, it reconstructs execution before anchors using recorded logs and only regenerates downstream trajectories, enabling reliable failure reproduction. Also creates SymFail dataset with 536 human-annotated failure trajectories.
AI.result: Empirical study across three mainstream MAS frameworks shows existing unguided rerun methods are highly unreliable (only 67.97% failure reproduction and 6.90% repair rates). Symptom-driven intervention method successfully repairs 20.15% of failed cases (191.89% improvement over state-of-the-art).
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates the limitations of current MAS debugging approaches and shows that systematic, controlled evaluation with intervention anchors enables more reliable failure reproduction and repair, providing actionable insights for robust MAS deployment.

title: SHSP: Structure-Aware Hierarchical Solution Prediction for Mixed-Integer Linear Programming
summary: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) is a fundamental optimization paradigm in combinatorial optimization and has been widely applied across real-world domains. Due to its NP-hard nature, obtaining optimal solutions for large-scale or highly constrained MILP instances remains computationally prohibitive. Learning-based solution prediction has therefore emerged as a promising approach to provide high-quality variable assignment for solver acceleration. However, existing methods typically adopt a one-shot prediction paradigm that predicts the marginal probabilities of all variables simultaneously. As a result, the conditional dependencies among variables are only implicitly captured through message passing, with the burden of modeling the combinatorial structure falling entirely on the representational capacity of graph neural networks. To address this limitation, we propose the Structure-Aware Hierarchical Solution Prediction (SHSP) framework that replaces the parallel marginal decoding of one-shot methods with a novel hierarchical conditional decoding mechanism. Specifically, SHSP constructs a variable coupling graph from the constraint structure, decodes variables sequentially along a hierarchy of increasing coupling strength, and conditions each hierarchy on previously predicted assignments. To mitigate error accumulation during the decoding process, SHSP further incorporates a confidence-aware mask-and-repair mechanism to identify and correct unreliable intermediate predictions. We integrate SHSP with multiple learning-guided search methods, and evaluate it on four standard MILP benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that SHSP significantly outperforms existing one-shot prediction baselines, achieving a 54% average reduction in solution gap.

AI.tldr: SHSP is a hierarchical conditional decoding framework for MILP solution prediction that sequentially decodes variables along coupling strength hierarchies and uses mask-and-repair to correct errors, achieving 54% better solution quality than one-shot methods.
AI.motivation: Existing MILP solution prediction methods use one-shot prediction that predicts all variables simultaneously, which only implicitly captures variable dependencies through message passing and places heavy modeling burden on graph neural networks, limiting solution quality.
AI.method: SHSP constructs a variable coupling graph from constraint structure, decodes variables sequentially along hierarchies of increasing coupling strength (not parallel like one-shot methods), conditions each hierarchy on previously predicted assignments, and uses a confidence-aware mask-and-repair mechanism to identify and correct unreliable intermediate predictions.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on four standard MILP benchmarks shows SHSP significantly outperforms existing one-shot prediction baselines, achieving a 54% average reduction in solution gap when integrated with multiple learning-guided search methods.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical conditional decoding approach of SHSP effectively addresses the limitations of one-shot MILP solution prediction by explicitly modeling variable dependencies through sequential hierarchical prediction, leading to substantially improved solution quality for combinatorial optimization problems.

title: Formal, Executable and Explainable Runtime Monitoring of Spoken Air Traffic Control Operational Procedures
summary: Air traffic control procedures are executed through spoken exchanges between controllers and pilots. These interactions are essential to the safety of air transportation: failures in their execution can create severe operational hazards, as evidenced by past fatal accidents. Assessing whether an instruction has been followed requires relating what was said to the aircraft concerned, its state, and the obligations that pilots must meet. We present a runtime verification framework that monitors such procedures by checking controller-pilot exchanges, surveillance data, and onboard observations. The framework parses radio communications into events linked to the entities they concern and merges them with surveillance and onboard observations into a time-stamped trace. The ICAO-derived obligations as formalized as temporal formulas with explicit time bounds and evaluated over execution traces. Every violation is reported along with the breached obligations and the observations that support the verdict. With real traffic, the complete pipeline reaches an F1 of 0.85 against blind human-annotated violations; in 1,495 synthetic situations derived from two public corpora, the monitor logic returns the expected verdict in every case. In two historical accidents reconstructed from official investigation reports, the monitor identifies the same procedural deviations documented by the investigators.

AI.tldr: Runtime verification framework monitors air traffic control procedures by checking controller-pilot communications, surveillance data, and onboard observations against formalized ICAO obligations to detect safety violations.
AI.motivation: Air traffic control procedures rely on spoken exchanges that are critical for aviation safety, with past fatal accidents demonstrating severe consequences when these exchanges fail. Current methods for assessing instruction compliance are inadequate, requiring automated monitoring that can relate communications to aircraft state and obligations.
AI.method: Framework parses radio communications into events linked to entities, merges them with surveillance and onboard observations into time-stamped traces, and evaluates these against formalized ICAO-derived temporal formulas with explicit time bounds using runtime verification techniques.
AI.result: Achieved F1 score of 0.85 against human-annotated violations on real traffic; correctly identified violations in 1,495 synthetic situations from two public corpora; successfully detected procedural deviations in two reconstructed historical accidents matching official investigation findings.
AI.conclusion: The runtime verification framework effectively monitors air traffic control procedures, demonstrating high accuracy in detecting violations and potential for improving aviation safety by automating compliance checking and early warning of procedural deviations.

title: InsightSR: Refining Symbolic Regression Search Spaces via Parallel Semantic and Structural LLM Guidance
summary: Symbolic regression (SR) seeks to discover parsimonious mathematical laws from observational data, yet conventional approaches often struggle with the vast combinatorial search space of physically meaningful expressions. We present InsightSR, a framework that embeds Large Language Models (LLMs) as a guiding layer around the PySR genetic programming engine. Rather than relying on LLMs to generate expressions directly, InsightSR uses LLMs to progressively transform the search space itself through two complementary pathways: a Semantic Seed Pathway that proposes dimensionally consistent functional skeletons, and a Structural Feature Pathway that recommends nonlinear feature transformations. These transformations accumulate over iterations, broadening the input space and shifting the symbolic search from constructing deep expression trees over raw variables to assembling shallow trees over a rich, semantically informed feature set. A post-generation feedback loop evaluates candidates, categorizes features by their empirical utility, and refines the guidance for the next iteration, transforming the discovery process from open-ended generation into iterative, self-correcting refinement. Across three benchmarks, InsightSR achieves a 95% exact recovery rate on the Feynman benchmark and 80.18% accuracy on the LLM-SRBench LSR-Transform task, substantially outperforming state-of-the-art genetic programming and neural-symbolic methods while maintaining strong out-of-distribution generalization on real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: InsightSR integrates LLMs with genetic programming for symbolic regression, using LLMs to transform the search space rather than directly generate expressions, achieving state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Conventional symbolic regression approaches struggle with the vast combinatorial search space of physically meaningful expressions, limiting their effectiveness in discovering parsimonious mathematical laws from observational data.
AI.method: InsightSR embeds LLMs as a guiding layer around PySR genetic programming. It uses two pathways: 1) Semantic Seed Pathway for dimensionally consistent functional skeletons, and 2) Structural Feature Pathway for nonlinear feature transformations. The framework includes iterative refinement with post-generation feedback that evaluates candidates, categorizes features by utility, and refines guidance.
AI.result: Achieved 95% exact recovery rate on the Feynman benchmark and 80.18% accuracy on the LLM-SRBench LSR-Transform task, substantially outperforming state-of-the-art genetic programming and neural-symbolic methods while maintaining strong out-of-distribution generalization on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: InsightSR transforms symbolic regression from open-ended generation into iterative, self-correcting refinement by using LLMs to progressively transform the search space, resulting in significantly improved performance and generalization capabilities compared to existing methods.

title: How Robust Are Automated Fact-Checking Systems? A Cross-Benchmark Evaluation
summary: Automated fact-checking (AFC) systems retrieve evidence and predict claim veracity, yet evaluations omit simple baselines, systems are developed for a single benchmark and cannot be trusted to generalise across domains. No prior work cross-evaluates the full two-stage retrieve-then-verify pipeline across diverse datasets, complementing retrieval-only studies (Thakur et al., 2021) and single-stage benchmarking studies (Calamai et al., 2025). We benchmark nine models, ranging from random and sparse baselines to fine-tuned transformers, zero-shot LLMs, and the two highest-ranked systems from the AVeriTeC 2025 shared task, across four datasets spanning scientific, open-web, and climate domains. Three findings stand out: (1) on ClimateCheck claim-only and fine-tuned models outperform zero-shot LLM and top-performing AVeriTeC 2025 systems, highlighting that noisy evidence can degrade veracity prediction; (2) system rankings are strongly domain- and metric-dependent: the best model on SciFact (macro-F1 0.70) drops to 0.31 on ClimateCheck, while the AVeriTeC 2025 winner and runner-up swap rankings based on evaluation metrics and datasets; (3) replacing retrieved evidence with gold annotations improves veracity accuracy by 14-22 points across models, confirming retrieval remains primary bottleneck. We release code, pre-processed datasets, and all results to support reproducible AFC research.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks automated fact-checking systems across diverse domains, finding that performance varies significantly by domain and metric, retrieval quality remains the primary bottleneck, and simple baselines can outperform complex systems when evidence is noisy.
AI.motivation: Current automated fact-checking systems lack comprehensive cross-domain evaluation, with evaluations omitting simple baselines, systems being developed for single benchmarks, and inability to generalize across domains. No prior work cross-evaluates the full two-stage retrieve-then-verify pipeline across diverse datasets.
AI.method: Benchmarked nine models including random/sparse baselines, fine-tuned transformers, zero-shot LLMs, and top AVeriTeC 2025 systems across four datasets spanning scientific, open-web, and climate domains. Cross-evaluated the full retrieve-then-verify pipeline across diverse domains.
AI.result: Three key findings: 1) On ClimateCheck, claim-only and fine-tuned models outperform zero-shot LLMs and top AVeriTeC systems; 2) System rankings are strongly domain- and metric-dependent; 3) Replacing retrieved evidence with gold annotations improves veracity accuracy by 14-22 points across models, confirming retrieval is primary bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval quality remains the primary bottleneck in automated fact-checking systems, and performance varies significantly across domains and metrics. The authors release code, pre-processed datasets, and results to support reproducible AFC research, highlighting the need for better generalization and domain-agnostic systems.

title: Prefix-Denoising Consistency: Test-Time Verification for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently become increasingly competitive with autoregressive (AR) models, and even outperform them on certain tasks. Unlike AR models, DLMs produce output through iterative denoising without a left-to-right order. To further improve the performance of DLMs, we introduce PDC (\emph{Prefix-Denoising Consistency}), a test-time self-verification method for DLMs. PDC exploits a distinctive test-time signal in DLMs under prefix conditioned regeneration, correct trajectories are more stable and reproducible than incorrect ones. Concretely, given an initially generated sample, PDC splits the sentence at an intermediate position and regenerates the remaining tokens conditioned on the fixed prefix. Across mathematical reasoning and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, PDC consistently improves upon the initial sample, outperforms independent generations under a computational constrained comparison, and is robust to different unmasking strategies and parameter settings. These results highlight prefix-conditioned regeneration as an effective DLM-specific primitive for test-time verification.

AI.tldr: PDC is a test-time self-verification method for Diffusion Language Models that uses prefix-conditioned regeneration to distinguish correct from incorrect generations based on their stability and reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Despite Diffusion Language Models becoming competitive with autoregressive models, there's a need to further improve their performance. Unlike AR models, DLMs produce output through iterative denoising without left-to-right order, which provides opportunities for DLM-specific improvement methods that exploit their unique generation characteristics.
AI.method: PDC (Prefix-Denoising Consistency) works by: 1) Taking an initially generated sample, 2) Splitting it at an intermediate position, 3) Regenerating the remaining tokens conditioned on the fixed prefix, 4) Comparing the stability and reproducibility of trajectories - correct trajectories show more consistency during this prefix-conditioned regeneration process.
AI.result: PDC consistently improves upon initial samples, outperforms independent generations under computational constraints, and shows robustness to different unmasking strategies and parameter settings across mathematical reasoning and commonsense reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Prefix-conditioned regeneration is an effective DLM-specific primitive for test-time verification, exploiting unique test-time signals in DLMs where correct trajectories are more stable and reproducible than incorrect ones.

title: Activation-Space Order-Swap Geometry: A Site-Asymmetry Audit
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures. Under review at the NeurReps Proceedings Track
summary: Order-dependent activation statistics are often interpreted as evidence of interaction, but that interpretation can be confounded by where interventions enter the network. We introduce a no-fit site-asymmetry audit. For a twice-differentiable readout, the open-path order-swap decomposes into a canonical additive response measured by single interventions and an antisymmetrized second difference free of first-order and pure self-curvature terms to second order. Across six open-weight language-model families, the single-intervention baseline explains 84.3-97.7 percent of the bracket norm (mean 93.7 percent), while the no-interaction self-curvature term is 1.8-5.2 times larger than the corrected residual in the two families with the plus/minus injection split. The corrected residual clears a generic-interaction null in three of six families under a confound-free prompt split and two of six after configuration robustness. A known-positive surrogate recovers planted mixed interaction, while a matched site-separation test changes the baseline share and a random architecture reproduces the first-order regime. The same estimator transfers to released non-language references: trained residual fractions fall below a fixed Gaussian-direction null in 11/12 contrasts (5/6 ViT-B/16, 6/6 ResNet-50), a portability check rather than pooled evidence. The contribution is a reusable measurement criterion: run the single-intervention baseline before reading an order-swap vector as interaction or geometric structure; if it explains the vector, form the second difference instead. All claims are scoped to activation-space interventions at distinct sites; we do not claim that representation geometry is globally Abelian.

AI.tldr: Paper introduces a no-fit site-asymmetry audit to separate genuine interaction effects from single-intervention baselines in activation statistics, showing that single interventions explain most order-swap variance in language models.
AI.motivation: Order-dependent activation statistics are often misinterpreted as evidence of interaction when they could be confounded by where interventions enter the network. Need to distinguish between genuine interaction effects and baseline effects from single interventions.
AI.method: Introduces a no-fit site-asymmetry audit with open-path order-swap decomposition into canonical additive response (single interventions) and antisymmetrized second difference free of first-order and pure self-curvature terms. Tests across six language-model families and other architectures (ViT-B/16, ResNet-50).
AI.result: Single-intervention baseline explains 84.3-97.7% of bracket norm (mean 93.7%) across language models. Corrected residual clears generic-interaction null in 3/6 families with confound-free prompt split. Method transfers to other architectures where trained residual fractions fall below Gaussian-direction null in 11/12 contrasts.
AI.conclusion: Provides reusable measurement criterion: first run single-intervention baseline before interpreting order-swap vectors as interaction; if baseline explains vector, use second difference instead. Claims are scoped to activation-space interventions at distinct sites, not claiming global Abelian representation geometry.

title: LivingRAG: Augmenting Graph RAG with Experience
summary: Graph-based RAG improves multi-hop question answering by organizing evidence as a knowledge graph.
