We instead compose the observables' likelihoods in per-task free-routed last-layer beliefs on a shared backbone; this absorbs unit-dependent loss scaling into likelihood parameters learned in the same gradient pass. Stochastic dynamics supply what static benchmarks cannot: computable ground truth for the predictive variance. Results land where theory puts them: on the well-specified, homoscedastic Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process the learned predictive law recovers the analytic kernel and correctly specified baselines tie. On heteroscedastic systems (stochastic Lorenz-63, real air-quality data) the belief's input-dependent variance separates: best single-run NLL on the state and regime tasks, calibration matched only by arms whose NLL it beats, at a fraction of the tuned grids' cost. On the real series the state margin holds across five rolling origins.

AI.tldr: A novel multi-task learning framework for stochastic dynamical systems that composes observable likelihoods through per-task free-routed last-layer beliefs on a shared backbone, achieving superior performance on heteroscedastic systems with efficient learning.
AI.motivation: Standard multi-task learning approaches balance per-task losses through tuning or learning, but forecasting stochastic dynamical systems requires predicting multiple observables (future state, threshold events, regime labels) each with its own likelihood. The authors seek a more principled approach that can handle heteroscedastic uncertainty and provide calibrated predictions.
AI.method: Proposes composing observable likelihoods through per-task free-routed last-layer beliefs on a shared backbone architecture. The method absorbs unit-dependent loss scaling into likelihood parameters learned in the same gradient pass. Leverages stochastic dynamics to provide computable ground truth for predictive variance, which static benchmarks cannot offer.
AI.result: On well-specified homoscedastic systems (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process), the method recovers the analytic kernel and ties with correctly specified baselines. On heteroscedastic systems (stochastic Lorenz-63 and real air-quality data), achieves best single-run negative log-likelihood on state and regime tasks with calibration matched only by methods it outperforms. Maintains performance across five rolling origins on real data at a fraction of tuned grid search costs.
AI.conclusion: The free-routed belief composition approach provides an efficient, well-calibrated multi-task learning framework for stochastic dynamical systems that naturally handles heteroscedastic uncertainty while avoiding costly hyperparameter tuning procedures.

title: One Symptom, Three Levers: A Critical Review of On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation trains a language model on its own generations while a teacher scores them token by token. It combines the dense supervision of imitation learning with the on-policy sampling of reinforcement learning. But it requires a second, larger model to act as teacher. On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) removes that cost. The teacher is the model itself, conditioned on privileged information the student will not have at test time, such as a reference solution, a plan, or environment feedback. The teacher is no stronger than the student, only better informed. Early results were promising, with accuracy comparable to reinforcement learning at a fraction of the generated tokens. But the same asymmetry that produces the signal also biases it. One failure mode now dominates the field: collapse, the progressive narrowing of the set of reasoning paths the model can produce. Collapse is not specific to OPSD, though privileged information aggravates it. This review treats collapse as a symptom governed by three levers: (i) where the signal is applied, that is, how tokens are weighted; (ii) what the teacher is shown, that is, the nature of the privileged information; and (iii) when the signal changes, that is, the teacher's dynamics and the decay of guidance. We restrict our scope to mathematical reasoning, where the method originated and where its failure modes are best documented. We report no new experiments. The contribution is structural: a shared vocabulary for phenomena named differently across papers, and a clear line between what is settled and what is still disputed.

AI.tldr: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) is a method where a language model trains on its own generations using privileged information as a teacher signal, avoiding the need for a larger teacher model but suffering from collapse - progressive narrowing of reasoning paths.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to combine the benefits of imitation learning (dense supervision) and reinforcement learning (on-policy sampling) without requiring a larger, expensive teacher model as in traditional on-policy distillation methods.
AI.method: OPSD uses the model itself as teacher by conditioning it on privileged information (reference solutions, plans, environment feedback) that the student won't have at test time. The teacher isn't stronger than student, just better informed.
AI.result: Early results showed comparable accuracy to reinforcement learning with far fewer generated tokens. However, the method suffers from collapse - progressive narrowing of reasoning paths. The review identifies three key levers controlling collapse: token weighting, privileged information nature, and teacher signal dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The main contribution is structural: providing shared vocabulary for phenomena across different papers and clarifying what's settled vs. disputed about OPSD, particularly focusing on mathematical reasoning where collapse is best documented.

title: Quantum-Inspired Modeling of Driving Behavior
comment: 44 pages (including Appendices), 27 figures. Submitted to Transportation Research Part B: Methodological. Code and toolkit: https://github.com/mselayan/quantum-driver-representation
summary: Driver behavior is heterogeneous, context-dependent, and changes over time, and these properties shape the traffic phenomena we observe. Most models, however, fix in advance which behavioral variables interact and how. Behavior outside that form is absorbed as noise, while models flexible enough to capture it tend to lose interpretability. We introduce a quantum-inspired representation of driver behavior that combines properties usually treated separately or in part: it is continuous, probabilistic, context-dependent, history-dependent, and represents interactions among behavioral variables as learned from data. Each driver is encoded as an evolving density matrix, providing a unified representation of behavioral uncertainty, temporal evolution, and context-dependent behavioral variation. Trained without supervision on the I-24 MOTION dataset, the framework recovers three interpretable driving profiles representing three regimes: free flow, transition, and congestion. The profiles capture the behavioral range of the data and the smooth transitions drivers make between regimes as conditions change. The same representation also reproduces known macroscopic phenomena, aligning with the fundamental diagram and reproducing hysteresis loops. We also show how the representation supports practical use: it supplies context-dependent parameters to classical car-following models, and gives an autonomous vehicle a live behavioral read of the surrounding drivers with a short-horizon forecast of their motion. The framework points toward models of traffic that are interpretable and trustworthy by construction. We release an open-source toolkit on GitHub (https://github.com/mselayan/quantum-driver-representation) spanning data processing, training, inference, and analysis.

AI.tldr: Quantum-inspired representation of driver behavior using evolving density matrices captures continuous, probabilistic, context-dependent, and history-dependent aspects of driving, enabling interpretable profiles that align with traffic phenomena.
AI.motivation: Driver behavior is heterogeneous, context-dependent, and changes over time, but most models fix behavioral interactions in advance, treating deviations as noise. Flexible models lose interpretability, creating a need for a unified representation that maintains interpretability while capturing complex behavioral dynamics.
AI.method: Introduces a quantum-inspired representation encoding each driver as an evolving density matrix, trained unsupervised on the I-24 MOTION dataset. This continuous, probabilistic representation captures behavioral uncertainty, temporal evolution, and context-dependent variation, learning interactions among behavioral variables from data.
AI.result: The framework recovers three interpretable driving profiles corresponding to free flow, transition, and congestion regimes. It captures behavioral range and smooth transitions between regimes, aligns with fundamental diagrams, reproduces hysteresis loops, and provides practical applications including context-dependent parameters for classical models and live behavioral reads for autonomous vehicles.
AI.conclusion: The quantum-inspired framework enables interpretable and trustworthy traffic models by construction, providing a unified representation of driver behavior that bridges microscopic individual behavior with macroscopic traffic phenomena, with open-source implementation available for wider adoption.

title: DualOPSD: Adaptive Privileged Teachers for On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses a privileged copy of the student model to provide dense supervision without an external teacher. OPSD keeps this privileged teacher fixed, even though the student distribution and output style change during training. We propose DualOPSD, an asymmetric alternating framework that adapts both policies. The student first learns from the privileged teacher. The teacher then moves toward the updated student distribution on the same student trajectory. This update makes later supervision responsive to the learner and does not require another rollout. On Qwen3-8B in non-thinking mode, DualOPSD improves avg@12 over OPSD by 23.61, 13.89, and 10.00 points on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025. Results at 1.7B and 4B show that the accuracy gain depends on model scale. Across all three scales, DualOPSD reduces truncation. The 4B diagnostic also shows lower KL in both directions between the teacher and student.

AI.tldr: DualOPSD enhances self-distillation by making teacher supervision responsive to the student's evolving distribution through an alternating update framework, achieving substantial performance improvements across multiple benchmarks and model scales.
AI.motivation: Traditional on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) keeps the privileged teacher fixed throughout training, despite changes in student distribution and output style during learning, limiting the effectiveness of supervision.
AI.method: Proposes DualOPSD, an asymmetric alternating framework where: 1) The student learns from a privileged teacher, 2) The teacher then moves toward the updated student distribution on the same student trajectory without requiring additional rollouts, enabling supervision responsive to the learner's current state.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B in non-thinking mode, DualOPSD improves average performance by 23.61, 13.89, and 10.00 points over OPSD on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 benchmarks. Results at 1.7B and 4B scales show accuracy gains depend on model scale, with DualOPSD reducing truncation across all scales and showing lower KL divergence in both directions between teacher and student at 4B scale.
AI.conclusion: DualOPSD introduces an effective asymmetric alternating framework that improves upon traditional on-policy self-distillation by dynamically adapting both student and teacher policies, leading to significant performance gains across multiple model scales and benchmarks.

title: How Much Rank Does LoRA Need? Rank-Error Bounds for Transformer Attention
summary: Choosing the rank of a low-rank adaptation (LoRA) update is usually an empirical task. In this paper, we provide a task-dependent theory of the approximation error achievable at each LoRA rank for Transformer attention. We fix a pretrained attention head, a target attention function, and a distribution over inputs from the downstream task, and bound the smallest expected Kullback--Leibler (KL) error achievable by a rank-$r$ query LoRA update. When target attention probabilities are bounded away from zero, we prove a lower bound of the error proportional to $ψ(\|d\|_2)$, where $d$ is the difference between candidate and target attention scores and $ψ(t)=\min\{t^2,t\}$. We also prove an unconditional upper bound $\min\{\|d\|_2^2/4,\sqrt2\|d\|_2\}$. Under explicit realizability, geometry, and moment conditions, we then bound the best rank-$r$ error between an explicit multiple of $ψ(\sqrt{T_r})$ and $\min\{T_r/4,\sqrt{2T_r}\}$, where $T_r$ is the downstream-weighted tail energy of the target update. We also provide target-Fisher bounds when candidate scores remain within a fixed range of the target scores, and an unrestricted lower bound when a subset of tokens carries most of the probability mass. These spectral bounds describe finite-score approximation. We then construct explicit families in which softmax saturation makes the rank required to match the attention function strictly smaller than the rank required to match the finite logits. Finally, we extend the analysis to fused multi-head LoRA and joint query/key updates, exposing the effects of rank sharing and query/key factorization constraints.

AI.tldr: Theoretical analysis of LoRA rank selection for Transformer attention, providing task-dependent bounds on approximation error and showing that softmax saturation allows lower ranks to match attention functions than logits.
AI.motivation: Choosing LoRA rank is usually empirical; this paper aims to provide theoretical foundations for task-dependent rank selection in Transformer attention, analyzing approximation errors and practical implications.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis with lower/upper bounds on KL error for rank-r LoRA updates, examining conditions like target probabilities bounded away from zero, explicit realizability/geometry conditions, softmax saturation effects, and extensions to multi-head LoRA and joint query/key updates.
AI.result: Proved error bounds proportional to ψ(‖d‖₂) for target attention with non-zero probabilities; under specific conditions, bounded rank-r error between explicit multiples of ψ(√Tᵣ) and min{Tᵣ/4,√2Tᵣ}; showed softmax saturation reduces required rank compared to matching logits; extended analysis to multi-head settings.
AI.conclusion: Provides first theoretical framework for LoRA rank selection in attention, showing task-dependent bounds and that softmax saturation enables practical rank reduction, with implications for multi-head LoRA design and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

title: When Pruning Meets Interpretability: Preserving Sparse Autoencoder Robustness in LLMs
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to interpret the internal representations of large language models (LLMs), yet their reliability under post-hoc model compression remains poorly understood. We present a systematic study of how pruning affects SAE behavior and theoretically show that, for a fixed SAE, its impact is governed by perturbation energy, a covariance-weighted norm. This perspective exposes a key limitation of magnitude pruning: by ignoring activation geometry, it distorts the learned representation space and degrades SAE functionality. Activation-aware methods such as Wanda and SparseGPT, in contrast, implicitly control perturbation energy and are therefore substantially more robust at preserving SAE behavior. We further reveal a consistent structural vulnerability across all pruning methods: middle layers are significantly more sensitive to pruning than early or late layers. Guided by this insight, we propose a layer-wise sparsity allocation strategy, achieving lower perplexity under the same average pruning sparsity. Experiments across four model architectures validate our theoretical findings. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/osu-srml/sae-robustness-under-pruning/tree/main.

AI.tldr: SAEs are used to interpret LLMs, but their reliability after model compression is unclear. The paper shows pruning affects SAEs through perturbation energy, magnitude pruning distorts representations while activation-aware methods preserve them better, and middle layers are most vulnerable to pruning.
AI.motivation: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are important tools for interpreting large language models (LLMs), but there's limited understanding of how reliable they remain after model compression techniques like pruning are applied. The paper aims to systematically study how different pruning methods affect SAE behavior and functionality.
AI.method: The authors present theoretical analysis showing pruning's impact on SAEs is governed by "perturbation energy" - a covariance-weighted norm. They compare different pruning methods (magnitude pruning vs. activation-aware methods like Wanda and SparseGPT), conduct experiments across four model architectures, and develop a layer-wise sparsity allocation strategy based on discovered structural vulnerabilities.
AI.result: Magnitude pruning distorts learned representation space and degrades SAE functionality, while activation-aware methods implicitly control perturbation energy and preserve SAE behavior better. Middle layers are consistently more sensitive to pruning than early or late layers. The proposed layer-wise sparsity allocation achieves lower perplexity under the same average pruning sparsity.
AI.conclusion: The reliability of SAEs under model compression depends on the pruning method used and layer-wise sensitivity patterns. Activation-aware pruning methods are more robust for preserving SAE behavior, and careful layer-wise sparsity allocation can improve model performance under pruning while maintaining interpretability tools.

title: ICON Decomposition: Multivariate Concept-Level Explanations of Deep Representations for Model Auditing
comment: 44 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Includes Extended Data (7 figures, 2 tables). Code: https://github.com/RoshanRane/ICON_decomposition
summary: Deep neural networks often exploit spurious associations in their training data, a failure known as shortcut learning. Concept-based explainability methods screen for shortcuts by testing whether concepts such as a patient's sex or scanner settings can be decoded from a network layer. Because each concept is evaluated in isolation, these methods can mistake correlations between concepts as evidence that the model uses them. We introduce ICON decomposition, which instead quantifies how much of a layer's variance each concept explains after accounting for all other concepts and the outcome. On synthetic data with known ground truth, ICON recovers concept importance more accurately than seven alternative baseline methods. On skin-lesion and brain-imaging models, it isolates the concepts on which a model genuinely relies, quantifies the representation unexplained by any of the supplied concepts, and yields sparse explanations that we validate by retraining and out-of-distribution testing.

AI.tldr: ICON decomposition is a new explainability method that accurately quantifies how much each concept contributes to a neural network layer's variance after accounting for other concepts, preventing false attribution due to correlations between concepts.
AI.motivation: Current concept-based explainability methods have a critical flaw: they evaluate concepts in isolation, which can mistake correlations between concepts as evidence that the model actually uses them. This is problematic because deep neural networks often learn spurious associations (shortcut learning), and we need accurate methods to detect which concepts models genuinely rely on.
AI.method: The authors introduce ICON decomposition, which quantifies how much of a layer's variance each concept explains after accounting for all other concepts and the outcome. This differs from existing methods that evaluate concepts individually without considering inter-concept correlations.
AI.result: On synthetic data with known ground truth, ICON recovered concept importance more accurately than seven alternative baseline methods. On real-world skin-lesion and brain-imaging models, ICON successfully isolated the concepts on which models genuinely rely, quantified the representation unexplained by any supplied concepts, and produced sparse explanations that were validated through retraining and out-of-distribution testing.
AI.conclusion: ICON decomposition provides a more accurate approach for detecting shortcut learning and understanding what concepts neural networks actually use, addressing the limitations of existing concept-based explainability methods by properly accounting for correlations between concepts.

title: Spectral Allocation: Why Muon Outperforms Adam, and How to Improve Muon
summary: Orthogonal optimisers such as Muon can substantially accelerate large language model pretraining relative to Adam, yet the mechanism remains incompletely understood. We investigate this through an out-of-sample spectral probing analysis of Transformer loss landscapes. At checkpoints along real training trajectories, we decompose each momentum buffer into its singular directions and estimate the loss-optimal step size along each direction on held-out data. The resulting spectral profile is anisotropic yet stable across batches and training stages, and consistent across the optimisers and model scales: a volatile head operating at the Edge-of-Stability supports a much smaller step size than the tolerant bulk, which permits substantially larger steps. This profile provides a unified spectral allocation account of why Muon outperforms Adam, which outperforms SGD. It also exposes a limitation of Muon's uniform scaling: it still underutilises the bulk. Guided by this finding, we introduce Spectral-Aware Muon (SAMuon), which holds the head at the Muon scale and amplifies the bulk using a static spectral prior. We provide two variants: the complete SAMuon follows the measured profile using a low-rank randomised SVD and the simplified SAMuon-lite uses a two-level approximation via rank-one power iteration. Neither method adds persistent optimiser state or notable extra FLOPs beyond Muon at scale, and the idealised exact-whitening versions of both retain Muon's asymptotic convergence rate under standard assumptions. Across "modded-nanogpt" models from 124M to 1B parameters, both variants outperform tuned AdamW and Muon (Scion implementation) baselines in all evaluated model-scale and batch-size configurations. SAMuon requires 13.3% to 24.0% fewer training tokens to reach the same validation loss as Muon, while SAMuon-lite retains most of this gain with near-zero wall-clock overhead.

AI.tldr: SAMuon optimizes LLM pretraining by using spectral analysis to allocate different step sizes to different singular directions of the loss landscape, outperforming both Adam and Muon.
AI.motivation: While orthogonal optimizers like Muon accelerate LLM pretraining over Adam, the mechanism is poorly understood. Existing methods like Muon use uniform scaling which may underutilize certain directions in the loss landscape.
AI.method: The paper conducts spectral probing analysis to decompose momentum buffers into singular directions and estimate optimal step sizes. Based on finding that different directions have different optimal step sizes (volatile head vs tolerant bulk), they propose Spectral-Aware Muon (SAMuon) which applies different scaling: holding the head at Muon scale while amplifying the bulk using a static spectral prior. Two variants: SAMuon (using low-rank randomized SVD) and SAMuon-lite (two-level approximation via rank-one power iteration).
AI.result: Spectral analysis reveals a stable anisotropic profile across batches, training stages, optimizers and model scales. SAMuon outperforms both AdamW and Muon across 124M to 1B parameter models, requiring 13.3-24.0% fewer training tokens than Muon. SAMuon-lite retains most gains with near-zero overhead. Both variants improve in all evaluated model-scale and batch-size configurations.
AI.conclusion: Spectral allocation explains optimizer performance differences (Muon > Adam > SGD). The proposed SAMuon variants exploit this insight by adapting step sizes to different spectral components, achieving superior efficiency without adding significant computational overhead, offering practical improvements for LLM pretraining.

title: TraceML: An Empirical Analysis of Human-Agent Planning in Machine Learning Development
summary: Large language models write correct code for isolated problems but remain far weaker at autonomous machine-learning development, where an agent must revise data pipelines, models, and validation over hours of feedback, and on most competitions still finishes below strong human competitors. Outcome-based benchmarks record this gap but not its cause, because they grade the final submission and discard the development process behind it. We introduce TraceML, which pairs human and agent work on the same competitions under one version-level schema: 4,465 human Kaggle trajectories across 134 competitions, seven of which are also worked by two agent scaffolds, giving 430 paired human and 207 agent trajectories. Every code version carries its score, its timestamp, and labels for the action taken, its intent, the edit size, and the score effect. Read this way, the gap becomes concrete. Experts alternate data work, validation, model changes, and ensembling, and return to approaches they had set aside. Each agent scaffold instead collapses into a narrow loop: Codex spends its steps re-weighting ensembles and tuning submissions, MLEvolve mutates its model in place, and neither pivots at the human rate nor reopens abandoned work. A short planning prompt distilled from human practice moves the behaviors it names toward the human profile and lifts scores, but the effort profile stays agent-shaped: instruction closes only the part of the gap that reduces to instructions. We release the corpus, the schema, the labelers, and the extraction pipeline at https://huggingface.co/datasets/jerryyan/TraceML.

AI.tldr: TraceML introduces a dataset and schema to compare human vs AI agent machine learning development processes on Kaggle competitions, revealing fundamental differences in how humans vs agents approach iterative coding and problem-solving.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs generate correct code for isolated problems but perform poorly at autonomous ML development requiring iterative refinement over hours. Outcome-based benchmarks only measure final results, not the development process causing the performance gap.
AI.method: TraceML pairs human and agent work on same Kaggle competitions using a version-level schema: 4,465 human trajectories across 134 competitions, with 430 paired human and 207 agent trajectories. Each code version includes score, timestamp, action labels (action taken, intent, edit size, score effect). Two agent scaffolds (Codex and MLEvolve) were tested.
AI.result: Experts alternate diverse activities (data work, validation, model changes, ensembling, revisiting abandoned approaches), while agents collapse into narrow loops: Codex re-weights ensembles/tunes submissions, MLEvolve mutates models in place. Planning prompts based on human practices improve scores but can't replicate human's flexible effort profile.
AI.conclusion: The ML development gap stems from fundamental differences in how humans vs agents approach iterative problem-solving. While instructions can close parts of the gap, agents fundamentally lack humans' ability to pivot, revisit abandoned work, and balance diverse development activities organically.

title: Robust CurveMoE: Multi-Norm Adversarial Defense for Mixture-of-Experts Models via Mode Connectivity
summary: Multi-norm adversarial defense aims to protect neural networks against perturbations defined by different norm constraints, but existing methods typically optimize competing robustness objectives within a single parameter configuration, leading to substantial training cost and unfavorable robustness trade-offs. We propose Robust CurveMoE, an efficient mixture-of-experts framework that connects models specialized for different perturbation norms through a low-loss path and exploits the complementary robustness profiles of models along this path. Robust CurveMoE derives clean and norm-specialized experts from robustness-constrained curve locations and selectively expertizes only influential layers, while sharing the remaining parameters across routing paths. To further reduce curve-construction cost, we introduce contribution-guided partial updating, which selects influential curve parameters using initialization-based gradient scores. We also theoretically bound the objective gap between partial and full curve optimization. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100 with WideResNet and Vision Transformer architectures show that Robust CurveMoE consistently improves clean, norm-specific, and Union accuracy over MSD and ERMC. In particular, it improves Union accuracy by 2.37 and 2.13 percentage points over the strongest baseline on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100, respectively. Extensive ablations further validate the effectiveness of partial updating, selective expertization, and robustness-constrained expert selection.

AI.tldr: Robust CurveMoE is a mixture-of-experts framework that efficiently defends against multi-norm adversarial attacks by connecting specialized models through a low-loss curve, using selective expertization and partial parameter updates.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-norm adversarial defense methods typically optimize competing robustness objectives within a single parameter configuration, leading to high training costs and suboptimal robustness trade-offs.
AI.method: Proposes Robust CurveMoE: 1) connects norm-specialized models via a low-loss curve, 2) selectively expertizes only influential layers while sharing remaining parameters, 3) introduces contribution-guided partial updating for efficient curve construction, 4) theoretically bounds optimization gaps.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100 with WideResNet and Vision Transformers, Robust CurveMoE consistently improves clean, norm-specific, and Union accuracy over baselines (MSD and ERMC). Achieves 2.37% and 2.13% Union accuracy improvements on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100 respectively.
AI.conclusion: Robust CurveMoE provides an efficient and effective framework for multi-norm adversarial defense with improved robustness trade-offs and reduced training costs through selective expertization and partial curve optimization.

title: Group-Shared Low-Rank Approximation for Mobile-Efficient Pointwise Convolutions in Large-Kernel CNNs
summary: Large-kernel Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) deliver remarkable performance in vision tasks by significantly expanding receptive fields, yet their quadratic parameter growth critically impedes storage-efficient edge deployment. While existing efficient architectures adopt parameter-efficient depthwise separable convolution backbones that leverage techniques like low-rank approximation and weight sharing to compress depthwise convolutions, we identify a critical oversight: pointwise convolutions dominate parameter volume (>87% in models like RepLKNet-31B) and constitute the primary deployment bottleneck on resource-constrained edge devices. This results in prohibitive storage costs and severe memory-loading constraints on resource-limited devices (e.g., smartphones with 4-12 GB Random Access Memory (RAM)). To overcome this, we propose Channel Group-Shared (CGS) low-rank approximation, a novel Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)-based parameter-sharing strategy. CGS constructs a structured low-rank paradigm isomorphic to SVD decomposition, comprising shared (high-parameter-cost) down/up-projection matrices across channel groups within a layer and channel-group-specific (low-parameter-cost) scalable diagonal matrices. This group-sharing design achieves significant parameter reduction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that large-kernel CNNs (RepLKNet, ConvNeXt, SLaK) enhanced with CGS strike an empirically favorable balance between competitive performance and substantially reduced storage costs. Crucially, by alleviating storage constraints, reducing memory bandwidth pressure during loading, and minimizing model loading latency, CGS enables the feasible deployment of pre-trained large-kernel CNN models on edge devices, thereby bridging the gap between high-performance vision models and practical edge deployment.

AI.tldr: CGS (Channel Group-Shared) low-rank approximation reduces parameter count in large-kernel CNNs by sharing projection matrices across channel groups, enabling efficient edge deployment without significant performance loss.
AI.motivation: Large-kernel CNNs deliver excellent performance but suffer from quadratic parameter growth, making them impractical for edge deployment due to storage constraints. While existing methods compress depthwise convolutions, they overlook that pointwise convolutions dominate parameter volume (over 87% in models like RepLKNet-31B), creating deployment bottlenecks on resource-constrained devices with limited RAM.
AI.method: CGS uses Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)-based parameter sharing with a structured low-rank paradigm: shared down/up-projection matrices across channel groups within layers (high parameter cost) combined with channel-group-specific scalable diagonal matrices (low parameter cost). This group-sharing design significantly reduces parameters.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show large-kernel CNNs (RepLKNet, ConvNeXt, SLaK) enhanced with CGS achieve competitive performance with substantially reduced storage costs. CGS alleviates storage constraints, reduces memory bandwidth pressure during loading, and minimizes model loading latency.
AI.conclusion: CGS enables feasible deployment of pre-trained large-kernel CNN models on edge devices by bridging the gap between high-performance vision models and practical edge deployment through efficient parameter reduction and storage optimization.

title: Agentic Autoresearch for Cell-Edge Power Control: Radically Redefining the Researcher's Role
summary: Designing machine learning algorithms for wireless resource management is labour-intensive: the architecture, the loss function and the training recipe are all specified by hand. We demonstrate that this design layer can be surrendered to an autonomous agent in its entirety. We adopt the autoresearch protocol, in which an AI coding agent edits a training script, runs a fixed-budget experiment, and retains or discards the change according to a single immutable metric. We grant the agent authority over the architecture family, the input representation, the output parameterization, the loss function and the task-sampling law, and set it a target chosen for its difficulty: sum-least-percentile-rate power control across a multicell network. The formulation targets cell-edge throughput and is non-convex, non-smooth and strongly NP-hard away from its max-min vertex. Safeguards render the results trustworthy: a hash-pinned evaluator, an enforced inference contract and a pre-registered falsifier per experiment. In eighty-one unattended experiments over twenty-six hours, the agent reached $99.5\%$ of a converged minorization-maximization reference in one fixed-cost inference pass, at roughly $600\times$ lower inference cost, closing $94\%$ of the gap from its first working architecture, with one parameter set serving every network size and percentile target. It recovered provable structure rather than tuned constants: the output parameterization it discovered reproduces the exact max-min-optimal allocation at the minimum percentile, for every value of the trained weights.

AI.tldr: An autonomous AI agent designs wireless power control algorithms through automated code editing and experimentation, achieving near-optimal performance with significantly lower inference cost compared to conventional methods.
AI.motivation: Manual design of machine learning algorithms for wireless resource management is labor-intensive and requires expertise in architecture, loss functions, and training recipes. The paper aims to automate this entire design process using AI agents.
AI.method: Uses the autoresearch protocol where an AI coding agent edits training scripts, runs fixed-budget experiments, and retains/discards changes based on a single immutable metric. The agent controls architecture family, input representation, output parameterization, loss function, and task-sampling law. Safeguards include hash-pinned evaluator, enforced inference contract, and pre-registered falsifier per experiment.
AI.result: In 81 unattended experiments over 26 hours, the agent reached 99.5% of a converged minorization-maximization reference in one fixed-cost inference pass, with roughly 600× lower inference cost. It closed 94% of the gap from its first working architecture, with one parameter set serving every network size and percentile target. The agent discovered provable structure rather than tuned constants.
AI.conclusion: The design layer for wireless resource management algorithms can be fully automated using autonomous AI agents, achieving near-optimal performance with dramatically reduced inference costs while maintaining trustworthy results through rigorous safeguards.
